cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is Vijayanagara?
cards.back: Vijayanagara or "city of victory" was the name of both a city and an empire.
cards.quote: Vijayanagara or "city of victory" was the name of both a city and an empire.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In its heyday it stretched from the river ____ in the north to the extreme south of the peninsula.
cards.back: In its heyday it stretched from the river Krishna in the north to the extreme south of the peninsula.
cards.quote: In its heyday it stretched from the river Krishna in the north to the extreme south of the peninsula.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In ____ the city was sacked and subsequently deserted.
cards.back: In 1565 the city was sacked and subsequently deserted.
cards.quote: In 1565 the city was sacked and subsequently deserted.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The name Hampi is derived from that of which local mother goddess?
cards.back: Hampi, a name derived from that of the local mother goddess, Pampadevi.
cards.quote: Hampi, a name derived from that of the local mother goddess, Pampadevi.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who brought the ruins at Hampi to light, and in which year?
cards.back: The ruins at Hampi were brought to light in 1800 by an engineer and antiquarian named Colonel Colin Mackenzie.
cards.quote: The ruins at Hampi were brought to light in 1800 by an engineer and antiquarian named Colonel Colin Mackenzie.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was the basis of the initial information Mackenzie received about Hampi?
cards.back: An employee of the English East India Company, he prepared the first survey map of the site. Much of the initial information he received was based on the memories of priests of the Virupaksha temple and the shrine of Pampadevi.
cards.quote: An employee of the English East India Company, he prepared the first survey map of the site. Much of the initial information he received was based on the memories of priests of the Virupaksha temple and the shrine of Pampadevi.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Subsequently, from ____, photographers began to record the monuments which enabled scholars to study them.
cards.back: Subsequently, from 1856, photographers began to record the monuments which enabled scholars to study them.
cards.quote: Subsequently, from 1856, photographers began to record the monuments which enabled scholars to study them.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: As early as 1836 ____ began collecting several dozen inscriptions found at this and other temples at Hampi.
cards.back: As early as 1836 epigraphists began collecting several dozen inscriptions found at this and other temples at Hampi.
cards.quote: As early as 1836 epigraphists began collecting several dozen inscriptions found at this and other temples at Hampi.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which literature did historians collate with other sources to reconstruct Vijayanagara's history?
cards.back: In an effort to reconstruct the history of the city and the empire, historians collated information from these sources with accounts of foreign travellers and other literature written in Telugu, Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit.
cards.quote: In an effort to reconstruct the history of the city and the empire, historians collated information from these sources with accounts of foreign travellers and other literature written in Telugu, Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which post did Colin Mackenzie hold from 1815 till his death in 1821?
cards.back: In 1815 he was appointed the first Surveyor General of India, a post he held till his death in 1821.
cards.quote: In 1815 he was appointed the first Surveyor General of India, a post he held till his death in 1821.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who founded the Vijayanagara Empire, and in which year?
cards.back: According to tradition and epigraphic evidence two brothers, Harihara and Bukka, founded the Vijayanagara Empire in 1336.
cards.quote: According to tradition and epigraphic evidence two brothers, Harihara and Bukka, founded the Vijayanagara Empire in 1336.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did interaction between Vijayanagara and the Deccan Sultanates lead to?
cards.back: At the same time, interaction between these states led to sharing of ideas, especially in the field of architecture.
cards.quote: At the same time, interaction between these states led to sharing of ideas, especially in the field of architecture.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: While historians use the term Vijayanagara Empire, contemporaries described it as the ____.
cards.back: While historians use the term Vijayanagara Empire, contemporaries described it as the karnataka samrajyamu.
cards.quote: While historians use the term Vijayanagara Empire, contemporaries described it as the karnataka samrajyamu.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What does Gajapati mean?
cards.back: Gajapati literally means lord of elephants. This was the name of a ruling lineage that was very powerful in Orissa in the fifteenth century.
cards.quote: Gajapati literally means lord of elephants. This was the name of a ruling lineage that was very powerful in Orissa in the fifteenth century.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In popular traditions, what are the Deccan Sultans and the rayas called?
cards.back: In the popular traditions of Vijayanagara the Deccan Sultans are termed as ashvapati or lord of horses and the rayas are called narapati or lord of men.
cards.quote: In the popular traditions of Vijayanagara the Deccan Sultans are termed as ashvapati or lord of horses and the rayas are called narapati or lord of men.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which elaborate temples did earlier ruling elites in the empire's areas patronise?
cards.back: Ruling elites in these areas had extended patronage to elaborate temples such as the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur and the Chennakeshava temple at Belur.
cards.quote: Ruling elites in these areas had extended patronage to elaborate temples such as the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur and the Chennakeshava temple at Belur.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: As warfare during these times depended upon effective ____, the import of horses from Arabia and Central Asia was very important for rival kingdoms.
cards.back: As warfare during these times depended upon effective cavalry, the import of horses from Arabia and Central Asia was very important for rival kingdoms.
cards.quote: As warfare during these times depended upon effective cavalry, the import of horses from Arabia and Central Asia was very important for rival kingdoms.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Local communities of merchants known as ____ or horse merchants also participated in these exchanges.
cards.back: Local communities of merchants known as kudirai chettis or horse merchants also participated in these exchanges.
cards.quote: Local communities of merchants known as kudirai chettis or horse merchants also participated in these exchanges.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who arrived on the west coast of the subcontinent from 1498?
cards.back: From 1498 other actors appeared on the scene. These were the Portuguese, who arrived on the west coast of the subcontinent and attempted to establish trading and military stations.
cards.quote: From 1498 other actors appeared on the scene. These were the Portuguese, who arrived on the west coast of the subcontinent and attempted to establish trading and military stations.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In which goods were Vijayanagara's markets noted for dealing?
cards.back: In fact, Vijayanagara was also noted for its markets dealing in spices, textiles and precious stones.
cards.quote: In fact, Vijayanagara was also noted for its markets dealing in spices, textiles and precious stones.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the first three dynasties of Vijayanagara in order.
cards.back:
The first dynasty, known as the Sangama dynasty, exercised control till 1485.
They were supplanted by the Saluvas, military commanders, who remained in power till 1503 when they were replaced by the Tuluvas.
cards.quote: The first dynasty, known as the Sangama dynasty, exercised control till 1485. They were supplanted by the Saluvas, military commanders, who remained in power till 1503 when they were replaced by the Tuluvas.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The apogee and decline of the empire

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Krishnadeva Raya belonged to the ____ dynasty.
cards.back: Krishnadeva Raya belonged to the Tuluva dynasty.
cards.quote: Krishnadeva Raya belonged to the Tuluva dynasty.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The apogee and decline of the empire

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Krishnadeva Raya's rule was characterised by ____.
cards.back: Krishnadeva Raya's rule was characterised by expansion and consolidation.
cards.quote: Krishnadeva Raya's rule was characterised by expansion and consolidation.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The apogee and decline of the empire

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the three gains of Krishnadeva Raya's rule, with the years.
cards.back:
the land between the Tungabhadra and Krishna rivers (the Raichur doab) was acquired (1512)
the rulers of Orissa were subdued (1514)
severe defeats were inflicted on the Sultan of Bijapur (1520)
cards.quote: This was the time when the land between the Tungabhadra and Krishna rivers (the Raichur doab) was acquired (1512), the rulers of Orissa were subdued (1514) and severe defeats were inflicted on the Sultan of Bijapur (1520).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The apogee and decline of the empire

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is Krishnadeva Raya credited with in temple building?
cards.back: Krishnadeva Raya is credited with building some fine temples and adding impressive gopurams to many important south Indian temples.
cards.quote: Krishnadeva Raya is credited with building some fine temples and adding impressive gopurams to many important south Indian temples.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The apogee and decline of the empire

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Strain began to show within the imperial structure following Krishnadeva Raya's death in ____.
cards.back: Strain began to show within the imperial structure following Krishnadeva Raya's death in 1529.
cards.quote: Strain began to show within the imperial structure following Krishnadeva Raya's death in 1529.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The apogee and decline of the empire

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which ruling lineage controlled the centre from 1542?
cards.back: By 1542 control at the centre had shifted to another ruling lineage, that of the Aravidu, which remained in power till the end of the seventeenth century.
cards.quote: By 1542 control at the centre had shifted to another ruling lineage, that of the Aravidu, which remained in power till the end of the seventeenth century.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The apogee and decline of the empire

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What happened in 1565 at Rakshasi-Tangadi (Talikota)?
cards.back: In 1565 Rama Raya, the chief minister of Vijayanagara, led the army into battle at Rakshasi-Tangadi (also known as Talikota), where his forces were routed by the combined armies of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda.
cards.quote: In 1565 Rama Raya, the chief minister of Vijayanagara, led the army into battle at Rakshasi-Tangadi (also known as Talikota), where his forces were routed by the combined armies of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The apogee and decline of the empire

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What policy of Rama Raya led the Sultans to combine and defeat him?
cards.back: It was the adventurous policy of Rama Raya who tried to play off one Sultan against another that led the Sultans to combine together and decisively defeat him.
cards.quote: It was the adventurous policy of Rama Raya who tried to play off one Sultan against another that led the Sultans to combine together and decisively defeat him.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The apogee and decline of the empire

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which work on statecraft did Krishnadeva Raya compose in Telugu?
cards.back: Krishnadeva Raya (ruled 1509-29), the most famous ruler of Vijayanagara, composed a work on statecraft in Telugu known as the Amuktamalyada.
cards.quote: Krishnadeva Raya (ruled 1509-29), the most famous ruler of Vijayanagara, composed a work on statecraft in Telugu known as the Amuktamalyada.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Krishnadeva Raya write that a king should improve to encourage commerce?
cards.back: A king should improve the harbours of his country and so encourage its commerce that horses, elephants, precious gems, sandalwood, pearls and other articles are freely imported
cards.quote: A king should improve the harbours of his country and so encourage its commerce that horses, elephants, precious gems, sandalwood, pearls and other articles are freely imported

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which title did Krishnadeva Raya take pride in after supporting claimants in the Sultanates?
cards.back: Krishnadeva Raya, for example, supported some claimants to power in the Sultanates and took pride in the title "establisher of the Yavana kingdom".
cards.quote: Krishnadeva Raya, for example, supported some claimants to power in the Sultanates and took pride in the title "establisher of the Yavana kingdom".

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The apogee and decline of the empire

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is the word Yavana used for?
cards.back: Yavana is a Sanskrit word used for the Greeks and other peoples who entered the subcontinent from the north west.
cards.quote: Yavana is a Sanskrit word used for the Greeks and other peoples who entered the subcontinent from the north west.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The apogee and decline of the empire

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who were the nayakas in the Vijayanagara Empire?
cards.back: Among those who exercised power in the empire were military chiefs who usually controlled forts and had armed supporters. These chiefs often moved from one area to another, and in many cases were accompanied by peasants looking for fertile land on which to settle. These chiefs were known as nayakas and they usually spoke Telugu or Kannada.
cards.quote: Among those who exercised power in the empire were military chiefs who usually controlled forts and had armed supporters. These chiefs often moved from one area to another, and in many cases were accompanied by peasants looking for fertile land on which to settle. These chiefs were known as nayakas and they usually spoke Telugu or Kannada.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did many nayakas behave towards the kings of Vijayanagara?
cards.back: Many nayakas submitted to the authority of the kings of Vijayanagara but they often rebelled and had to be subdued by military action.
cards.quote: Many nayakas submitted to the authority of the kings of Vijayanagara but they often rebelled and had to be subdued by military action.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The ____ system was a major political innovation of the Vijayanagara Empire.
cards.back: The amara-nayaka system was a major political innovation of the Vijayanagara Empire.
cards.quote: The amara-nayaka system was a major political innovation of the Vijayanagara Empire.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Many features of the Vijayanagara amara-nayaka system were likely derived from which Delhi Sultanate system?
cards.back: The amara-nayaka system was a major political innovation of the Vijayanagara Empire. It is likely that many features of this system were derived from the iqta system of the Delhi Sultanate.
cards.quote: The amara-nayaka system was a major political innovation of the Vijayanagara Empire. It is likely that many features of this system were derived from the iqta system of the Delhi Sultanate.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who were the amara-nayakas?
cards.back: The amara-nayakas were military commanders who were given territories to govern by the raya. They collected taxes and other dues from peasants, craftspersons and traders in the area.
cards.quote: The amara-nayakas were military commanders who were given territories to govern by the raya. They collected taxes and other dues from peasants, craftspersons and traders in the area.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did the amara-nayakas do with part of the revenue they collected?
cards.back: They retained part of the revenue for personal use and for maintaining a stipulated contingent of horses and elephants.
cards.quote: They retained part of the revenue for personal use and for maintaining a stipulated contingent of horses and elephants.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The amara-nayakas sent ____ to the king annually and personally appeared in the royal court with gifts to express their loyalty.
cards.back: The amara-nayakas sent tribute to the king annually and personally appeared in the royal court with gifts to express their loyalty.
cards.quote: The amara-nayakas sent tribute to the king annually and personally appeared in the royal court with gifts to express their loyalty.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did many nayakas do in the seventeenth century, and with what result?
cards.back: However, during the course of the seventeenth century, many of these nayakas established independent kingdoms. This hastened the collapse of the central imperial structure.
cards.quote: However, during the course of the seventeenth century, many of these nayakas established independent kingdoms. This hastened the collapse of the central imperial structure.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What do the inscriptions of Vijayanagara kings and their nayakas record?
cards.back: A large number of inscriptions of the kings of Vijayanagara and their nayakas recording donations to temples as well as describing important events have been recovered.
cards.quote: A large number of inscriptions of the kings of Vijayanagara and their nayakas recording donations to temples as well as describing important events have been recovered.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which travellers from Portugal visited Vijayanagara in the sixteenth century?
cards.back: Duarte Barbosa, Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz from Portugal, who came in the sixteenth century.
cards.quote: Duarte Barbosa, Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz from Portugal, who came in the sixteenth century.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which merchant from Russia visited Vijayanagara in the fifteenth century?
cards.back: a merchant named Afanasii Nikitin from Russia
cards.quote: a merchant named Afanasii Nikitin from Russia

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The most striking feature about the location of Vijayanagara is the natural basin formed by the river ____ which flows in a north-easterly direction.
cards.back: The most striking feature about the location of Vijayanagara is the natural basin formed by the river Tungabhadra which flows in a north-easterly direction.
cards.quote: The most striking feature about the location of Vijayanagara is the natural basin formed by the river Tungabhadra which flows in a north-easterly direction.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which was the most important tank of Vijayanagara, and what did its water do?
cards.back: The most important such tank was built in the early years of the fifteenth century and is now called Kamalapuram tank. Water from this tank not only irrigated fields nearby but was also conducted through a channel to the "royal centre".
cards.quote: The most important such tank was built in the early years of the fifteenth century and is now called Kamalapuram tank. Water from this tank not only irrigated fields nearby but was also conducted through a channel to the "royal centre".

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was the Hiriya canal and who apparently built it?
cards.back: One of the most prominent waterworks to be seen among the ruins is the Hiriya canal. This canal drew water from a dam across the Tungabhadra and irrigated the cultivated valley that separated the "sacred centre" from the "urban core". This was apparently built by kings of the Sangama dynasty.
cards.quote: One of the most prominent waterworks to be seen among the ruins is the Hiriya canal. This canal drew water from a dam across the Tungabhadra and irrigated the cultivated valley that separated the "sacred centre" from the "urban core". This was apparently built by kings of the Sangama dynasty.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How many lines of forts did Abdur Razzaq mention at Vijayanagara?
cards.back: Abdur Razzaq, an ambassador sent by the ruler of Persia to Calicut (present-day Kozhikode) in the fifteenth century, was greatly impressed by the fortifications, and mentioned seven lines of forts.
cards.quote: Abdur Razzaq, an ambassador sent by the ruler of Persia to Calicut (present-day Kozhikode) in the fifteenth century, was greatly impressed by the fortifications, and mentioned seven lines of forts.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: No ____ or cementing agent was employed anywhere in the construction.
cards.back: No mortar or cementing agent was employed anywhere in the construction.
cards.quote: No mortar or cementing agent was employed anywhere in the construction.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How were the stone blocks of the Vijayanagara fortification walls held in place?
cards.back: The stone blocks were wedge shaped, which held them in place, and the inner portion of the walls was of earth packed with rubble.
cards.quote: The stone blocks were wedge shaped, which held them in place, and the inner portion of the walls was of earth packed with rubble.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was most significant about this fortification is that it enclosed ____.
cards.back: What was most significant about this fortification is that it enclosed agricultural tracts.
cards.quote: What was most significant about this fortification is that it enclosed agricultural tracts.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Against sieges, what strategy did Vijayanagara adopt instead of large granaries?
cards.back: Normally rulers tried to be prepared for such situations by building large granaries within fortified areas. The rulers of Vijayanagara adopted a more expensive and elaborate strategy of protecting the agricultural belt itself.
cards.quote: Normally rulers tried to be prepared for such situations by building large granaries within fortified areas. The rulers of Vijayanagara adopted a more expensive and elaborate strategy of protecting the agricultural belt itself.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did the second and third lines of fortification enclose?
cards.back: A second line of fortification went round the inner core of the urban complex, and a third line surrounded the royal centre, within which each set of major buildings was surrounded by its own high walls.
cards.quote: A second line of fortification went round the inner core of the urban complex, and a third line surrounded the royal centre, within which each set of major buildings was surrounded by its own high walls.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is the Indo-Islamic style seen in Vijayanagara's gateways?
cards.back: The arch on the gateway leading into the fortified settlement as well as the dome over the gate (Fig. 7.6) are regarded as typical features of the architecture introduced by the Turkish Sultans. Art historians refer to this style as Indo-Islamic, as it grew continually through interaction with local building practices in different regions.
cards.quote: The arch on the gateway leading into the fortified settlement as well as the dome over the gate (Fig. 7.6) are regarded as typical features of the architecture introduced by the Turkish Sultans. Art historians refer to this style as Indo-Islamic, as it grew continually through interaction with local building practices in different regions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Where did the most important roads of Vijayanagara extend from?
cards.back: Roads generally wound around through the valleys, avoiding rocky terrain. Some of the most important roads extended from temple gateways, and were lined by bazaars.
cards.quote: Roads generally wound around through the valleys, avoiding rocky terrain. Some of the most important roads extended from temple gateways, and were lined by bazaars.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did archaeologists find in the north-eastern urban core, suggesting rich traders lived there?
cards.back: found fine Chinese porcelain in some areas, including in the north-eastern corner of the urban core and suggest that these areas may have been occupied by rich traders.
cards.quote: found fine Chinese porcelain in some areas, including in the north-eastern corner of the urban core and suggest that these areas may have been occupied by rich traders.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Whose residential quarter was the north-eastern part of the urban core, and what did its tombs and mosques resemble?
cards.back: This was also the Muslim residential quarter. Tombs and mosques located here have distinctive functions, yet their architecture resembles that of the mandapas found in the temples of Hampi.
cards.quote: This was also the Muslim residential quarter. Tombs and mosques located here have distinctive functions, yet their architecture resembles that of the mandapas found in the temples of Hampi.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did Barbosa describe the houses of ordinary people?
cards.back: The other houses of the people are thatched, but nonetheless well built and arranged according to occupations, in long streets with many open places.
cards.quote: The other houses of the people are thatched, but nonetheless well built and arranged according to occupations, in long streets with many open places.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Where was the royal centre located, and how many temples did it include?
cards.back: The royal centre was located in the south-western part of the settlement. Although designated as a royal centre, it included over 60 temples.
cards.quote: The royal centre was located in the south-western part of the settlement. Although designated as a royal centre, it included over 60 temples.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why was patronage of temples and cults important for the rulers of Vijayanagara?
cards.back: Clearly, the patronage of temples and cults was important for rulers who were trying to establish and legitimise their authority through association with the divinities housed in the shrines.
cards.quote: Clearly, the patronage of temples and cults was important for rulers who were trying to establish and legitimise their authority through association with the divinities housed in the shrines.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: About ____ building complexes have been identified as palaces.
cards.back: About thirty building complexes have been identified as palaces.
cards.quote: About thirty building complexes have been identified as palaces.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Palaces vs temples in the royal centre: the difference in building material.
cards.back: One difference between these structures and temples is that the latter were constructed entirely of masonry, while the superstructure of the secular buildings was made of perishable materials.
cards.quote: One difference between these structures and temples is that the latter were constructed entirely of masonry, while the superstructure of the secular buildings was made of perishable materials.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which two impressive platforms does the "king's palace" have?
cards.back: The "king's palace" is the largest of the enclosures but has not yielded definitive evidence of being a royal residence. It has two of the most impressive platforms, usually called the "audience hall" and the "mahanavami dibba".
cards.quote: The "king's palace" is the largest of the enclosures but has not yielded definitive evidence of being a royal residence. It has two of the most impressive platforms, usually called the "audience hall" and the "mahanavami dibba".

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are the dimensions of the "mahanavami dibba"?
cards.back: Located on one of the highest points in the city, the "mahanavami dibba" is a massive platform rising from a base of about 11,000 sq. ft to a height of 40 ft.
cards.quote: Located on one of the highest points in the city, the "mahanavami dibba" is a massive platform rising from a base of about 11,000 sq. ft to a height of 40 ft.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: With which festival did the rituals of the "mahanavami dibba" probably coincide?
cards.back: Rituals associated with the structure probably coincided with Mahanavami (literally, the great ninth day) of the ten-day Hindu festival during the autumn months of September and October
cards.quote: Rituals associated with the structure probably coincided with Mahanavami (literally, the great ninth day) of the ten-day Hindu festival during the autumn months of September and October

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What ceremonies were performed during Mahanavami at Vijayanagara?
cards.back: The ceremonies performed on the occasion included worship of the image, worship of the state horse, and the sacrifice of buffaloes and other animals.
cards.quote: The ceremonies performed on the occasion included worship of the image, worship of the state horse, and the sacrifice of buffaloes and other animals.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What three things did the Vijayanagara kings display at the Mahanavami festival?
cards.back: The Vijayanagara kings displayed their prestige, power and suzerainty on this occasion.
cards.quote: The Vijayanagara kings displayed their prestige, power and suzerainty on this occasion.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What happened on the last day of the Mahanavami festival?
cards.back: On the last day of the festival the king inspected his army and the armies of the nayakas in a grand ceremony in an open field. On this occasion the nayakas brought rich gifts for the king as well as the stipulated tribute.
cards.quote: On the last day of the festival the king inspected his army and the armies of the nayakas in a grand ceremony in an open field. On this occasion the nayakas brought rich gifts for the king as well as the stipulated tribute.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who named the Lotus Mahal, and in which century?
cards.back: One of the most beautiful buildings in the royal centre is the Lotus Mahal, so named by British travellers in the nineteenth century.
cards.quote: One of the most beautiful buildings in the royal centre is the Lotus Mahal, so named by British travellers in the nineteenth century.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Other buildings in the royal centre

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Mackenzie's map suggest the Lotus Mahal may have been?
cards.back: One suggestion, found in a map drawn by Mackenzie, is that it may have been a council chamber, a place where the king met his advisers.
cards.quote: One suggestion, found in a map drawn by Mackenzie, is that it may have been a council chamber, a place where the king met his advisers.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Other buildings in the royal centre

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: For whom was the Hazara Rama temple probably meant?
cards.back: One of the most spectacular of these is one known as the Hazara Rama temple. This was probably meant to be used only by the king and his family.
cards.quote: One of the most spectacular of these is one known as the Hazara Rama temple. This was probably meant to be used only by the king and his family.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Other buildings in the royal centre

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: According to local tradition, what did the hills of the sacred centre shelter?
cards.back: According to local tradition, these hills sheltered the monkey kingdom of Vali and Sugriva mentioned in the Ramayana.
cards.quote: According to local tradition, these hills sheltered the monkey kingdom of Vali and Sugriva mentioned in the Ramayana.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why did Pampadevi do penance in the hills, according to local tradition?
cards.back: Other traditions suggest that Pampadevi, the local mother goddess, did penance in these hills in order to marry Virupaksha, the guardian deity of the kingdom, also recognised as a form of Shiva. To this day this marriage is celebrated annually in the Virupaksha temple.
cards.quote: Other traditions suggest that Pampadevi, the local mother goddess, did penance in these hills in order to marry Virupaksha, the guardian deity of the kingdom, also recognised as a form of Shiva. To this day this marriage is celebrated annually in the Virupaksha temple.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did temples develop into as significant centres?
cards.back: Temples also functioned as centres of learning. Besides, rulers and others often granted land and other resources for the maintenance of temples. Consequently, temples developed as significant religious, social, cultural and economic centres.
cards.quote: Temples also functioned as centres of learning. Besides, rulers and others often granted land and other resources for the maintenance of temples. Consequently, temples developed as significant religious, social, cultural and economic centres.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: On behalf of which god did the Vijayanagara kings claim to rule?
cards.back: In fact the Vijayanagara kings claimed to rule on behalf of the god Virupaksha. All royal orders were signed "Shri Virupaksha", usually in the Kannada script.
cards.quote: In fact the Vijayanagara kings claimed to rule on behalf of the god Virupaksha. All royal orders were signed "Shri Virupaksha", usually in the Kannada script.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is the title "Hindu Suratrana"?
cards.back: Rulers also indicated their close links with the gods by using the title "Hindu Suratrana". This was a Sanskritisation of the Arabic term Sultan, meaning king, so it literally meant Hindu Sultan.
cards.quote: Rulers also indicated their close links with the gods by using the title "Hindu Suratrana". This was a Sanskritisation of the Arabic term Sultan, meaning king, so it literally meant Hindu Sultan.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What innovations did Vijayanagara rulers introduce in their relation to temples?
cards.back: Royal portrait sculpture was now displayed in temples, and the king's visits to temples were treated as important state occasions on which he was accompanied by the important nayakas of the empire.
cards.quote: Royal portrait sculpture was now displayed in temples, and the king's visits to temples were treated as important state occasions on which he was accompanied by the important nayakas of the empire.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are raya gopurams?
cards.back: best exemplified by the raya gopurams (Fig. 7.7) or royal gateways that often dwarfed the towers on the central shrines
cards.quote: best exemplified by the raya gopurams (Fig. 7.7) or royal gateways that often dwarfed the towers on the central shrines

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Other distinctive features include ____ or pavilions and long, pillared corridors that often ran around the shrines within the temple complex.
cards.back: Other distinctive features include mandapas or pavilions and long, pillared corridors that often ran around the shrines within the temple complex.
cards.quote: Other distinctive features include mandapas or pavilions and long, pillared corridors that often ran around the shrines within the temple complex.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: When did the earliest shrine of the Virupaksha temple date to, according to inscriptions?
cards.back: The Virupaksha temple was built over centuries. While inscriptions suggest that the earliest shrine dated to the ninth-tenth centuries, it was substantially enlarged with the establishment of the Vijayanagara Empire.
cards.quote: The Virupaksha temple was built over centuries. While inscriptions suggest that the earliest shrine dated to the ninth-tenth centuries, it was substantially enlarged with the establishment of the Vijayanagara Empire.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who built the hall in front of the main shrine of the Virupaksha temple, and why?
cards.back: The hall in front of the main shrine was built by Krishnadeva Raya to mark his accession. This was decorated with delicately carved pillars.
cards.quote: The hall in front of the main shrine was built by Krishnadeva Raya to mark his accession. This was decorated with delicately carved pillars.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: For what purposes were the halls in the Virupaksha temple used?
cards.back: The halls in the temple were used for a variety of purposes. Some were spaces in which the images of gods were placed to witness special programmes of music, dance, drama, etc. Others were used to celebrate the marriages of deities, and yet others were meant for the deities to swing in.
cards.quote: The halls in the temple were used for a variety of purposes. Some were spaces in which the images of gods were placed to witness special programmes of music, dance, drama, etc. Others were used to celebrate the marriages of deities, and yet others were meant for the deities to swing in.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who was the principal deity of the Vitthala temple?
cards.back: Another shrine, the Vitthala temple, is also interesting. Here, the principal deity was Vitthala, a form of Vishnu generally worshipped in Maharashtra.
cards.quote: Another shrine, the Vitthala temple, is also interesting. Here, the principal deity was Vitthala, a form of Vishnu generally worshipped in Maharashtra.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What does the worship of Vitthala in Karnataka indicate?
cards.back: The introduction of the worship of the deity in Karnataka is another indication of the ways in which the rulers of Vijayanagara drew on different traditions to create an imperial culture.
cards.quote: The introduction of the worship of the deity in Karnataka is another indication of the ways in which the rulers of Vijayanagara drew on different traditions to create an imperial culture.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The Vitthala temple at Vijayanagara has several halls and a unique shrine designed as what?
cards.back: As in the case of other temples, this temple too has several halls and a unique shrine designed as a chariot (Fig. 7.24).
cards.quote: As in the case of other temples, this temple too has several halls and a unique shrine designed as a chariot (Fig. 7.24).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are the chariot streets of the temple complexes?
cards.back: A characteristic feature of the temple complexes is the chariot streets that extended from the temple gopuram in a straight line. These streets were paved with stone slabs and lined with pillared pavilions in which merchants set up their shops.
cards.quote: A characteristic feature of the temple complexes is the chariot streets that extended from the temple gopuram in a straight line. These streets were paved with stone slabs and lined with pillared pavilions in which merchants set up their shops.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are the towering temple gateways called, some of whose most spectacular examples the local nayakas built?
cards.back: Just as the nayakas continued with and elaborated on traditions of fortification, so they did with traditions of temple building. In fact, some of the most spectacular gopurams were also built by the local nayakas.
cards.quote: Just as the nayakas continued with and elaborated on traditions of fortification, so they did with traditions of temple building. In fact, some of the most spectacular gopurams were also built by the local nayakas.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In which year was Hampi recognised as a site of national importance?
cards.back: In 1976, Hampi was recognised as a site of national importance.
cards.quote: In 1976, Hampi was recognised as a site of national importance.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What project was launched in the early 1980s at Vijayanagara?
cards.back: Then, in the early 1980s, an important project was launched to document the material remains at Vijayanagara in detail, through extensive and intensive surveys, using a variety of recording techniques.
cards.quote: Then, in the early 1980s, an important project was launched to document the material remains at Vijayanagara in detail, through extensive and intensive surveys, using a variety of recording techniques.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was the first step in mapping Vijayanagara?
cards.back: The first step was to divide the entire area into a set of 25 squares, each designated by a letter of the alphabet.
cards.quote: The first step was to divide the entire area into a set of 25 squares, each designated by a letter of the alphabet.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: For example, we can assess the defence requirements and military preparedness of a city by studying its ____.
cards.back: For example, we can assess the defence requirements and military preparedness of a city by studying its fortifications.
cards.quote: For example, we can assess the defence requirements and military preparedness of a city by studying its fortifications.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What do buildings tell us when compared with buildings in other places?
cards.back: Buildings also tell us about the spread of ideas and cultural influences if we compare them with buildings in other places.
cards.quote: Buildings also tell us about the spread of ideas and cultural influences if we compare them with buildings in other places.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Timeline c. 1300-1400: which empire and kingdom were established in 1336? and 1347?
cards.back: Establishment of the Vijayanagara Empire (1336?); establishment of the Bahmani kingdom (1347); Sultanates in Jaunpur, Kashmir and Madura
cards.quote: Establishment of the Vijayanagara Empire (1336?); establishment of the Bahmani kingdom (1347); Sultanates in Jaunpur, Kashmir and Madura

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Timeline c. 1500-1600: the events of 1510, 1518 and 1526.
cards.back:
Conquest of Goa by the Portuguese (1510)
Collapse of the Bahmani kingdom, emergence of the Sultanate of Golconda (1518)
Establishment of the Mughal empire by Babur (1526)
cards.quote: Conquest of Goa by the Portuguese (1510); Collapse of the Bahmani kingdom, emergence of the Sultanate of Golconda (1518); Establishment of the Mughal empire by Babur (1526)

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the five landmarks, with years, in the discovery and conservation of Vijayanagara.
cards.back:
1800 Colin Mackenzie visits Vijayanagara
1856 Alexander Greenlaw takes the first detailed photographs of archaeological remains at Hampi
1876 J.F. Fleet begins documenting the inscriptions on the temple walls at the site
1902 Conservation begins under John Marshall
1986 Hampi declared a World Heritage site by UNESCO

Fleet begins documenting the inscriptions on the temple walls at the site 1902 Conservation begins under John Marshall 1986 Hampi declared a World Heritage site by UNESCO

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What made the traditions of the poet-saints “fluid” as a source for historians?
cards.back: generations of devotees tended to elaborate on the original message, and occasionally modified or even abandoned some of the ideas that appeared problematic or irrelevant in different political, social or cultural contexts.
cards.quote: generations of devotees tended to elaborate on the original message, and occasionally modified or even abandoned some of the ideas that appeared problematic or irrelevant in different political, social or cultural contexts.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Historians also draw on ____ or biographies of saints written by their followers (or members of their religious sect).
cards.back: Historians also draw on hagiographies or biographies of saints written by their followers (or members of their religious sect).
cards.quote: Historians also draw on hagiographies or biographies of saints written by their followers (or members of their religious sect).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In what kind of languages did most poet-saints express themselves orally?
cards.back: New textual sources available from this period include compositions attributed to poet-saints, most of whom expressed themselves orally in regional languages used by ordinary people.
cards.quote: New textual sources available from this period include compositions attributed to poet-saints, most of whom expressed themselves orally in regional languages used by ordinary people.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Two processes at work in the integration of cults, as historians suggest.
cards.back:
a process of disseminating Brahmanical ideas
that of the Brahmanas accepting and reworking the beliefs and practices of these and other social categories
cards.quote: Historians who have tried to understand these developments suggest that there were at least two processes at work. One was a process of disseminating Brahmanical ideas. This is exemplified by the composition, compilation and preservation of Puranic texts in simple Sanskrit verse, explicitly meant to be accessible to women and Shudras, who were generally excluded from Vedic learning. At the same time, there was a second process at work – that of the Brahmanas accepting and reworking the beliefs and practices of these and other social categories.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are the “great” and “little” traditions, and who coined the terms?
cards.back: The terms great and little traditions were coined by a sociologist named Robert Redfield in the twentieth century to describe the cultural practices of peasant societies.
cards.quote: The terms great and little traditions were coined by a sociologist named Robert Redfield in the twentieth century to describe the cultural practices of peasant societies.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is a “great tradition” (Robert Redfield)?
cards.back: He found that peasants observed rituals and customs that emanated from dominant social categories, including priests and rulers. These he classified as part of a great tradition.
cards.quote: He found that peasants observed rituals and customs that emanated from dominant social categories, including priests and rulers. These he classified as part of a great tradition.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is a “little tradition” (Robert Redfield)?
cards.back: At the same time, peasants also followed local practices that did not necessarily correspond with those of the great tradition. These he included within the category of little tradition.
cards.quote: At the same time, peasants also followed local practices that did not necessarily correspond with those of the great tradition. These he included within the category of little tradition.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which deity at Puri, Orissa, was identified by the twelfth century as a form of Vishnu?
cards.back: One of the most striking examples of this process is evident at Puri, Orissa, where the principal deity was identified, by the twelfth century, as Jagannatha (literally, the lord of the world), a form of Vishnu.
cards.quote: One of the most striking examples of this process is evident at Puri, Orissa, where the principal deity was identified, by the twelfth century, as Jagannatha (literally, the lord of the world), a form of Vishnu.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Local goddesses were equated with which wife of Vishnu and which wife of Shiva?
cards.back: sometimes they were equated with Lakshmi, the wife of Vishnu, in other instances, with Parvati, the wife of Shiva.
cards.quote: sometimes they were equated with Lakshmi, the wife of Vishnu, in other instances, with Parvati, the wife of Shiva.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who were Tantric practices open to, and what did practitioners often ignore?
cards.back: Tantric practices were widespread in several parts of the subcontinent – they were open to women and men, and practitioners often ignored differences of caste and class within the ritual context.
cards.quote: Tantric practices were widespread in several parts of the subcontinent – they were open to women and men, and practitioners often ignored differences of caste and class within the ritual context.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which three principal deities of the Vedic pantheon does NCERT name as becoming marginal figures in Puranic traditions?
cards.back: The principal deities of the Vedic pantheon, Agni, Indra and Soma, become marginal figures, rarely visible in textual or visual representations.
cards.quote: The principal deities of the Vedic pantheon, Agni, Indra and Soma, become marginal figures, rarely visible in textual or visual representations.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Despite obvious discrepancies with Puranic traditions, how did the Vedas continue to be regarded?
cards.back: However, in spite of these obvious discrepancies, the Vedas continued to be revered as authoritative.
cards.quote: However, in spite of these obvious discrepancies, the Vedas continued to be revered as authoritative.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: All of these somewhat divergent and even disparate beliefs and practices would come to be classified as ____ over the course of the next millennium.
cards.back: All of these somewhat divergent and even disparate beliefs and practices would come to be classified as Hindu over the course of the next millennium.
cards.quote: All of these somewhat divergent and even disparate beliefs and practices would come to be classified as Hindu over the course of the next millennium.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The two broad categories into which historians classify bhakti traditions.
cards.back:
saguna (with attributes)
nirguna (without attributes)
cards.quote: At a different level, historians of religion often classify bhakti traditions into two broad categories: saguna (with attributes) and nirguna (without attributes).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Poems of Prayer: Early Traditions of Bhakti

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did saguna bhakti focus on?
cards.back: The former included traditions that focused on the worship of specific deities such as Shiva, Vishnu and his avatars (incarnations) and forms of the goddess or Devi, all often conceptualised in anthropomorphic forms.
cards.quote: The former included traditions that focused on the worship of specific deities such as Shiva, Vishnu and his avatars (incarnations) and forms of the goddess or Devi, all often conceptualised in anthropomorphic forms.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Poems of Prayer: Early Traditions of Bhakti

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: ____ bhakti on the other hand was worship of an abstract form of god.
cards.back: Nirguna bhakti on the other hand was worship of an abstract form of god.
cards.quote: Nirguna bhakti on the other hand was worship of an abstract form of god.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Poems of Prayer: Early Traditions of Bhakti

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Whom did bhakti traditions accommodate that the orthodox Brahmanical framework held ineligible for liberation?
cards.back: while Brahmanas remained important intermediaries between gods and devotees in several forms of bhakti, these traditions also accommodated and acknowledged women and the “lower castes”, categories considered ineligible for liberation within the orthodox Brahmanical framework.
cards.quote: while Brahmanas remained important intermediaries between gods and devotees in several forms of bhakti, these traditions also accommodated and acknowledged women and the “lower castes”, categories considered ineligible for liberation within the orthodox Brahmanical framework.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Poems of Prayer: Early Traditions of Bhakti

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who were the Alvars and Nayanars, and when did their movements begin?
cards.back: Some of the earliest bhakti movements (c. sixth century) were led by the Alvars (literally, those who are “immersed” in devotion to Vishnu) and Nayanars (literally, leaders who were devotees of Shiva).
cards.quote: Some of the earliest bhakti movements (c. sixth century) were led by the Alvars (literally, those who are “immersed” in devotion to Vishnu) and Nayanars (literally, leaders who were devotees of Shiva).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The Alvars and Nayanars of Tamil Nadu

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In which language did the Alvars and Nayanars sing hymns as they travelled from place to place?
cards.back: They travelled from place to place singing hymns in Tamil in praise of their gods.
cards.quote: They travelled from place to place singing hymns in Tamil in praise of their gods.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: The Alvars and Nayanars of Tamil Nadu

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
