cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What happened at the shrines the Alvars and Nayanars identified as abodes of their deities?
cards.back: During their travels the Alvars and Nayanars identified certain shrines as abodes of their chosen deities. Very often large temples were later built at these sacred places. These developed as centres of pilgrimage.
cards.quote: During their travels the Alvars and Nayanars identified certain shrines as abodes of their chosen deities. Very often large temples were later built at these sacred places. These developed as centres of pilgrimage.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Some historians suggest that the Alvars and Nayanars initiated a movement of protest against the ____ and the dominance of Brahmanas
cards.back: Some historians suggest that the Alvars and Nayanars initiated a movement of protest against the caste system and the dominance of Brahmanas
cards.quote: Some historians suggest that the Alvars and Nayanars initiated a movement of protest against the caste system and the dominance of Brahmanas

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Alvar and Nayanar bhaktas hailed from which social backgrounds?
cards.back: To some extent this is corroborated by the fact that bhaktas hailed from diverse social backgrounds ranging from Brahmanas to artisans and cultivators and even from castes considered “untouchable”.
cards.quote: To some extent this is corroborated by the fact that bhaktas hailed from diverse social backgrounds ranging from Brahmanas to artisans and cultivators and even from castes considered “untouchable”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which anthology of the Alvars was frequently described as the Tamil Veda?
cards.back: For instance, one of the major anthologies of compositions by the Alvars, the Nalayira Divyaprabandham, was frequently described as the Tamil Veda, thus claiming that the text was as significant as the four Vedas in Sanskrit that were cherished by the Brahmanas.
cards.quote: For instance, one of the major anthologies of compositions by the Alvars, the Nalayira Divyaprabandham, was frequently described as the Tamil Veda, thus claiming that the text was as significant as the four Vedas in Sanskrit that were cherished by the Brahmanas.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is the Nalayira Divyaprabandham and when was it compiled?
cards.back: By the tenth century the compositions of the 12 Alvars were compiled in an anthology known as the Nalayira Divyaprabandham (“Four Thousand Sacred Compositions”).
cards.quote: By the tenth century the compositions of the 12 Alvars were compiled in an anthology known as the Nalayira Divyaprabandham (“Four Thousand Sacred Compositions”).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Whose poems form the Tevaram, and on what basis was it classified?
cards.back: The poems of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar form the Tevaram, a collection that was compiled and classified in the tenth century on the basis of the music of the songs.
cards.quote: The poems of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar form the Tevaram, a collection that was compiled and classified in the tenth century on the basis of the music of the songs.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which woman Alvar saw herself as the beloved of Vishnu?
cards.back: Andal saw herself as the beloved of Vishnu; her verses express her love for the deity.
cards.quote: Andal saw herself as the beloved of Vishnu; her verses express her love for the deity.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which woman devotee of Shiva adopted the path of extreme asceticism?
cards.back: Another woman, Karaikkal Ammaiyar, a devotee of Shiva, adopted the path of extreme asceticism
cards.quote: Another woman, Karaikkal Ammaiyar, a devotee of Shiva, adopted the path of extreme asceticism

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did women bhaktas such as Andal and Karaikkal Ammaiyar challenge society?
cards.back: These women renounced their social obligations, but did not join an alternative order or become nuns. Their very existence and their compositions posed a challenge to patriarchal norms.
cards.quote: These women renounced their social obligations, but did not join an alternative order or become nuns. Their very existence and their compositions posed a challenge to patriarchal norms.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: From the second half of the first millennium there is evidence for states, including those of the ____ and ____ (c. sixth to ninth centuries CE).
cards.back: From the second half of the first millennium there is evidence for states, including those of the Pallavas and Pandyas (c. sixth to ninth centuries CE).
cards.quote: From the second half of the first millennium there is evidence for states, including those of the Pallavas and Pandyas (c. sixth to ninth centuries CE).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Interestingly, one of the major themes in Tamil bhakti hymns is the poets’ opposition to ____.
cards.back: Interestingly, one of the major themes in Tamil bhakti hymns is the poets’ opposition to Buddhism and Jainism.
cards.quote: Interestingly, one of the major themes in Tamil bhakti hymns is the poets’ opposition to Buddhism and Jainism.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How have historians explained the Tamil bhakti poets’ hostility to Buddhism and Jainism?
cards.back: Historians have attempted to explain this hostility by suggesting that it was due to competition between members of other religious traditions for royal patronage.
cards.quote: Historians have attempted to explain this hostility by suggesting that it was due to competition between members of other religious traditions for royal patronage.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did the powerful Chola rulers (ninth to thirteenth centuries) support bhakti traditions?
cards.back: What is evident is that the powerful Chola rulers (ninth to thirteenth centuries) supported Brahmanical and bhakti traditions, making land grants and constructing temples for Vishnu and Shiva.
cards.quote: What is evident is that the powerful Chola rulers (ninth to thirteenth centuries) supported Brahmanical and bhakti traditions, making land grants and constructing temples for Vishnu and Shiva.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which magnificent Shiva temples were built under Chola patronage?
cards.back: In fact, some of the most magnificent Shiva temples, including those at Chidambaram, Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram, were constructed under the patronage of Chola rulers.
cards.quote: In fact, some of the most magnificent Shiva temples, including those at Chidambaram, Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram, were constructed under the patronage of Chola rulers.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Both Nayanars and Alvars were revered by the ____ peasants.
cards.back: Both Nayanars and Alvars were revered by the Vellala peasants.
cards.quote: Both Nayanars and Alvars were revered by the Vellala peasants.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did the Chola kings introduce in temples, and which text did they help compile?
cards.back: These kings also introduced the singing of Tamil Shaiva hymns in the temples under royal patronage, taking the initiative to collect and organise them into a text (Tevaram).
cards.quote: These kings also introduced the singing of Tamil Shaiva hymns in the temples under royal patronage, taking the initiative to collect and organise them into a text (Tevaram).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which Chola ruler, around 945, consecrated metal images of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar?
cards.back: Further, inscriptional evidence from around 945 suggests that the Chola ruler Parantaka I had consecrated metal images of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar in a Shiva temple.
cards.quote: Further, inscriptional evidence from around 945 suggests that the Chola ruler Parantaka I had consecrated metal images of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar in a Shiva temple.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who led the twelfth-century Virashaiva movement in Karnataka?
cards.back: The twelfth century witnessed the emergence of a new movement in Karnataka, led by a Brahmana named Basavanna (1106-68) who was a minister in the court of a Kalachuri ruler.
cards.quote: The twelfth century witnessed the emergence of a new movement in Karnataka, led by a Brahmana named Basavanna (1106-68) who was a minister in the court of a Kalachuri ruler.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who were the Virashaivas or Lingayats?
cards.back: His followers were known as Virashaivas (heroes of Shiva) or Lingayats (wearers of the linga).
cards.quote: His followers were known as Virashaivas (heroes of Shiva) or Lingayats (wearers of the linga).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How do the Lingayats worship Shiva?
cards.back: They worship Shiva in his manifestation as a linga, and men usually wear a small linga in a silver case on a loop strung over the left shoulder.
cards.quote: They worship Shiva in his manifestation as a linga, and men usually wear a small linga in a silver case on a loop strung over the left shoulder.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why do the Lingayats ceremonially bury their dead instead of cremating them?
cards.back: Lingayats believe that on death the devotee will be united with Shiva and will not return to this world. Therefore they do not practise funerary rites such as cremation, prescribed in the Dharmashastras. Instead, they ceremonially bury their dead.
cards.quote: Lingayats believe that on death the devotee will be united with Shiva and will not return to this world. Therefore they do not practise funerary rites such as cremation, prescribed in the Dharmashastras. Instead, they ceremonially bury their dead.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did the Lingayats challenge and question?
cards.back: The Lingayats challenged the idea of caste and the “pollution” attributed to certain groups by Brahmanas. They also questioned the theory of rebirth.
cards.quote: The Lingayats challenged the idea of caste and the “pollution” attributed to certain groups by Brahmanas. They also questioned the theory of rebirth.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which practices disapproved in the Dharmashastras did the Lingayats encourage?
cards.back: The Lingayats also encouraged certain practices disapproved in the Dharmashastras, such as post-puberty marriage and the remarriage of widows.
cards.quote: The Lingayats also encouraged certain practices disapproved in the Dharmashastras, such as post-puberty marriage and the remarriage of widows.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are vachanas, and what do they tell us?
cards.back: Our understanding of the Virashaiva tradition is derived from vachanas (literally, sayings) composed in Kannada by women and men who joined the movement.
cards.quote: Our understanding of the Virashaiva tradition is derived from vachanas (literally, sayings) composed in Kannada by women and men who joined the movement.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who composed this vachana: “When they see a serpent carved in stone they pour milk on it.”?
cards.back: Here is a vachana composed by Basavanna
cards.quote: Here is a vachana composed by Basavanna

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What two major developments does NCERT list under 'New religious developments', after the twelfth-century Virashaiva movement?
cards.back:
many ideas of the Tamil bhaktas (especially the Vaishnavas) were incorporated within the Sanskritic tradition, culminating in the composition of one of the best-known Puranas, the Bhagavata Purana
the development of traditions of bhakti in Maharashtra in the thirteenth century
cards.quote: This period also witnessed two major developments. On the one hand, many ideas of the Tamil bhaktas (especially the Vaishnavas) were incorporated within the Sanskritic tradition, culminating in the composition of one of the best-known Puranas, the Bhagavata Purana. Second, we find the development of traditions of bhakti in Maharashtra in the thirteenth century.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Till which century have historians found no north Indian compositions resembling those of the Alvars and Nayanars?
cards.back: However, historians have not found evidence of anything resembling the compositions of the Alvars and Nayanars till the fourteenth century.
cards.quote: However, historians have not found evidence of anything resembling the compositions of the Alvars and Nayanars till the fourteenth century.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What position did Brahmanas hold in the Rajput states that emerged in north India?
cards.back: In most of these states Brahmanas occupied positions of importance, performing a range of secular and ritual functions.
cards.quote: In most of these states Brahmanas occupied positions of importance, performing a range of secular and ritual functions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Religious leaders outside the orthodox Brahmanical framework who gained ground in north India.
cards.back:
Naths
Jogis
Siddhas
cards.quote: At the same time other religious leaders, who did not function within the orthodox Brahmanical framework, were gaining ground. These included the Naths, Jogis and Siddhas.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which artisanal group does NCERT name among those from which many Naths, Jogis and Siddhas came?
cards.back: These included the Naths, Jogis and Siddhas. Many of them came from artisanal groups, including weavers, who were becoming increasingly important with the development of organised craft production.
cards.quote: These included the Naths, Jogis and Siddhas. Many of them came from artisanal groups, including weavers, who were becoming increasingly important with the development of organised craft production.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which scriptures' authority did many of the Naths, Jogis and Siddhas question, speaking in the languages of ordinary people?
cards.back: Many of these new religious leaders questioned the authority of the Vedas, and expressed themselves in languages spoken by ordinary people
cards.quote: Many of these new religious leaders questioned the authority of the Vedas, and expressed themselves in languages spoken by ordinary people

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was the new element in north India that culminated in the thirteenth century?
cards.back: A new element in this situation was the coming of the Turks which culminated in the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate (thirteenth century).
cards.quote: A new element in this situation was the coming of the Turks which culminated in the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate (thirteenth century).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did the Delhi Sultanate undermine?
cards.back: This undermined the power of many of the Rajput states and the Brahmanas who were associated with these kingdoms.
cards.quote: This undermined the power of many of the Rajput states and the Brahmanas who were associated with these kingdoms.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which Arab general conquered Sind in 711?
cards.back: In 711 an Arab general named Muhammad Qasim conquered Sind, which became part of the Caliph’s domain.
cards.quote: In 711 an Arab general named Muhammad Qasim conquered Sind, which became part of the Caliph’s domain.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Later (c. thirteenth century) the ____ established the Delhi Sultanate.
cards.back: Later (c. thirteenth century) the Turks and Afghans established the Delhi Sultanate.
cards.quote: Later (c. thirteenth century) the Turks and Afghans established the Delhi Sultanate.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Theoretically, Muslim rulers were to be guided by the ____, who were expected to ensure that they ruled according to the shari‘a.
cards.back: Theoretically, Muslim rulers were to be guided by the ulama, who were expected to ensure that they ruled according to the shari‘a.
cards.quote: Theoretically, Muslim rulers were to be guided by the ulama, who were expected to ensure that they ruled according to the shari‘a.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What does the category of zimmi mean, and for whom did it develop?
cards.back: It is in this context that the category of the zimmi, meaning protected (derived from the Arabic word zimma, protection) developed for people who followed revealed scriptures, such as the Jews and Christians, and lived under Muslim rulership.
cards.quote: It is in this context that the category of the zimmi, meaning protected (derived from the Arabic word zimma, protection) developed for people who followed revealed scriptures, such as the Jews and Christians, and lived under Muslim rulership.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What tax did zimmis pay, and to whom was the status extended in India?
cards.back: They paid a tax called jizya and gained the right to be protected by Muslims. In India this status was extended to Hindus as well.
cards.quote: They paid a tax called jizya and gained the right to be protected by Muslims. In India this status was extended to Hindus as well.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who are the ulama?
cards.back: Ulama (plural of alim, or one who knows) are scholars of Islamic studies.
cards.quote: Ulama (plural of alim, or one who knows) are scholars of Islamic studies.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is the shari‘a?
cards.back: The shari‘a is the law governing the Muslim community. It is based on the Qur’an and the hadis, traditions of the Prophet including a record of his remembered words and deeds.
cards.quote: The shari‘a is the law governing the Muslim community. It is based on the Qur’an and the hadis, traditions of the Prophet including a record of his remembered words and deeds.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The four sources from which the shari‘a evolved.
cards.back:
Qur’an
hadis
qiyas (reasoning by analogy)
ijma (consensus of the community)
cards.quote: With the expansion of Islamic rule outside Arabia, in areas where customs and traditions were different, qiyas (reasoning by analogy) and ijma (consensus of the community) were recognised as two other sources of legislation. Thus, the shari‘a evolved from the Qur’an, hadis, qiyas and ijma.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which two kinds of grants did several rulers make to Hindu, Jaina, Zoroastrian, Christian and Jewish religious institutions?
cards.back: In effect, rulers often adopted a fairly flexible policy towards their subjects. For instance, several rulers gave land endowments and granted tax exemptions to Hindu, Jaina, Zoroastrian, Christian and Jewish religious institutions
cards.quote: In effect, rulers often adopted a fairly flexible policy towards their subjects. For instance, several rulers gave land endowments and granted tax exemptions to Hindu, Jaina, Zoroastrian, Christian and Jewish religious institutions

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Akbar's 1598 farman allow the padris of the Society of Jesus to build in Khambat?
cards.back: Whereas it reached our eminent and holy notice that the padris (fathers) of the Holy Society of Jesus wish to build a house of prayer (church) in the city of Kambayat (Khambat, in Gujarat)
cards.quote: Whereas it reached our eminent and holy notice that the padris (fathers) of the Holy Society of Jesus wish to build a house of prayer (church) in the city of Kambayat (Khambat, in Gujarat)

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: To whom did Aurangzeb write a respectful letter in 1661-62?
cards.back: Here is an excerpt from a letter written by Aurangzeb to a Jogi in 1661-62
cards.quote: Here is an excerpt from a letter written by Aurangzeb to a Jogi in 1661-62

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the five “pillars” of Islam.
cards.back:
that there is one God, Allah, and Prophet Muhammad is his messenger (shahada)
offering prayers five times a day (namaz/salat)
giving alms (zakat)
fasting during the month of Ramzan (sawm)
performing the pilgrimage to Mecca (hajj)
cards.quote: All those who adopted Islam accepted, in principle, the five “pillars” of the faith: that there is one God, Allah, and Prophet Muhammad is his messenger (shahada); offering prayers five times a day (namaz/salat ); giving alms (zakat); fasting during the month of Ramzan (sawm ); and performing the pilgrimage to Mecca (hajj ).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who were the Khojahs and how did they spread ideas from the Qur’an?
cards.back: For example, the Khojahs, a branch of the Ismailis (a Shi‘a sect), developed new modes of communication, disseminating ideas derived from the Qur’an through indigenous literary genres.
cards.quote: For example, the Khojahs, a branch of the Ismailis (a Shi‘a sect), developed new modes of communication, disseminating ideas derived from the Qur’an through indigenous literary genres.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are ginan?
cards.back: These included the ginan (derived from the Sanskrit jnana, meaning “knowledge”), devotional poems in Punjabi, Multani, Sindhi, Kachchi, Hindi and Gujarati, sung in special ragas during daily prayer meetings.
cards.quote: These included the ginan (derived from the Sanskrit jnana, meaning “knowledge”), devotional poems in Punjabi, Multani, Sindhi, Kachchi, Hindi and Gujarati, sung in special ragas during daily prayer meetings.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In which script were the ginan recorded after being transmitted orally?
cards.back: The ginan were transmitted orally before being recorded in the Khojaki script that was derived from the local landa (“clipped” mercantile script) used by the linguistically diverse community of Khojahs in the Punjab, Sind and Gujarat.
cards.quote: The ginan were transmitted orally before being recorded in the Khojaki script that was derived from the local landa (“clipped” mercantile script) used by the linguistically diverse community of Khojahs in the Punjab, Sind and Gujarat.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which language and customs did Arab Muslim traders on the Malabar coast adopt?
cards.back: Elsewhere, Arab Muslim traders who settled along the Malabar coast (Kerala) adopted the local language, Malayalam. They also adopted local customs such as matriliny (Chapter 3) and matrilocal residence.
cards.quote: Elsewhere, Arab Muslim traders who settled along the Malabar coast (Kerala) adopted the local language, Malayalam. They also adopted local customs such as matriliny (Chapter 3) and matrilocal residence.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is matrilocal residence?
cards.back: Matrilocal residence is a practice where women after marriage remain in their natal home with their children and the husbands may come to stay with them.
cards.quote: Matrilocal residence is a practice where women after marriage remain in their natal home with their children and the husbands may come to stay with them.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The complex blend of a universal faith with local traditions is perhaps best exemplified in the ____.
cards.back: The complex blend of a universal faith with local traditions is perhaps best exemplified in the architecture of mosques.
cards.quote: The complex blend of a universal faith with local traditions is perhaps best exemplified in the architecture of mosques.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which universal feature of mosques is seen in the mihrab and minbar?
cards.back: such as their orientation towards Mecca, evident in the placement of the mihrab (prayer niche) and the minbar (pulpit)
cards.quote: such as their orientation towards Mecca, evident in the placement of the mihrab (prayer niche) and the minbar (pulpit)

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which features of mosques show variations?
cards.back: However, there are several features that show variations – such as roofs and building materials (see Figs. 6.9, 6.10 and 6.11).
cards.quote: However, there are several features that show variations – such as roofs and building materials (see Figs. 6.9, 6.10 and 6.11).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What does the study of Sanskrit texts and inscriptions of the eighth to fourteenth centuries show about the term Muslim?
cards.back: Historians who have studied Sanskrit texts and inscriptions dating between the eighth and fourteenth centuries point out that the term musalman or Muslim was virtually never used.
cards.quote: Historians who have studied Sanskrit texts and inscriptions dating between the eighth and fourteenth centuries point out that the term musalman or Muslim was virtually never used.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Terms for the Turkish rulers, people from Tajikistan and people from Persia in Sanskrit texts.
cards.back:
Turushka
Tajika
Parashika
cards.quote: So, the Turkish rulers were designated as Turushka, Tajika were people from Tajikistan and Parashika were people from Persia.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which terms were used for the Turks and Afghans, borrowed from other peoples?
cards.back: For instance, the Turks and Afghans were referred to as Shakas (Chapters 2 and 3) and Yavanas (a term used for Greeks).
cards.quote: For instance, the Turks and Afghans were referred to as Shakas (Chapters 2 and 3) and Yavanas (a term used for Greeks).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What does the term mlechchha indicate?
cards.back: A more general term for these migrant communities was mlechchha, indicating that they did not observe the norms of caste society and spoke languages that were not derived from Sanskrit.
cards.quote: A more general term for these migrant communities was mlechchha, indicating that they did not observe the norms of caste society and spoke languages that were not derived from Sanskrit.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who were the sufis, and what were they protesting against?
cards.back: In the early centuries of Islam a group of religious-minded people called sufis turned to asceticism and mysticism in protest against the growing materialism of the Caliphate as a religious and political institution.
cards.quote: In the early centuries of Islam a group of religious-minded people called sufis turned to asceticism and mysticism in protest against the growing materialism of the Caliphate as a religious and political institution.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Whose example did the sufis follow, regarding him as a perfect human being?
cards.back: Instead, they laid emphasis on seeking salvation through intense devotion and love for God by following His commands, and by following the example of the Prophet Muhammad whom they regarded as a perfect human being.
cards.quote: Instead, they laid emphasis on seeking salvation through intense devotion and love for God by following His commands, and by following the example of the Prophet Muhammad whom they regarded as a perfect human being.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is a khanqah, and who controlled it?
cards.back: Institutionally, the sufis began to organise communities around the hospice or khanqah (Persian) controlled by a teaching master known as shaikh (in Arabic), pir or murshid (in Persian).
cards.quote: Institutionally, the sufis began to organise communities around the hospice or khanqah (Persian) controlled by a teaching master known as shaikh (in Arabic), pir or murshid (in Persian).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: He enrolled disciples (____) and appointed a successor (____).
cards.back: He enrolled disciples (murids) and appointed a successor (khalifa).
cards.quote: He enrolled disciples (murids) and appointed a successor (khalifa).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What does the word silsila mean?
cards.back: The word silsila literally means a chain, signifying a continuous link between master and disciple, stretching as an unbroken spiritual genealogy to the Prophet Muhammad.
cards.quote: The word silsila literally means a chain, signifying a continuous link between master and disciple, stretching as an unbroken spiritual genealogy to the Prophet Muhammad.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Sufi silsilas began to crystallise in different parts of the Islamic world around the ____.
cards.back: Sufi silsilas began to crystallise in different parts of the Islamic world around the twelfth century.
cards.quote: Sufi silsilas began to crystallise in different parts of the Islamic world around the twelfth century.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did initiates do in the special sufi rituals of initiation?
cards.back: Special rituals of initiation were developed in which initiates took an oath of allegiance, wore a patched garment, and shaved their hair.
cards.quote: Special rituals of initiation were developed in which initiates took an oath of allegiance, wore a patched garment, and shaved their hair.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is a dargah?
cards.back: When the shaikh died, his tomb-shrine (dargah, a Persian term meaning court) became the centre of devotion for his followers.
cards.quote: When the shaikh died, his tomb-shrine (dargah, a Persian term meaning court) became the centre of devotion for his followers.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are ziyarat and urs?
cards.back: This encouraged the practice of pilgrimage or ziyarat to his grave, particularly on his death anniversary or urs (or marriage, signifying the union of his soul with God).
cards.quote: This encouraged the practice of pilgrimage or ziyarat to his grave, particularly on his death anniversary or urs (or marriage, signifying the union of his soul with God).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: A sufi shaikh’s tomb-shrine became a centre of devotion. By what term was the shaikh revered in this cult?
cards.back: Thus evolved the cult of the shaikh revered as wali.
cards.quote: Thus evolved the cult of the shaikh revered as wali.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What word is used for Sufism in Islamic texts?
cards.back: Sufism is an English word coined in the nineteenth century. The word used for Sufism in Islamic texts is tasawwuf.
cards.quote: Sufism is an English word coined in the nineteenth century. The word used for Sufism in Islamic texts is tasawwuf.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Three possible derivations of the word tasawwuf.
cards.back:
suf, meaning wool
safa, meaning purity
suffa, the platform outside the Prophet’s mosque
cards.quote: According to some scholars, it is derived from suf, meaning wool, referring to the coarse woollen clothes worn by sufis. Others derive it from safa, meaning purity. It may also have been derived from suffa, the platform outside the Prophet’s mosque, where a group of close followers assembled to learn about the faith.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: After what was the Chishti order named, unlike the Qadiri order?
cards.back: However, some like the Chishti order, were named after their place of origin, in this case the town of Chisht in central Afghanistan.
cards.quote: However, some like the Chishti order, were named after their place of origin, in this case the town of Chisht in central Afghanistan.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who is a wali (plural auliya)?
cards.back: Wali (plural auliya) or friend of God was a sufi who claimed proximity to Allah, acquiring His Grace (barakat) to perform miracles (karamat).
cards.quote: Wali (plural auliya) or friend of God was a sufi who claimed proximity to Allah, acquiring His Grace (barakat) to perform miracles (karamat).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Names of the mystics who scorned the khanqah and took to mendicancy.
cards.back:
Qalandars
Madaris
Malangs
Haidaris
cards.quote: They were known by different names – Qalandars, Madaris, Malangs, Haidaris, etc.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: be-shari‘a vs ba-shari‘a sufis: the difference.
cards.back: Because of their deliberate defiance of the shari‘a they were often referred to as be-shari‘a, in contrast to the ba-shari‘a sufis who complied with it.
cards.quote: Because of their deliberate defiance of the shari‘a they were often referred to as be-shari‘a, in contrast to the ba-shari‘a sufis who complied with it.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why were the Chishtis the most influential of the sufi groups that migrated to India in the late twelfth century?
cards.back: Of the groups of sufis who migrated to India in the late twelfth century, the Chishtis were the most influential. This was because they adapted successfully to the local environment and adopted several features of Indian devotional traditions.
cards.quote: Of the groups of sufis who migrated to India in the late twelfth century, the Chishtis were the most influential. This was because they adapted successfully to the local environment and adopted several features of Indian devotional traditions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Where was Shaikh Nizamuddin's hospice located?
cards.back: We know about Shaikh Nizamuddin’s hospice (c. fourteenth century) on the banks of the river Yamuna in Ghiyaspur, on the outskirts of what was then the city of Delhi.
cards.quote: We know about Shaikh Nizamuddin’s hospice (c. fourteenth century) on the banks of the river Yamuna in Ghiyaspur, on the outskirts of what was then the city of Delhi.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was the big hall of Shaikh Nizamuddin’s hospice called, where inmates and visitors lived and prayed?
cards.back: We know about Shaikh Nizamuddin’s hospice (c. fourteenth century) on the banks of the river Yamuna in Ghiyaspur, on the outskirts of what was then the city of Delhi. It comprised several small rooms and a big hall ( jama’at khana) where the inmates and visitors lived and prayed.
cards.quote: We know about Shaikh Nizamuddin’s hospice (c. fourteenth century) on the banks of the river Yamuna in Ghiyaspur, on the outskirts of what was then the city of Delhi. It comprised several small rooms and a big hall ( jama’at khana) where the inmates and visitors lived and prayed.

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is the langar of a Chishti khanqah?
cards.back: There was an open kitchen (langar), run on futuh (unasked-for charity).
cards.quote: There was an open kitchen (langar), run on futuh (unasked-for charity).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which practices adopted in the Chishti khanqah show assimilation of local traditions?
cards.back: Practices that were adopted, including bowing before the Shaikh, offering water to visitors, shaving the heads of initiates, and yogic exercises, represented attempts to assimilate local traditions.
cards.quote: Practices that were adopted, including bowing before the Shaikh, offering water to visitors, shaving the heads of initiates, and yogic exercises, represented attempts to assimilate local traditions.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Pilgrimage, called ____, to tombs of sufi saints is prevalent all over the Muslim world.
cards.back: Pilgrimage, called ziyarat, to tombs of sufi saints is prevalent all over the Muslim world.
cards.quote: Pilgrimage, called ziyarat, to tombs of sufi saints is prevalent all over the Muslim world.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which Chishti shrine is the most revered, and by what name is its saint popularly known?
cards.back: Amongst these, the most revered shrine is that of Khwaja Muinuddin, popularly known as “Gharib Nawaz” (comforter of the poor).
cards.quote: Amongst these, the most revered shrine is that of Khwaja Muinuddin, popularly known as “Gharib Nawaz” (comforter of the poor).

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who funded the earliest construction to house Khwaja Muinuddin's tomb?
cards.back: the earliest construction to house the tomb was funded in the late fifteenth century by Sultan Ghiyasuddin Khalji of Malwa
cards.quote: the earliest construction to house the tomb was funded in the late fifteenth century by Sultan Ghiyasuddin Khalji of Malwa

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which Persian book did al Hujwiri write to explain the meaning of tasawwuf?
cards.back: He settled in Lahore and wrote a book in Persian called the Kashful-Mahjub (Unveiling of the Veiled) to explain the meaning of tasawwuf, and those who practised it, that is, the sufi.
cards.quote: He settled in Lahore and wrote a book in Persian called the Kashful-Mahjub (Unveiling of the Veiled) to explain the meaning of tasawwuf, and those who practised it, that is, the sufi.

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: By what name is Hujwiri revered, and what is his mausoleum called?
cards.back: Even today Hujwiri is revered as Data Ganj Bakhsh or “Giver who bestows treasures” and his mausoleum is called Data Darbar or “Court of the Giver”.
cards.quote: Even today Hujwiri is revered as Data Ganj Bakhsh or “Giver who bestows treasures” and his mausoleum is called Data Darbar or “Court of the Giver”.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What inspired Akbar to visit the Ajmer tomb?
cards.back: By the sixteenth century the shrine had become very popular; in fact it was the spirited singing of pilgrims bound for Ajmer that inspired Akbar to visit the tomb.
cards.quote: By the sixteenth century the shrine had become very popular; in fact it was the spirited singing of pilgrims bound for Ajmer that inspired Akbar to visit the tomb.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How many times did Akbar visit the Ajmer shrine, and until when?
cards.back: He went there fourteen times, sometimes two or three times a year, to seek blessings for new conquests, fulfilment of vows, and the birth of sons. He maintained this tradition until 1580.
cards.quote: He went there fourteen times, sometimes two or three times a year, to seek blessings for new conquests, fulfilment of vows, and the birth of sons. He maintained this tradition until 1580.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Akbar offer in 1568 at Ajmer, and what did he have constructed in the dargah compound?
cards.back: For example, in 1568 he offered a huge cauldron (degh) to facilitate cooking for pilgrims. He also had a mosque constructed within the compound of the dargah.
cards.quote: For example, in 1568 he offered a huge cauldron (degh) to facilitate cooking for pilgrims. He also had a mosque constructed within the compound of the dargah.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How do the sufis remember God (zikr and sama‘)?
cards.back: The sufis remember God either by reciting the zikr (the Divine Names) or evoking His Presence through sama‘ (literally, “audition”) or performance of mystical music.
cards.quote: The sufis remember God either by reciting the zikr (the Divine Names) or evoking His Presence through sama‘ (literally, “audition”) or performance of mystical music.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which sufi practice, literally "audition", was integral to the Chishtis and showed interaction with indigenous devotional traditions?
cards.back: The sufis remember God either by reciting the zikr (the Divine Names) or evoking His Presence through sama‘ (literally, “audition”) or performance of mystical music. Sama‘ was integral to the Chishtis, and exemplified interaction with indigenous devotional traditions.
cards.quote: The sufis remember God either by reciting the zikr (the Divine Names) or evoking His Presence through sama‘ (literally, “audition”) or performance of mystical music. Sama‘ was integral to the Chishtis, and exemplified interaction with indigenous devotional traditions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who performs mystical chants during ziyarat to evoke divine ecstasy?
cards.back: Also part of ziyarat is the use of music and dance including mystical chants performed by specially trained musicians or qawwals to evoke divine ecstasy.
cards.quote: Also part of ziyarat is the use of music and dance including mystical chants performed by specially trained musicians or qawwals to evoke divine ecstasy.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Amir Khusrau introduce into the Chishti sama‘?
cards.back: Amir Khusrau (1253-1325), the great poet, musician and disciple of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya, gave a unique form to the Chishti sama‘ by introducing the qaul (Arabic word meaning “saying”), a hymn sung at the opening or closing of qawwali.
cards.quote: Amir Khusrau (1253-1325), the great poet, musician and disciple of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya, gave a unique form to the Chishti sama‘ by introducing the qaul (Arabic word meaning “saying”), a hymn sung at the opening or closing of qawwali.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Qawwals (those who sing these songs) at the shrine of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya always start their recital with the ____.
cards.back: Qawwals (those who sing these songs) at the shrine of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya always start their recital with the qaul.
cards.quote: Qawwals (those who sing these songs) at the shrine of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya always start their recital with the qaul.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In Delhi, those associated with the Chishti silsila conversed in ____, the language of the people.
cards.back: In Delhi, those associated with the Chishti silsila conversed in Hindavi, the language of the people.
cards.quote: In Delhi, those associated with the Chishti silsila conversed in Hindavi, the language of the people.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Whose verses in the local language were incorporated in the Guru Granth Sahib?
cards.back: Other sufis such as Baba Farid composed verses in the local language, which were incorporated in the Guru Granth Sahib.
cards.quote: Other sufis such as Baba Farid composed verses in the local language, which were incorporated in the Guru Granth Sahib.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are masnavis in sufi poetry?
cards.back: Yet others composed long poems or masnavis to express ideas of divine love using human love as an allegory.
cards.quote: Yet others composed long poems or masnavis to express ideas of divine love using human love as an allegory.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which prem-akhyan did Malik Muhammad Jayasi compose, and whose romance does it tell?
cards.back: For example, the prem-akhyan (love story) Padmavat composed by Malik Muhammad Jayasi revolved around the romance of Padmini and Ratansen, the king of Chittor.
cards.quote: For example, the prem-akhyan (love story) Padmavat composed by Malik Muhammad Jayasi revolved around the romance of Padmini and Ratansen, the king of Chittor.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In which language and region were short sufi poems attributed to Chishti sufis composed?
cards.back: A different genre of sufi poetry was composed in and around the town of Bijapur, Karnataka. These were short poems in Dakhani (a variant of Urdu) attributed to Chishti sufis who lived in this region during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
cards.quote: A different genre of sufi poetry was composed in and around the town of Bijapur, Karnataka. These were short poems in Dakhani (a variant of Urdu) attributed to Chishti sufis who lived in this region during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are lurinama and shadinama?
cards.back: Other compositions were in the form of lurinama or lullabies and shadinama or wedding songs.
cards.quote: Other compositions were in the form of lurinama or lullabies and shadinama or wedding songs.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is a charkhanama?
cards.back: Charkhanama A song set to the rhythm of the spinning wheel
cards.quote: Charkhanama A song set to the rhythm of the spinning wheel

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did the Sultans set up as endowments for hospices, and what land did they grant?
cards.back: The sufis accepted unsolicited grants and donations from the political elites. The Sultans in turn set up charitable trusts (auqaf ) as endowments for hospices and granted tax-free land (inam).
cards.quote: The sufis accepted unsolicited grants and donations from the political elites. The Sultans in turn set up charitable trusts (auqaf ) as endowments for hospices and granted tax-free land (inam).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did the Chishtis use the donations they accepted?
cards.back: Rather than accumulate donations, they preferred to use these fully on immediate requirements such as food, clothes, living quarters and ritual necessities (such as sama‘ ).
cards.quote: Rather than accumulate donations, they preferred to use these fully on immediate requirements such as food, clothes, living quarters and ritual necessities (such as sama‘ ).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why did the Turks of the Delhi Sultanate resist the ulama's insistence on the shari‘a as state law?
cards.back: When the Turks set up the Delhi Sultanate, they resisted the insistence of the ulama on imposing shari‘a as state law because they anticipated opposition from their subjects, the majority of whom were non-Muslims.
cards.quote: When the Turks set up the Delhi Sultanate, they resisted the insistence of the ulama on imposing shari‘a as state law because they anticipated opposition from their subjects, the majority of whom were non-Muslims.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why did kings often want their tombs near sufi shrines and hospices?
cards.back: Besides, it was believed that the auliya could intercede with God in order to improve the material and spiritual conditions of ordinary human beings. This explains why kings often wanted their tombs to be in the vicinity of sufi shrines and hospices.
cards.quote: Besides, it was believed that the auliya could intercede with God in order to improve the material and spiritual conditions of ordinary human beings. This explains why kings often wanted their tombs to be in the vicinity of sufi shrines and hospices.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: By what title did the disciples of Nizamuddin Auliya address him?
cards.back: For example, the disciples of Nizamuddin Auliya addressed him as sultan-ul-mashaikh (literally, Sultan amongst shaikhs).
cards.quote: For example, the disciples of Nizamuddin Auliya addressed him as sultan-ul-mashaikh (literally, Sultan amongst shaikhs).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which sufi orders were associated with the Delhi Sultans and with the Mughals?
cards.back: Other sufis such as the Suhrawardi under the Delhi Sultans and the Naqshbandi under the Mughals were also associated with the state.
cards.quote: Other sufis such as the Suhrawardi under the Delhi Sultans and the Naqshbandi under the Mughals were also associated with the state.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which dargah at Fatehpur Sikri symbolised the bond between the Chishtis and the Mughal state?
cards.back: The dargah of Shaikh Salim Chishti (a direct descendant of Baba Farid) constructed in Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar’s capital, symbolised the bond between the Chishtis and the Mughal state.
cards.quote: The dargah of Shaikh Salim Chishti (a direct descendant of Baba Farid) constructed in Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar’s capital, symbolised the bond between the Chishtis and the Mughal state.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which poet-saint (c. fourteenth-fifteenth centuries) is an outstanding example of the new devotional paths in north India?
cards.back: Kabir (c. fourteenth-fifteenth centuries) is perhaps one of the most outstanding examples of a poet-saint who emerged within this context.
cards.quote: Kabir (c. fourteenth-fifteenth centuries) is perhaps one of the most outstanding examples of a poet-saint who emerged within this context.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Three overlapping traditions in which Kabir’s verses were compiled.
cards.back:
The Kabir Bijak is preserved by the Kabirpanth (the path or sect of Kabir) in Varanasi and elsewhere in Uttar Pradesh
the Kabir Granthavali is associated with the Dadupanth in Rajasthan
many of his compositions are found in the Adi Granth Sahib
cards.quote: Verses ascribed to Kabir have been compiled in three distinct but overlapping traditions. The Kabir Bijak is preserved by the Kabirpanth (the path or sect of Kabir) in Varanasi and elsewhere in Uttar Pradesh; the Kabir Granthavali is associated with the Dadupanth in Rajasthan, and many of his compositions are found in the Adi Granth Sahib (see Section 8.2).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Kabir’s poems have survived in several languages and dialects; and some are composed in the special language of nirguna poets, the ____.
cards.back: Kabir’s poems have survived in several languages and dialects; and some are composed in the special language of nirguna poets, the sant bhasha.
cards.quote: Kabir’s poems have survived in several languages and dialects; and some are composed in the special language of nirguna poets, the sant bhasha.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are ulatbansi in Kabir’s poems?
cards.back: Others, known as ulatbansi (upside-down sayings), are written in a form in which everyday meanings are inverted.
cards.quote: Others, known as ulatbansi (upside-down sayings), are written in a form in which everyday meanings are inverted.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Traditions Kabir drew on to describe the Ultimate Reality, with their terms.
cards.back:
he described the Ultimate Reality as Allah, Khuda, Hazrat and Pir
terms drawn from Vedantic traditions, alakh (the unseen), nirakar (formless), Brahman, Atman, etc.
shabda (sound) or shunya (emptiness) were drawn from yogic traditions
cards.quote: These include Islam: he described the Ultimate Reality as Allah, Khuda, Hazrat and Pir. He also used terms drawn from Vedantic traditions, alakh (the unseen), nirakar (formless), Brahman, Atman, etc. Other terms with mystical connotations such as shabda (sound) or shunya (emptiness) were drawn from yogic traditions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Whose composition: “God is called by many names: Names like Allah, Ram, Karim, Keshav, Hari, and Hazrat.”?
cards.back: Here is a composition attributed to Kabir
cards.quote: Here is a composition attributed to Kabir

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which sufi concepts were used in some poems to express the Hindu practice of nam-simaran?
cards.back: others use the sufi concept of zikr and ishq (love) to express the Hindu practice of nam-simaran (remembrance of God’s name).
cards.quote: others use the sufi concept of zikr and ishq (love) to express the Hindu practice of nam-simaran (remembrance of God’s name).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Vaishnava hagiographies suggest about Kabir's birth and upbringing?
cards.back: Hagiographies within the Vaishnava tradition attempted to suggest that he was born a Hindu, Kabirdas (Kabir itself is an Arabic word meaning “great”), but was raised by a poor Muslim family belonging to the community of weavers or julahas, who were relatively recent converts to Islam.
cards.quote: Hagiographies within the Vaishnava tradition attempted to suggest that he was born a Hindu, Kabirdas (Kabir itself is an Arabic word meaning “great”), but was raised by a poor Muslim family belonging to the community of weavers or julahas, who were relatively recent converts to Islam.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Where and in what family was Baba Guru Nanak (1469-1539) born?
cards.back: Baba Guru Nanak (1469-1539) was born in a Hindu merchant family in a village called Nankana Sahib near the river Ravi in the predominantly Muslim Punjab.
cards.quote: Baba Guru Nanak (1469-1539) was born in a Hindu merchant family in a village called Nankana Sahib near the river Ravi in the predominantly Muslim Punjab.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The message of Baba Guru Nanak is spelt out in his hymns and teachings. These suggest that he advocated a form of ____.
cards.back: The message of Baba Guru Nanak is spelt out in his hymns and teachings. These suggest that he advocated a form of nirguna bhakti.
cards.quote: The message of Baba Guru Nanak is spelt out in his hymns and teachings. These suggest that he advocated a form of nirguna bhakti.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Baba Guru Nanak reject?
cards.back:
sacrifices
ritual baths
image worship
austerities
the scriptures of both Hindus and Muslims
cards.quote: He rejected sacrifices, ritual baths, image worship, austerities and the scriptures of both Hindus and Muslims.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did Baba Guru Nanak conceive the Absolute or “rab”?
cards.back: For Baba Guru Nanak, the Absolute or “rab” had no gender or form.
cards.quote: For Baba Guru Nanak, the Absolute or “rab” had no gender or form.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Through which hymns, and in which language, did Baba Guru Nanak express his ideas?
cards.back: He proposed a simple way to connect to the Divine by remembering and repeating the Divine Name, expressing his ideas through hymns called “shabad” in Punjabi, the language of the region.
cards.quote: He proposed a simple way to connect to the Divine by remembering and repeating the Divine Name, expressing his ideas through hymns called “shabad” in Punjabi, the language of the region.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which attendant of Baba Guru Nanak played the rabab?
cards.back: Baba Guru Nanak would sing these compositions in various ragas while his attendant Mardana played the rabab.
cards.quote: Baba Guru Nanak would sing these compositions in various ragas while his attendant Mardana played the rabab.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Whom did Baba Guru Nanak appoint as his successor, and what rules did he set for worship?
cards.back: Baba Guru Nanak organised his followers into a community. He set up rules for congregational worship (sangat ) involving collective recitation. He appointed one of his disciples, Angad, to succeed him as the preceptor (guru), and this practice was followed for nearly 200 years.
cards.quote: Baba Guru Nanak organised his followers into a community. He set up rules for congregational worship (sangat ) involving collective recitation. He appointed one of his disciples, Angad, to succeed him as the preceptor (guru), and this practice was followed for nearly 200 years.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What happened after Baba Guru Nanak’s death, though he did not wish to establish a new religion?
cards.back: It appears that Baba Guru Nanak did not wish to establish a new religion, but after his death his followers consolidated their own practices and distinguished themselves from both Hindus and Muslims.
cards.quote: It appears that Baba Guru Nanak did not wish to establish a new religion, but after his death his followers consolidated their own practices and distinguished themselves from both Hindus and Muslims.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who compiled the Adi Granth Sahib, and whose hymns did it include?
cards.back: The fifth preceptor, Guru Arjan, compiled Baba Guru Nanak’s hymns along with those of his four successors and other religious poets like Baba Farid, Ravidas (also known as Raidas) and Kabir in the Adi Granth Sahib.
cards.quote: The fifth preceptor, Guru Arjan, compiled Baba Guru Nanak’s hymns along with those of his four successors and other religious poets like Baba Farid, Ravidas (also known as Raidas) and Kabir in the Adi Granth Sahib.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who included Guru Tegh Bahadur's compositions, and what was the scripture then called?
cards.back: In the late seventeenth century the tenth preceptor, Guru Gobind Singh, included the compositions of the ninth guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, and this scripture was called the Guru Granth Sahib.
cards.quote: In the late seventeenth century the tenth preceptor, Guru Gobind Singh, included the compositions of the ninth guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, and this scripture was called the Guru Granth Sahib.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The five symbols of the Khalsa Panth defined by Guru Gobind Singh.
cards.back:
uncut hair
a dagger
a pair of shorts
a comb
a steel bangle
cards.quote: Guru Gobind Singh also laid the foundation of the Khalsa Panth (army of the pure) and defined its five symbols: uncut hair, a dagger, a pair of shorts, a comb and a steel bangle.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What kind of force did the Sikh community become consolidated as under Guru Gobind Singh, founder of the Khalsa Panth?
cards.back: Guru Gobind Singh also laid the foundation of the Khalsa Panth (army of the pure) and defined its five symbols: uncut hair, a dagger, a pair of shorts, a comb and a steel bangle. Under him the community got consolidated as a socio-religious and military force.
cards.quote: Guru Gobind Singh also laid the foundation of the Khalsa Panth (army of the pure) and defined its five symbols: uncut hair, a dagger, a pair of shorts, a comb and a steel bangle. Under him the community got consolidated as a socio-religious and military force.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Baba Guru Nanak and the Sacred Word

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who is perhaps the best-known woman poet within the bhakti tradition?
cards.back: Mirabai (c. fifteenth-sixteenth centuries) is perhaps the best-known woman poet within the bhakti tradition. Biographies have been reconstructed primarily from the bhajans attributed to her, which were transmitted orally for centuries.
cards.quote: Mirabai (c. fifteenth-sixteenth centuries) is perhaps the best-known woman poet within the bhakti tradition. Biographies have been reconstructed primarily from the bhajans attributed to her, which were transmitted orally for centuries.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Where was Mirabai from, and into which clan was she married against her wishes?
cards.back: According to these, she was a Rajput princess from Merta in Marwar who was married against her wishes to a prince of the Sisodia clan of Mewar, Rajasthan.
cards.quote: According to these, she was a Rajput princess from Merta in Marwar who was married against her wishes to a prince of the Sisodia clan of Mewar, Rajasthan.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Whom did Mirabai recognise as her lover instead of submitting to the role of wife and mother?
cards.back: She defied her husband and did not submit to the traditional role of wife and mother, instead recognising Krishna, the avatar of Vishnu, as her lover.
cards.quote: She defied her husband and did not submit to the traditional role of wife and mother, instead recognising Krishna, the avatar of Vishnu, as her lover.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Mirabai’s in-laws try to do, and how did she live afterwards?
cards.back: Her in-laws tried to poison her, but she escaped from the palace to live as a wandering saint composing songs that are characterised by intense expressions of emotion.
cards.quote: Her in-laws tried to poison her, but she escaped from the palace to live as a wandering saint composing songs that are characterised by intense expressions of emotion.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: According to some traditions, who was Mirabai’s preceptor, and what would it indicate?
cards.back: According to some traditions, her preceptor was Raidas, a leather worker. This would indicate her defiance of the norms of caste society.
cards.quote: According to some traditions, her preceptor was Raidas, a leather worker. This would indicate her defiance of the norms of caste society.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who especially continue to sing Mirabai’s songs, and where?
cards.back: Her songs continue to be sung by women and men, especially those who are poor and considered “low caste” in Gujarat and Rajasthan.
cards.quote: Her songs continue to be sung by women and men, especially those who are poor and considered “low caste” in Gujarat and Rajasthan.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who emerged in the late fifteenth century as a leading proponent of Vaishnavism in Assam?
cards.back: In the late fifteenth century, Shankaradeva emerged as one of the leading proponents of Vaishnavism in Assam.
cards.quote: In the late fifteenth century, Shankaradeva emerged as one of the leading proponents of Vaishnavism in Assam.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is the Bhagavati dharma of Shankaradeva based on, and what did it focus on?
cards.back: His teachings, often known as the Bhagavati dharma because they were based on the Bhagavad Gita and the Bhagavata Purana, focused on absolute surrender to the supreme deity, in this case Vishnu.
cards.quote: His teachings, often known as the Bhagavati dharma because they were based on the Bhagavad Gita and the Bhagavata Purana, focused on absolute surrender to the supreme deity, in this case Vishnu.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Shankaradeva emphasise, and which institutions did he encourage?
cards.back: He emphasised the need for naam kirtan, recitation of the names of the lord in sat sanga or congregations of pious devotees. He also encouraged the establishment of satra or monasteries for the transmission of spiritual knowledge, and naam ghar or prayer halls.
cards.quote: He emphasised the need for naam kirtan, recitation of the names of the lord in sat sanga or congregations of pious devotees. He also encouraged the establishment of satra or monasteries for the transmission of spiritual knowledge, and naam ghar or prayer halls.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which is a major composition of Shankaradeva?
cards.back: His major compositions include the Kirtana-ghosha.
cards.quote: His major compositions include the Kirtana-ghosha.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which treatise of Ali bin Usman Hujwiri is an example of sufi treatises or manuals?
cards.back: Treatises or manuals dealing with sufi thought and practices – The Kashf-ul-Mahjub of Ali bin Usman Hujwiri (died c. 1071) is an example of this genre.
cards.quote: Treatises or manuals dealing with sufi thought and practices – The Kashf-ul-Mahjub of Ali bin Usman Hujwiri (died c. 1071) is an example of this genre.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are malfuzat, and which is an early text on them?
cards.back: Malfuzat (literally, “uttered”; conversations of sufi saints) – An early text on malfuzat is the Fawa’id-al-Fu’ad, a collection of conversations of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya, compiled by Amir Hasan Sijzi Dehlavi, a noted Persian poet.
cards.quote: Malfuzat (literally, “uttered”; conversations of sufi saints) – An early text on malfuzat is the Fawa’id-al-Fu’ad, a collection of conversations of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya, compiled by Amir Hasan Sijzi Dehlavi, a noted Persian poet.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are maktubat?
cards.back: Maktubat (literally, “written” collections of letters); letters written by sufi masters, addressed to their disciples and associates
cards.quote: Maktubat (literally, “written” collections of letters); letters written by sufi masters, addressed to their disciples and associates

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Whose letters are known as the Maktubat-i Imam Rabbani?
cards.back: The letters, known as Maktubat-i Imam Rabbani, of the noted seventeenth-century Naqshbandi Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (d.1624), whose ideology is often contrasted with the liberal and non-sectarian views of Akbar, are amongst those most frequently discussed by scholars.
cards.quote: The letters, known as Maktubat-i Imam Rabbani, of the noted seventeenth-century Naqshbandi Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (d.1624), whose ideology is often contrasted with the liberal and non-sectarian views of Akbar, are amongst those most frequently discussed by scholars.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are tazkiras?
cards.back: Tazkiras (literally, “to mention and memorialise”; biographical accounts of saints)
cards.quote: Tazkiras (literally, “to mention and memorialise”; biographical accounts of saints)

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which was the first sufi tazkira written in India, and whom did it deal with?
cards.back: The fourteenth-century Siyar-ul-Auliya of Mir Khwurd Kirmani was the first sufi tazkira written in India. It dealt principally with the Chishti saints.
cards.quote: The fourteenth-century Siyar-ul-Auliya of Mir Khwurd Kirmani was the first sufi tazkira written in India. It dealt principally with the Chishti saints.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which is the most famous tazkira, and who wrote it?
cards.back: The most famous tazkira is the Akhbar-ul-Akhyar of Abdul Haqq Muhaddis Dehlavi (d. 1642).
cards.quote: The most famous tazkira is the Akhbar-ul-Akhyar of Abdul Haqq Muhaddis Dehlavi (d. 1642).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is the total time span of the Harappan civilisation?
cards.back: The total time span of the civilisation ranges from 6000 BCE to 1300 BCE.
cards.quote: The total time span of the civilisation ranges from 6000 BCE to 1300 BCE.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Phases of the Harappan civilisation, with their dates.
cards.back:
Early Harappan (6000 BCE-2600 BCE) is a formative phase of the civilisation.
Mature Harappan (2600 BCE-1900 BCE) is the most prosperous phase.
This decadent phase (1900 BCE-1300 BCE) is termed as Late Harappan.
cards.quote: The early phase, termed as Early Harappan (6000 BCE-2600 BCE) is a formative phase of the civilisation. The urban phase of the civilisation, termed as Mature Harappan (2600 BCE-1900 BCE) is the most prosperous phase. The decline of the civilisation starts around 1900 BCE. This decadent phase (1900 BCE-1300 BCE) is termed as Late Harappan.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The urban phase of the civilisation, termed as ____ (2600 BCE-1900 BCE) is the most prosperous phase.
cards.back: The urban phase of the civilisation, termed as Mature Harappan (2600 BCE-1900 BCE) is the most prosperous phase.
cards.quote: The urban phase of the civilisation, termed as Mature Harappan (2600 BCE-1900 BCE) is the most prosperous phase.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why is the Indus Valley Civilisation also called the Harappan Civilisation?
cards.back: The term Harappa is derived from the place where the civilization was identified.
cards.quote: The term Harappa is derived from the place where the civilization was identified.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Harappan seals were made of which stone, and what do they often contain?
cards.back: Made of a stone called steatite, seals like this one often contain animal motifs and signs from a script that remains undeciphered.
