cards.quote: Made of a stone called steatite, seals like this one often contain animal motifs and signs from a script that remains undeciphered.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What share of Harappan settlements lie in the Saraswati basin, and what does this suggest?
cards.back: Nearly two-thirds of these settlements are in the Saraswati basin, suggesting its immense importance for the Harappan Civilisation.
cards.quote: Nearly two-thirds of these settlements are in the Saraswati basin, suggesting its immense importance for the Harappan Civilisation.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Name the five major Harappan cities identified.
cards.back:
Rakhigarhi
Mohenjodaro
Harappa
Dholavira
Ganweriwala
cards.quote: Among these, five major cities have been identified. These are Rakhigarhi, Mohenjodaro, Harappa, Dholavira and Ganweriwala.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Categories of the remaining Harappan sites.
cards.back:
Regional Centres
agricultural villages
ports
manufacturing centres
cards.quote: The remaining sites come under different categories such as Regional Centres, agricultural villages, ports and manufacturing centres.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The recent archaeological evidences also indicate the emergence of Harappan culture from early farming communities dated around ____.
cards.back: The recent archaeological evidences also indicate the emergence of Harappan culture from early farming communities dated around 7000 BCE.
cards.quote: The recent archaeological evidences also indicate the emergence of Harappan culture from early farming communities dated around 7000 BCE.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who are archaeo-botanists, and what do they study?
cards.back: Archaeologists have been able to reconstruct dietary practices from finds of charred grains and seeds. These are studied by archaeo-botanists, who are specialists in ancient plant remains.
cards.quote: Archaeologists have been able to reconstruct dietary practices from finds of charred grains and seeds. These are studied by archaeo-botanists, who are specialists in ancient plant remains.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Where are millets found, and how common is rice, at Harappan sites?
cards.back: Millets are found from sites in Gujarat. Finds of rice are relatively rare.
cards.quote: Millets are found from sites in Gujarat. Finds of rice are relatively rare.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Name the five domesticated animals whose bones NCERT lists as found at Harappan sites.
cards.back:
cattle
sheep
goat
buffalo
pig
cards.quote: Animal bones found at Harappan sites include those of cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What do archaeo-zoologists or zooarchaeologists conclude about the animal bones?
cards.back: Studies done by archaeo-zoologists or zooarchaeologists indicate that these animals were domesticated.
cards.quote: Studies done by archaeo-zoologists or zooarchaeologists indicate that these animals were domesticated.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What do archaeologists infer from the bull on seals and terracotta sculpture?
cards.back: Representations on seals and terracotta sculpture indicate that the bull was known, and archaeologists extrapolate from this that oxen were used for ploughing.
cards.quote: Representations on seals and terracotta sculpture indicate that the bull was known, and archaeologists extrapolate from this that oxen were used for ploughing.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What did the two sets of furrows at right angles at Kalibangan suggest?
cards.back: The field had two sets of furrows at right angles to each other, suggesting that two different crops were grown together.
cards.quote: The field had two sets of furrows at right angles to each other, suggesting that two different crops were grown together.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: At which Harappan site have traces of canals been found?
cards.back: Traces of canals have been found at the Harappan site of Shortughai in Afghanistan, but not in Punjab or Sind.
cards.quote: Traces of canals have been found at the Harappan site of Shortughai in Afghanistan, but not in Punjab or Sind.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What may the water reservoirs at Dholavira have been used for?
cards.back: Besides, water reservoirs found in Dholavira (Gujarat) may have been used to store water for agriculture.
cards.quote: Besides, water reservoirs found in Dholavira (Gujarat) may have been used to store water for agriculture.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Of what materials were Harappan grinding equipment and food vessels made?
cards.back: Processing of food required grinding equipment as well as vessels for mixing, blending and cooking. These were made of stone, metal and terracotta.
cards.quote: Processing of food required grinding equipment as well as vessels for mixing, blending and cooking. These were made of stone, metal and terracotta.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which was the first Harappan site to be discovered?
cards.back: Although Mohenjodaro is the most well-known site, the first site to be discovered was Harappa.
cards.quote: Although Mohenjodaro is the most well-known site, the first site to be discovered was Harappa.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why was Harappa badly destroyed?
cards.back: Although Harappa was the first site to be discovered, it was badly destroyed by brick robbers.
cards.quote: Although Harappa was the first site to be discovered, it was badly destroyed by brick robbers.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In Mohenjodaro, what do archaeologists call the smaller, higher section and the larger, lower one?
cards.back: Archaeologists designate these as the Citadel and the Lower Town respectively.
cards.quote: Archaeologists designate these as the Citadel and the Lower Town respectively.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.note: Citadel = smaller but higher section; Lower Town = much larger but lower section.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why was the Citadel higher, and was it walled?
cards.back: The Citadel owes its height to the fact that buildings were constructed on mud brick platforms. It was walled, which meant that it was physically separated from the Lower Town.
cards.quote: The Citadel owes its height to the fact that buildings were constructed on mud brick platforms. It was walled, which meant that it was physically separated from the Lower Town.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How much labour would the foundation platforms at Mohenjodaro have needed?
cards.back: It has been calculated that if one labourer moved roughly a cubic metre of earth daily, just to put the foundations in place it would have required four million person-days, in other words, mobilising labour on a very large scale.
cards.quote: It has been calculated that if one labourer moved roughly a cubic metre of earth daily, just to put the foundations in place it would have required four million person-days, in other words, mobilising labour on a very large scale.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What was the standardised ratio of Harappan bricks?
cards.back: Other signs of planning include bricks, which, whether sun-dried or baked, were of a standardised ratio, where the length and breadth were four times and twice the height respectively.
cards.quote: Other signs of planning include bricks, which, whether sun-dried or baked, were of a standardised ratio, where the length and breadth were four times and twice the height respectively.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In NCERT's section 'Laying out drains', what is called one of the most distinctive features of Harappan cities?
cards.back: One of the most distinctive features of Harappan cities was the carefully planned drainage system.
cards.quote: One of the most distinctive features of Harappan cities was the carefully planned drainage system.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In what pattern were the roads and streets of the Lower Town laid out?
cards.back: If you look at the plan of the Lower Town you will notice that roads and streets were laid out along an approximate "grid" pattern, intersecting at right angles.
cards.quote: If you look at the plan of the Lower Town you will notice that roads and streets were laid out along an approximate "grid" pattern, intersecting at right angles.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In Harappan cities, what seems to have been laid out first, with houses then built along them?
cards.back:
Streets with drains
It seems that streets with drains were laid out first and then houses built along them.
cards.quote: It seems that streets with drains were laid out first and then houses built along them.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: At which Gujarat sites was the entire settlement fortified?
cards.back: At sites such as Dholavira and Lothal (Gujarat), the entire settlement was fortified, and sections within the town were also separated by walls.
cards.quote: At sites such as Dholavira and Lothal (Gujarat), the entire settlement was fortified, and sections within the town were also separated by walls.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What was unusual about the Citadel within Lothal?
cards.back: The Citadel within Lothal was not walled off, but was built at a height.
cards.quote: The Citadel within Lothal was not walled off, but was built at a height.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is also interesting is an apparent concern for ____: there are no windows in the walls along the ground level.
cards.back: What is also interesting is an apparent concern for privacy: there are no windows in the walls along the ground level.
cards.quote: What is also interesting is an apparent concern for privacy: there are no windows in the walls along the ground level.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What did every Mohenjodaro house have, connected to the street drains?
cards.back: Every house had its own bathroom paved with bricks, with drains connected through the wall to the street drains.
cards.quote: Every house had its own bathroom paved with bricks, with drains connected through the wall to the street drains.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Scholars have estimated that the total number of wells in Mohenjodaro was about ____.
cards.back: Scholars have estimated that the total number of wells in Mohenjodaro was about 700.
cards.quote: Scholars have estimated that the total number of wells in Mohenjodaro was about 700.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who said of the Harappan drains: "It is certainly the most complete ancient system as yet discovered."?
cards.back: About the drains, Mackay noted: "It is certainly the most complete ancient system as yet discovered."
cards.quote: About the drains, Mackay noted: "It is certainly the most complete ancient system as yet discovered."

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Source 2: The most ancient system yet discovered

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How were the main drainage channels built and covered?
cards.back: The main channels were made of bricks set in mortar and were covered with loose bricks that could be removed for cleaning.
cards.quote: The main channels were made of bricks set in mortar and were covered with loose bricks that could be removed for cleaning.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Source 2: The most ancient system yet discovered

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Where did house drains first empty?
cards.back: House drains first emptied into a sump or cesspit into which solid matter settled while waste water flowed out into the street drains.
cards.quote: House drains first emptied into a sump or cesspit into which solid matter settled while waste water flowed out into the street drains.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Source 2: The most ancient system yet discovered

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: At Lothal, what were houses and drains made of?
cards.back: At Lothal for example, while houses were built of mud bricks, drains were made of burnt bricks.
cards.quote: At Lothal for example, while houses were built of mud bricks, drains were made of burnt bricks.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Source 2: The most ancient system yet discovered

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: On Mohenjodaro's Citadel, which two structures does NCERT name as probably used for special public purposes?
cards.back: It is on the Citadel that we find evidence of structures that were probably used for special public purposes. These include the warehouse – a massive structure of which the lower brick portions remain, while the upper portions, probably of wood, decayed long ago – and the Great Bath.
cards.quote: It is on the Citadel that we find evidence of structures that were probably used for special public purposes. These include the warehouse – a massive structure of which the lower brick portions remain, while the upper portions, probably of wood, decayed long ago – and the Great Bath.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What was the Great Bath of Mohenjodaro?
cards.back: The Great Bath was a large rectangular tank in a courtyard surrounded by a corridor on all four sides.
cards.quote: The Great Bath was a large rectangular tank in a courtyard surrounded by a corridor on all four sides.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How was the Great Bath made watertight?
cards.back: There were two flights of steps on the north and south leading into the tank, which was made watertight by setting bricks on edge and using a mortar of gypsum.
cards.quote: There were two flights of steps on the north and south leading into the tank, which was made watertight by setting bricks on edge and using a mortar of gypsum.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What have scholars suggested the Great Bath was meant for?
cards.back: The uniqueness of the structure, as well as the context in which it was found (the Citadel, with several distinctive buildings), has led scholars to suggest that it was meant for some kind of a special ritual bath.
cards.quote: The uniqueness of the structure, as well as the context in which it was found (the Citadel, with several distinctive buildings), has led scholars to suggest that it was meant for some kind of a special ritual bath.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How were the dead generally laid in Harappan burials?
cards.back: At burials in Harappan sites the dead were generally laid in pits.
cards.quote: At burials in Harappan sites the dead were generally laid in pits.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Was jewellery found in Harappan burials of men, women or both?
cards.back: Jewellery has been found in burials of both men and women.
cards.quote: Jewellery has been found in burials of both men and women.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is faience, and why were little faience pots considered precious?
cards.back: Thus, little pots of faience (a material made of ground sand or silica mixed with colour and a gum and then fired) were probably considered precious because they were difficult to make.
cards.quote: Thus, little pots of faience (a material made of ground sand or silica mixed with colour and a gum and then fired) were probably considered precious because they were difficult to make.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What are hoards?
cards.back: Hoards are objects kept carefully by people, often inside containers such as pots. Such hoards can be of jewellery or metal objects saved for reuse by metalworkers.
cards.quote: Hoards are objects kept carefully by people, often inside containers such as pots. Such hoards can be of jewellery or metal objects saved for reuse by metalworkers.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Where are rare objects made of valuable materials generally concentrated?
cards.back: If we study the distribution of such artefacts, we find that rare objects made of valuable materials are generally concentrated in large settlements like Mohenjodaro and Harappa and are rarely found in the smaller settlements.
cards.quote: If we study the distribution of such artefacts, we find that rare objects made of valuable materials are generally concentrated in large settlements like Mohenjodaro and Harappa and are rarely found in the smaller settlements.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: From where was all the gold jewellery found at Harappan sites recovered?
cards.back: all the gold jewellery found at Harappan sites was recovered from hoards.
cards.quote: all the gold jewellery found at Harappan sites was recovered from hoards.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Chanhudaro: how big was it and what was it devoted to?
cards.back: This is a tiny settlement (less than 7 hectares) as compared to Mohenjodaro (125 hectares), almost exclusively devoted to craft production, including bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making.
cards.quote: This is a tiny settlement (less than 7 hectares) as compared to Mohenjodaro (125 hectares), almost exclusively devoted to craft production, including bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Name the materials used to make beads in the Harappan civilisation.
cards.back:
stones like carnelian (of a beautiful red colour), jasper, crystal, quartz and steatite
metals like copper, bronze and gold
shell, faience and terracotta or burnt clay
cards.quote: The variety of materials used to make beads is remarkable: stones like carnelian (of a beautiful red colour), jasper, crystal, quartz and steatite; metals like copper, bronze and gold; and shell, faience and terracotta or burnt clay.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Steatite, a very ____ stone, was easily worked.
cards.back: Steatite, a very soft stone, was easily worked.
cards.quote: Steatite, a very soft stone, was easily worked.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How was the red colour of carnelian obtained?
cards.back: Archaeologists' experiments have revealed that the red colour of carnelian was obtained by firing the yellowish raw material and beads at various stages of production.
cards.quote: Archaeologists' experiments have revealed that the red colour of carnelian was obtained by firing the yellowish raw material and beads at various stages of production.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Steps in making a carnelian bead, in order.
cards.back:
Nodules were chipped into rough shapes, and then finely flaked into the final form.
Grinding, polishing and drilling completed the process.
cards.quote: Nodules were chipped into rough shapes, and then finely flaked into the final form. Grinding, polishing and drilling completed the process.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: At which sites have specialised drills been found?
cards.back: Specialised drills have been found at Chanhudaro, Lothal and more recently at Dholavira.
cards.quote: Specialised drills have been found at Chanhudaro, Lothal and more recently at Dholavira.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Nageshwar and Balakot were specialised centres for making what?
cards.back: These were specialised centres for making shell objects – including bangles, ladles and inlay – which were taken to other settlements.
cards.quote: These were specialised centres for making shell objects – including bangles, ladles and inlay – which were taken to other settlements.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What do archaeologists look for to identify centres of craft production?
cards.back:
raw material such as stone nodules, whole shells, copper ore
tools
unfinished objects
rejects and waste material
cards.quote: In order to identify centres of craft production, archaeologists usually look for the following: raw material such as stone nodules, whole shells, copper ore; tools; unfinished objects; rejects and waste material.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Archaeologists look for raw material, tools, unfinished objects, rejects, waste. Which is 'one of the best indicators' of craft work?
cards.back: In fact, waste is one of the best indicators of craft work.
cards.quote: In fact, waste is one of the best indicators of craft work.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What do terracotta toy models of bullock carts suggest?
cards.back: Terracotta toy models of bullock carts suggest that this was one important means of transporting goods and people across land routes.
cards.quote: Terracotta toy models of bullock carts suggest that this was one important means of transporting goods and people across land routes.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Terracotta models suggest bullock carts carried goods over land. Which other routes were probably used?
cards.back: Riverine routes along the Indus and its tributaries, as well as coastal routes were also probably used.
cards.quote: Terracotta toy models of bullock carts suggest that this was one important means of transporting goods and people across land routes. Riverine routes along the Indus and its tributaries, as well as coastal routes were also probably used.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why did the Harappans establish Nageshwar and Balakot?
cards.back: For instance, they established settlements such as Nageshwar and Balakot in areas where shell was available.
cards.quote: For instance, they established settlements such as Nageshwar and Balakot in areas where shell was available.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Materials from the subcontinent and beyond

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why were Shortughai and Lothal settled near particular sources?
cards.back: Other such sites were Shortughai, in far-off Afghanistan, near the best source of lapis lazuli, a blue stone that was apparently very highly valued, and Lothal which was near sources of carnelian (from Bharuch in Gujarat), steatite (from south Rajasthan and north Gujarat) and metal (from Rajasthan).
cards.quote: Other such sites were Shortughai, in far-off Afghanistan, near the best source of lapis lazuli, a blue stone that was apparently very highly valued, and Lothal which was near sources of carnelian (from Bharuch in Gujarat), steatite (from south Rajasthan and north Gujarat) and metal (from Rajasthan).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Materials from the subcontinent and beyond

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which regions did Harappan expeditions go to for copper and for gold?
cards.back: Another strategy for procuring raw materials may have been to send expeditions to areas such as the Khetri region of Rajasthan (for copper) and south India (for gold).
cards.quote: Another strategy for procuring raw materials may have been to send expeditions to areas such as the Khetri region of Rajasthan (for copper) and south India (for gold).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Materials from the subcontinent and beyond

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Beyond Rajasthan's Khetri region, from where outside the subcontinent was copper also probably brought to the Harappan region?
cards.back: Recent archaeological finds suggest that copper was also probably brought from Oman, on the southeastern tip of the Arabian peninsula.
cards.quote: Recent archaeological finds suggest that copper was also probably brought from Oman, on the southeastern tip of the Arabian peninsula.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What did chemical analyses of Omani copper and Harappan artefacts show?
cards.back: Chemical analyses have shown that both the Omani copper and Harappan artefacts have traces of nickel, suggesting a common origin.
cards.quote: Chemical analyses have shown that both the Omani copper and Harappan artefacts have traces of nickel, suggesting a common origin.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which regions do Mesopotamian texts name in contact with Mesopotamia, and which is Harappan?
cards.back: Mesopotamian texts mention contact with regions named Dilmun (probably the island of Bahrain), Magan and Meluhha, possibly the Harappan region.
cards.quote: Mesopotamian texts mention contact with regions named Dilmun (probably the island of Bahrain), Magan and Meluhha, possibly the Harappan region.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Name the products from Meluhha mentioned in Mesopotamian texts.
cards.back:
carnelian
lapis lazuli
copper
gold
varieties of wood
cards.quote: They mention the products from Meluhha: carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold, and varieties of wood.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Mesopotamian texts refer to Meluhha as a land of ____.
cards.back: Mesopotamian texts refer to Meluhha as a land of seafarers.
cards.quote: Mesopotamian texts refer to Meluhha as a land of seafarers.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What did an intact sealing on a bag of goods mean, and what else did it convey?
cards.back: If the bag reached with its sealing intact, it meant that it had not been tampered with. The sealing also conveyed the identity of the sender.
cards.quote: If the bag reached with its sealing intact, it meant that it had not been tampered with. The sealing also conveyed the identity of the sender.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What do Harappan seals usually have, and what does it probably contain?
cards.back: Harappan seals usually have a line of writing, probably containing the name and title of the owner.
cards.quote: Harappan seals usually have a line of writing, probably containing the name and title of the owner.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Most inscriptions are short, the longest containing about ____ signs.
cards.back: Most inscriptions are short, the longest containing about 26 signs.
cards.quote: Most inscriptions are short, the longest containing about 26 signs.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why was the Harappan script evidently not alphabetical?
cards.back: Although the script remains undeciphered to date, it was evidently not alphabetical (where each sign stands for a vowel or a consonant) as it has just too many signs – somewhere between 375 and 400.
cards.quote: Although the script remains undeciphered to date, it was evidently not alphabetical (where each sign stands for a vowel or a consonant) as it has just too many signs – somewhere between 375 and 400.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In which direction was the Harappan script written, and how is this apparent?
cards.back: It is apparent that the script was written from right to left as some seals show a wider spacing on the right and cramping on the left, as if the engraver began working from the right and then ran out of space.
cards.quote: It is apparent that the script was written from right to left as some seals show a wider spacing on the right and cramping on the left, as if the engraver began working from the right and then ran out of space.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Name the objects on which Harappan writing has been found.
cards.back:
seals
copper tools
rims of jars
copper and terracotta tablets
jewellery
bone rods
even an ancient signboard
cards.quote: Consider the variety of objects on which writing has been found: seals, copper tools, rims of jars, copper and terracotta tablets, jewellery, bone rods, even an ancient signboard!

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What were Harappan weights usually made of, and what shape were they?
cards.back: Exchanges were regulated by a precise system of weights, usually made of a stone called chert and generally cubical (Fig. 1.2), with no markings.
cards.quote: Exchanges were regulated by a precise system of weights, usually made of a stone called chert and generally cubical (Fig. 1.2), with no markings.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How were the lower and higher denominations of Harappan weights arranged?
cards.back: lower denominations of weights were binary (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32), while the higher denominations followed the decimal system (160, 200, 320, 640).
cards.quote: lower denominations of weights were binary (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32), while the higher denominations followed the decimal system (160, 200, 320, 640).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: For what were the smaller Harappan weights probably used?
cards.back: The smaller weights were probably used for weighing jewellery and beads.
cards.quote: The smaller weights were probably used for weighing jewellery and beads.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How uniform were Harappan bricks across the region?
cards.back: Notably, bricks, though obviously not produced in any single centre, were of a uniform ratio throughout the region, from Jammu to Gujarat.
cards.quote: Notably, bricks, though obviously not produced in any single centre, were of a uniform ratio throughout the region, from Jammu to Gujarat.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What was found with the large building at Mohenjodaro labelled a palace?
cards.back: A large building found at Mohenjodaro was labelled as a palace by archaeologists but no spectacular finds were associated with it.
cards.quote: A large building found at Mohenjodaro was labelled as a palace by archaeologists but no spectacular finds were associated with it.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why is the stone statue from Mohenjodaro called the "priest-king"?
cards.back: A stone statue was labelled and continues to be known as the "priest-king". This is because archaeologists were familiar with Mesopotamian history and its "priest-kings" and have found parallels in the Indus region.
cards.quote: A stone statue was labelled and continues to be known as the "priest-king". This is because archaeologists were familiar with Mesopotamian history and its "priest-kings" and have found parallels in the Indus region.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What three views do archaeologists hold on who ruled Harappan society, according to NCERT?
cards.back:
Some archaeologists are of the opinion that Harappan society had no rulers, and that everybody enjoyed equal status.
Others feel there was no single ruler but several, that Mohenjodaro had a separate ruler, Harappa another, and so forth.
Yet others argue that there was a single state, given the similarity in artefacts, the evidence for planned settlements, the standardised ratio of brick size, and the establishment of settlements near sources of raw material.
cards.quote: Some archaeologists are of the opinion that Harappan society had no rulers, and that everybody enjoyed equal status. Others feel there was no single ruler but several, that Mohenjodaro had a separate ruler, Harappa another, and so forth. Yet others argue that there was a single state, given the similarity in artefacts, the evidence for planned settlements, the standardised ratio of brick size, and the establishment of settlements near sources of raw material.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.note: A third view in NCERT: a single state, given the similarity in artefacts and planned settlements.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: There is evidence that by ____ most of the Mature Harappan sites in regions such as Cholistan had been abandoned.
cards.back: There is evidence that by c. 1800 BCE most of the Mature Harappan sites in regions such as Cholistan had been abandoned.
cards.quote: There is evidence that by c. 1800 BCE most of the Mature Harappan sites in regions such as Cholistan had been abandoned.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Where did population expand into new settlements as Cholistan sites were abandoned?
cards.back: Simultaneously, there was an expansion of population into new settlements in Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
cards.quote: Simultaneously, there was an expansion of population into new settlements in Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which distinctive artefacts disappeared after 1900 BCE?
cards.back: In the few Harappan sites that continued to be occupied after 1900 BCE there appears to have been a transformation of material culture, marked by the disappearance of the distinctive artefacts of the civilisation – weights, seals, special beads.
cards.quote: In the few Harappan sites that continued to be occupied after 1900 BCE there appears to have been a transformation of material culture, marked by the disappearance of the distinctive artefacts of the civilisation – weights, seals, special beads.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Name the explanations put forward for the end of the Harappan civilisation.
cards.back:
climatic change
deforestation
excessive floods
the shifting and/or drying up of rivers
overuse of the landscape
cards.quote: Several explanations have been put forward. These range from climatic change, deforestation, excessive floods, the shifting and/or drying up of rivers, to overuse of the landscape.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: At the end of the Harappan civilisation, what strong unifying element, perhaps, came to an end?
cards.back:
Perhaps the Harappan state
It appears that a strong unifying element, perhaps the Harappan state, came to an end.
cards.quote: It appears that a strong unifying element, perhaps the Harappan state, came to an end.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What way of life do Late Harappan artefacts and settlements indicate?
cards.back: Overall, artefacts and settlements indicate a rural way of life in what are called "Late Harappan" or "successor cultures".
cards.quote: Overall, artefacts and settlements indicate a rural way of life in what are called "Late Harappan" or "successor cultures".

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who questioned the evidence of a massacre at Mohenjodaro in the 1960s?
cards.back: In the 1960s, the evidence of a massacre in Mohenjodaro was questioned by an archaeologist named George Dales.
cards.quote: In the 1960s, the evidence of a massacre in Mohenjodaro was questioned by an archaeologist named George Dales.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In 1947, with what text did R.E.M. Wheeler try to correlate the archaeological evidence?
cards.back: Much later, in 1947, R.E.M. Wheeler, then Director-General of the ASI, tried to correlate this archaeological evidence with that of the Rigveda, the earliest known text in the subcontinent.
cards.quote: Much later, in 1947, R.E.M. Wheeler, then Director-General of the ASI, tried to correlate this archaeological evidence with that of the Rigveda, the earliest known text in the subcontinent.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What does the Rigveda call Indra, and what does pur mean?
cards.back: The Rigveda mentions pur, meaning rampart, fort or stronghold. Indra, the Aryan war-god is called puramdara, the fort-destroyer.
cards.quote: The Rigveda mentions pur, meaning rampart, fort or stronghold. Indra, the Aryan war-god is called puramdara, the fort-destroyer.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which is the biggest Harappan city, and where is it located?
cards.back: the recent archaeogenetic research carried out at the site of Rakhigarhi. The site, located in Hisar district of Haryana, is the biggest Harappan city, spread over an area of 550 Hectare.
cards.quote: In this respect, it is necessary to mention the recent archaeogenetic research carried out at the site of Rakhigarhi. The site, located in Hisar district of Haryana, is the biggest Harappan city, spread over an area of 550 Hectare.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What does the Rakhigarhi DNA analysis indicate about the Harappans?
cards.back: The analysis of the data indicates that the Harappans are the indigenous people of this region.
cards.quote: The analysis of the data indicates that the Harappans are the indigenous people of this region.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The genetic roots of the Harappans go back to ____.
cards.back: The genetic roots of the Harappans go back to 10,000 BCE.
cards.quote: The genetic roots of the Harappans go back to 10,000 BCE.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What does continuity in genetic and cultural history rule out?
cards.back: The continuity without any break in genetic history as well as cultural history rules out large scale immigration of the so-called Aryans.
cards.quote: The continuity without any break in genetic history as well as cultural history rules out large scale immigration of the so-called Aryans.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The Rakhigarhi archaeogenetic study indicated unbroken continuity for how many years in the region?
cards.back:
5000 years
Thus, this study has indicated unbroken continuity for 5000 years in this region.
cards.quote: Thus, this study has indicated unbroken continuity for 5000 years in this region.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is archaeogenetics?
cards.back: Archaeogenetics is the study of DNA of ancient population. It involves various methods of molecular genetics to understand population history.
cards.quote: Archaeogenetics is the study of DNA of ancient population. It involves various methods of molecular genetics to understand population history.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What guide to investigations did archaeologists prefer when Cunningham began excavating?
cards.back: When Cunningham, the first Director-General of the ASI, began archaeological excavations in the mid-nineteenth century, archaeologists preferred to use the written word (texts and inscriptions) as a guide to investigations.
cards.quote: When Cunningham, the first Director-General of the ASI, began archaeological excavations in the mid-nineteenth century, archaeologists preferred to use the written word (texts and inscriptions) as a guide to investigations.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Whose accounts did Cunningham use to locate early settlements?
cards.back: He used the accounts left by Chinese Buddhist pilgrims who had visited the subcontinent between the fourth and seventh centuries CE to locate early settlements.
cards.quote: He used the accounts left by Chinese Buddhist pilgrims who had visited the subcontinent between the fourth and seventh centuries CE to locate early settlements.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why did Cunningham miss the significance of the Harappan seal?
cards.back: This was because he, like many others, thought that Indian history began with the first cities in the Ganga valley (see Chapter 2).
cards.quote: This was because he, like many others, thought that Indian history began with the first cities in the Ganga valley (see Chapter 2).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is a mound in archaeology?
cards.back: When people continue to live in the same place, their constant use and reuse of the landscape results in the build up of occupational debris, called a mound.
cards.quote: When people continue to live in the same place, their constant use and reuse of the landscape results in the build up of occupational debris, called a mound.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What are "sterile layers"?
cards.back: Abandonment or desertions, what are called "sterile layers", can be identified by the absence of such traces.
cards.quote: Abandonment or desertions, what are called "sterile layers", can be identified by the absence of such traces.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is stratigraphy?
cards.back: Generally, the lowest layers are the oldest and the highest are the most recent. The study of these layers is called stratigraphy.
cards.quote: Generally, the lowest layers are the oldest and the highest are the most recent. The study of these layers is called stratigraphy.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who discovered seals at Harappa in the early decades of the twentieth century?
cards.back: Subsequently, seals were discovered at Harappa by archaeologists such as Daya Ram Sahni in the early decades of the twentieth century, in layers that were definitely much older than Early Historic levels.
cards.quote: Subsequently, seals were discovered at Harappa by archaeologists such as Daya Ram Sahni in the early decades of the twentieth century, in layers that were definitely much older than Early Historic levels.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who found similar seals at Mohenjodaro, suggesting a single archaeological culture?
cards.back: Another archaeologist, Rakhal Das Banerji found similar seals at Mohenjodaro, leading to the conjecture that these sites were part of a single archaeological culture.
cards.quote: Another archaeologist, Rakhal Das Banerji found similar seals at Mohenjodaro, leading to the conjecture that these sites were part of a single archaeological culture.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who announced the discovery of a new civilisation in the Indus valley, and when?
cards.back: Based on these finds, in 1924, John Marshall, Director-General of the ASI, announced the discovery of a new civilisation in the Indus valley to the world.
cards.quote: Based on these finds, in 1924, John Marshall, Director-General of the ASI, announced the discovery of a new civilisation in the Indus valley to the world.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who noted: "Marshall left India three thousand years older than he had found her."?
cards.back: As S.N. Roy noted in The Story of Indian Archaeology, "Marshall left India three thousand years older than he had found her."
cards.quote: As S.N. Roy noted in The Story of Indian Archaeology, "Marshall left India three thousand years older than he had found her."

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: With which civilisation was the Indus civilisation contemporaneous?
cards.back: It was then that the world knew not only of a new civilisation, but also of one contemporaneous with Mesopotamia.
cards.quote: It was then that the world knew not only of a new civilisation, but also of one contemporaneous with Mesopotamia.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What was special about John Marshall as an archaeologist in India?
cards.back: He was the first professional archaeologist to work in India, and brought his experience of working in Greece and Crete to the field.
cards.quote: He was the first professional archaeologist to work in India, and brought his experience of working in Greece and Crete to the field.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What mistake did Marshall make in excavating mounds?
cards.back: Marshall tended to excavate along regular horizontal units, measured uniformly throughout the mound, ignoring the stratigraphy of the site.
cards.quote: Marshall tended to excavate along regular horizontal units, measured uniformly throughout the mound, ignoring the stratigraphy of the site.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In which year did R.E.M. Wheeler take over as Director-General of the ASI?
cards.back:
1944
It was R.E.M. Wheeler, after he took over as Director-General of the ASI in 1944, who rectified this problem.
cards.quote: It was R.E.M. Wheeler, after he took over as Director-General of the ASI in 1944, who rectified this problem.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What did Wheeler recognise as necessary in digging a mound?
cards.back: Wheeler recognised that it was necessary to follow the stratigraphy of the mound rather than dig mechanically along uniform horizontal lines.
cards.quote: Wheeler recognised that it was necessary to follow the stratigraphy of the mound rather than dig mechanically along uniform horizontal lines.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What did Wheeler bring to archaeology as an ex-army brigadier?
cards.back: Moreover, as an ex-army brigadier, he brought with him a military precision to the practice of archaeology.
cards.quote: Moreover, as an ex-army brigadier, he brought with him a military precision to the practice of archaeology.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How did the partition of the subcontinent affect Indian archaeologists?
cards.back: However, with the partition of the subcontinent and the creation of Pakistan, the major known sites became part of Pakistan. This has spurred Indian archaeologists to try and locate sites in India.
cards.quote: However, with the partition of the subcontinent and the creation of Pakistan, the major known sites became part of Pakistan. This has spurred Indian archaeologists to try and locate sites in India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which Harappan sites in India were discovered and excavated in these efforts?
cards.back: While Kalibangan, Lothal, Rakhi Garhi and most recently Dholavira have been discovered, explored and excavated as part of these efforts, fresh explorations continue.
cards.quote: While Kalibangan, Lothal, Rakhi Garhi and most recently Dholavira have been discovered, explored and excavated as part of these efforts, fresh explorations continue.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which materials generally decompose, and which survive?
cards.back: Organic materials such as cloth, leather, wood and reeds generally decompose, especially in tropical regions. What survive are stone, burnt clay (or terracotta), metal, etc.
cards.quote: Organic materials such as cloth, leather, wood and reeds generally decompose, especially in tropical regions. What survive are stone, burnt clay (or terracotta), metal, etc.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Problems of Piecing Together the Past

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why are valuable artefacts found intact by archaeologists accidental rather than typical?
cards.back:
Lost in the past, or hoarded and never retrieved
Consequently, valuable artefacts that are found intact were either lost in the past or hoarded and never retrieved. In other words, such finds are accidental rather than typical.
cards.quote: Consequently, valuable artefacts that are found intact were either lost in the past or hoarded and never retrieved. In other words, such finds are accidental rather than typical.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Problems of Piecing Together the Past

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Principles on which archaeologists classify their finds.
cards.back:
in terms of material, such as stone, clay, metal, bone, ivory, etc.
in terms of function: archaeologists have to decide whether, for instance, an artefact is a tool or an ornament, or both, or something meant for ritual use.
cards.quote: One simple principle of classification is in terms of material, such as stone, clay, metal, bone, ivory, etc. The second, and more complicated, is in terms of function: archaeologists have to decide whether, for instance, an artefact is a tool or an ornament, or both, or something meant for ritual use.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What indirect evidence do we depend on to find out about Harappan clothing?
cards.back: Sometimes, archaeologists have to take recourse to indirect evidence. For instance, though there are traces of cotton at some Harappan sites, to find out about clothing we have to depend on indirect evidence including depictions in sculpture.
cards.quote: Sometimes, archaeologists have to take recourse to indirect evidence. For instance, though there are traces of cotton at some Harappan sites, to find out about clothing we have to depend on indirect evidence including depictions in sculpture.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which terracotta figurines were regarded as mother goddesses?
cards.back: These included terracotta figurines of women, heavily jewelled, some with elaborate head-dresses. These were regarded as mother goddesses.
cards.quote: These included terracotta figurines of women, heavily jewelled, some with elaborate head-dresses. These were regarded as mother goddesses.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which structures have been assigned ritual significance?
cards.back: In other instances, structures have been assigned ritual significance. These include the Great Bath and fire altars found at Kalibangan and Lothal.
cards.quote: In other instances, structures have been assigned ritual significance. These include the Great Bath and fire altars found at Kalibangan and Lothal.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which seal figure has been regarded as a depiction of "proto-Shiva"?
cards.back: In some seals, a figure shown seated cross-legged in a "yogic" posture, sometimes surrounded by animals, has been regarded as a depiction of "proto-Shiva", that is, an early form of one of the major deities of Hinduism.
cards.quote: In some seals, a figure shown seated cross-legged in a "yogic" posture, sometimes surrounded by animals, has been regarded as a depiction of "proto-Shiva", that is, an early form of one of the major deities of Hinduism.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is the one-horned animal on seals often called?
cards.back: Some animals – such as the one-horned animal, often called the "unicorn" – depicted on seals seem to be mythical, composite creatures.
cards.quote: Some animals – such as the one-horned animal, often called the "unicorn" – depicted on seals seem to be mythical, composite creatures.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What have conical stone objects been classified as?
cards.back: Besides, conical stone objects have been classified as lingas.
cards.quote: Besides, conical stone objects have been classified as lingas.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is a linga?
cards.back: A linga is a polished stone that is worshipped as a symbol of Shiva.
cards.quote: A linga is a polished stone that is worshipped as a symbol of Shiva.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why does the "proto-Shiva" seal not match Rudra of the Rigveda?
cards.back: However, unlike Shiva, Rudra in the Rigveda is neither depicted as Pashupati (lord of animals in general and cattle in particular), nor as a yogi.
cards.quote: However, unlike Shiva, Rudra in the Rigveda is neither depicted as Pashupati (lord of animals in general and cattle in particular), nor as a yogi.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who are shamans?
cards.back: Shamans are men and women who claim magical and healing powers, as well as an ability to communicate with the other world.
cards.quote: Shamans are men and women who claim magical and healing powers, as well as an ability to communicate with the other world.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What could help settle the question of the languages spoken by the Harappans?
cards.back: If a bilingual inscription is found, questions about the languages spoken by the Harappans could perhaps be put to rest.
cards.quote: If a bilingual inscription is found, questions about the languages spoken by the Harappans could perhaps be put to rest.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is described as a whole new area for future work in Harappan archaeology?
cards.back: Very few scholars have investigated issues of gender in the context of the Harappan civilisation and this is a whole new area for future work.
cards.quote: Very few scholars have investigated issues of gender in the context of the Harappan civilisation and this is a whole new area for future work.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When did the Permanent Settlement come into operation, and what had the Company fixed?
cards.back: The Permanent Settlement had come into operation in 1793. The East India Company had fixed the revenue that each zamindar had to pay.
cards.quote: The Permanent Settlement had come into operation in 1793. The East India Company had fixed the revenue that each zamindar had to pay.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: In the 1797 Burdwan auction, how much of the sale was fictitious?
cards.back: Over 95 per cent of the sale at the auction was fictitious. The raja's estates had been publicly sold, but he remained in control of his zamindari.
cards.quote: Over 95 per cent of the sale at the auction was fictitious. The raja's estates had been publicly sold, but he remained in control of his zamindari.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Over ____ of the zamindaris changed hands after the Permanent Settlement.
cards.back: Over 75 per cent of the zamindaris changed hands after the Permanent Settlement.
cards.quote: Over 75 per cent of the zamindaris changed hands after the Permanent Settlement.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: By the 1770s, the rural economy in Bengal was in crisis, with ____ and declining agricultural output.
cards.back: By the 1770s, the rural economy in Bengal was in crisis, with recurrent famines and declining agricultural output.
cards.quote: By the 1770s, the rural economy in Bengal was in crisis, with recurrent famines and declining agricultural output.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did officials want to fix the revenue demand permanently?
cards.back: If the revenue demand of the state was permanently fixed, then the Company could look forward to a regular flow of revenue, while entrepreneurs could feel sure of earning a profit from their investment, since the state would not siphon it off by increasing its claim.
cards.quote: If the revenue demand of the state was permanently fixed, then the Company could look forward to a regular flow of revenue, while entrepreneurs could feel sure of earning a profit from their investment, since the state would not siphon it off by increasing its claim.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What class did officials hope the Permanent Settlement would bring about?
cards.back: The process, officials hoped, would lead to the emergence of a class of yeomen farmers and rich landowners who would have the capital and enterprise to improve agriculture. Nurtured by the British, this class would also be loyal to the Company.
cards.quote: The process, officials hoped, would lead to the emergence of a class of yeomen farmers and rich landowners who would have the capital and enterprise to improve agriculture. Nurtured by the British, this class would also be loyal to the Company.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: With whom was the Permanent Settlement made, and how were they now classified?
cards.back: After a prolonged debate amongst Company officials, the Permanent Settlement was made with the rajas and taluqdars of Bengal. They were now classified as zamindars, and they had to pay the revenue demand that was fixed in perpetuity.
cards.quote: After a prolonged debate amongst Company officials, the Permanent Settlement was made with the rajas and taluqdars of Bengal. They were now classified as zamindars, and they had to pay the revenue demand that was fixed in perpetuity.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Under the Permanent Settlement, what was a zamindar?
cards.back: In terms of this definition, the zamindar was not a landowner in the village, but a revenue Collector of the state.
cards.quote: In terms of this definition, the zamindar was not a landowner in the village, but a revenue Collector of the state.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.note: A zamindar was a revenue collector for the state, not the owner of the village land.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Under the Permanent Settlement, how did a zamindar earn his income?
cards.back: The zamindar collected rent from the different villages, paid the revenue to the Company, and retained the difference as his income.
cards.quote: The zamindar collected rent from the different villages, paid the revenue to the Company, and retained the difference as his income.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why were the initial revenue demands under the Permanent Settlement so high?
cards.back: First: the initial demands were very high. This was because it was felt that if the demand was fixed for all time to come, the Company would never be able to claim a share of increased income from land when prices rose and cultivation expanded.
cards.quote: First: the initial demands were very high. This was because it was felt that if the demand was fixed for all time to come, the Company would never be able to claim a share of increased income from land when prices rose and cultivation expanded.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Besides the very high initial demand, name the three other reasons zamindars defaulted on revenue payments.
cards.back:
this high demand was imposed in the 1790s, a time when the prices of agricultural produce were depressed, making it difficult for the ryots to pay their dues to the zamindar
the revenue was invariable, regardless of the harvest, and had to be paid punctually
the Permanent Settlement initially limited the power of the zamindar to collect rent from the ryot and manage his zamindari
cards.quote: Second: this high demand was imposed in the 1790s, a time when the prices of agricultural produce were depressed, making it difficult for the ryots to pay their dues to the zamindar. If the zamindar could not collect the rent, how could he pay the Company? Third: the revenue was invariable, regardless of the harvest, and had to be paid punctually. In fact, according to the Sunset Law, if payment did not come in by sunset of the specified date, the zamindari was liable to be auctioned. Fourth: the Permanent Settlement initially limited the power of the zamindar to collect rent from the ryot and manage his zamindari.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was the Sunset Law?
cards.back: In fact, according to the Sunset Law, if payment did not come in by sunset of the specified date, the zamindari was liable to be auctioned.
cards.quote: In fact, according to the Sunset Law, if payment did not come in by sunset of the specified date, the zamindari was liable to be auctioned.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the Company curb the authority of the zamindars?
cards.back: The zamindars' troops were disbanded, customs duties abolished, and their "cutcheries" (courts) brought under the supervision of a Collector appointed by the Company. Zamindars lost their power to organise local justice and the local police.
cards.quote: The zamindars' troops were disbanded, customs duties abolished, and their "cutcheries" (courts) brought under the supervision of a Collector appointed by the Company. Zamindars lost their power to organise local justice and the local police.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Over time the ____ emerged as an alternative centre of authority, severely restricting what the zamindar could do.
cards.back: Over time the collectorate emerged as an alternative centre of authority, severely restricting what the zamindar could do.
cards.quote: Over time the collectorate emerged as an alternative centre of authority, severely restricting what the zamindar could do.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Rich ryots and village headmen – ____ – were only too happy to see the zamindar in trouble.
cards.back: Rich ryots and village headmen – jotedars and mandals – were only too happy to see the zamindar in trouble.
cards.quote: Rich ryots and village headmen – jotedars and mandals – were only too happy to see the zamindar in trouble.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who were the jotedars, and how powerful were they by the early nineteenth century?
cards.back: By the early nineteenth century, jotedars had acquired vast areas of land – sometimes as much as several thousand acres. They controlled local trade as well as moneylending, exercising immense power over the poorer cultivators of the region.
cards.quote: By the early nineteenth century, jotedars had acquired vast areas of land – sometimes as much as several thousand acres. They controlled local trade as well as moneylending, exercising immense power over the poorer cultivators of the region.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who cultivated the jotedars' land, and what share of the produce did they hand over?
cards.back: A large part of their land was cultivated through sharecroppers (adhiyars or bargadars) who brought their own ploughs, laboured in the field, and handed over half the produce to the jotedars after the harvest.
cards.quote: A large part of their land was cultivated through sharecroppers (adhiyars or bargadars) who brought their own ploughs, laboured in the field, and handed over half the produce to the jotedars after the harvest.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why was the power of jotedars within the villages more effective than that of zamindars?
cards.back: Unlike zamindars who often lived in urban areas, jotedars were located in the villages and exercised direct control over a considerable section of poor villagers.
cards.quote: Within the villages, the power of jotedars was more effective than that of zamindars. Unlike zamindars who often lived in urban areas, jotedars were located in the villages and exercised direct control over a considerable section of poor villagers.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Name the four ways in which the jotedars resisted the zamindars.
cards.back:
fiercely resisted efforts by zamindars to increase the jama of the village
prevented zamindari officials from executing their duties
mobilised ryots who were dependent on them
deliberately delayed payments of revenue to the zamindar
cards.quote: They fiercely resisted efforts by zamindars to increase the jama of the village, prevented zamindari officials from executing their duties, mobilised ryots who were dependent on them, and deliberately delayed payments of revenue to the zamindar.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What were zamindars responsible for (Fig. 9.5, Power in rural Bengal)?
cards.back:
(a) paying revenue to the company
(b) distributing the revenue demand (jama) over villages
cards.quote: Zamindars were responsible for: (a) paying revenue to the company (b) distributing the revenue demand (jama) over villages.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Jotedars gave out ____ to other ryots and sold their produce.
cards.back: Jotedars gave out loans to other ryots and sold their produce.
cards.quote: Jotedars gave out loans to other ryots and sold their produce.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Steps in the Raja of Burdwan's fictitious sale, in order.
cards.back:
first transferred some of his zamindari to his mother
Then, as a second move, his agents manipulated the auctions.
The revenue demand of the Company was deliberately withheld, and unpaid balances were allowed to accumulate.
When a part of the estate was auctioned, the zamindar's men bought the property, outbidding other purchasers.
Subsequently they refused to pay up the purchase money, so that the estate had to be resold.
This process was repeated endlessly, exhausting the state, and the other bidders at the auction.
At last the estate was sold at a low price back to the zamindar.
cards.quote: The Raja of Burdwan, for instance, first transferred some of his zamindari to his mother, since the Company had decreed that the property of women would not be taken over. Then, as a second move, his agents manipulated the auctions. The revenue demand of the Company was deliberately withheld, and unpaid balances were allowed to accumulate. When a part of the estate was auctioned, the zamindar's men bought the property, outbidding other purchasers. Subsequently they refused to pay up the purchase money, so that the estate had to be resold. Once again it was bought by the zamindar's agents, once again the purchase money was not paid, and once again there was an auction. This process was repeated endlessly, exhausting the state, and the other bidders at the auction. At last the estate was sold at a low price back to the zamindar.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did the Raja of Burdwan first transfer part of his zamindari to his mother?
cards.back: The Raja of Burdwan, for instance, first transferred some of his zamindari to his mother, since the Company had decreed that the property of women would not be taken over.
cards.quote: The Raja of Burdwan, for instance, first transferred some of his zamindari to his mother, since the Company had decreed that the property of women would not be taken over.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did four big zamindaris gain through benami purchases between 1793 and 1801?
cards.back: Between 1793 and 1801 four big zamindaris of Bengal, including Burdwan, made benami purchases that collectively yielded as much as Rs 30 lakh. Of the total sales at the auctions, over 15 per cent were fictitious.
cards.quote: Between 1793 and 1801 four big zamindaris of Bengal, including Burdwan, made benami purchases that collectively yielded as much as Rs 30 lakh. Of the total sales at the auctions, over 15 per cent were fictitious.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What happened when outsiders bought an estate at auction and tried to take possession?
cards.back: When people from outside the zamindari bought an estate at an auction, they could not always take possession. At times their agents would be attacked by lathyals of the former zamindar.
cards.quote: When people from outside the zamindari bought an estate at an auction, they could not always take possession. At times their agents would be attacked by lathyals of the former zamindar.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Ryots who felt loyal to their own zamindar perceived themselves as his what? (give the term)
cards.back:
Proja (subjects)
Sometimes even the ryots resisted the entry of outsiders. They felt bound to their own zamindar through a sense of loyalty and perceived him as a figure of authority and themselves as his proja (subjects).
cards.quote: Sometimes even the ryots resisted the entry of outsiders. They felt bound to their own zamindar through a sense of loyalty and perceived him as a figure of authority and themselves as his proja (subjects).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: During what did the zamindars’ power over the villages finally collapse, as the jotedars consolidated theirs?
cards.back:
The Great Depression of the 1930s
As a result, the zamindar’s power over the villages was strengthened. It was only during the Great Depression of the 1930s that they finally collapsed and the jotedars consolidated their power in the countryside.
cards.quote: As a result, the zamindar’s power over the villages was strengthened. It was only during the Great Depression of the 1930s that they finally collapsed and the jotedars consolidated their power in the countryside.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What does the term raja mean in this chapter?
cards.back: Raja (literally king) was a term that was often used to designate powerful zamindars.
cards.quote: Raja (literally king) was a term that was often used to designate powerful zamindars.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What does taluqdar literally mean?
cards.back: Taluqdar literally means "one who holds a taluq" or a connection. Taluq came to refer to a territorial unit.
cards.quote: Taluqdar literally means "one who holds a taluq" or a connection. Taluq came to refer to a territorial unit.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What is a ryot?
cards.back: Ryot is the way the term raiyat, used to designate peasants (Chapter 8), was spelt in British records.
