cards.quote: Ryot is the way the term raiyat, used to designate peasants (Chapter 8), was spelt in British records.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What is a benami transaction?
cards.back: Benami, literally anonymous, is a term used in Hindi and several other Indian languages for transactions made in the name of a fictitious or relatively insignificant person, whereas the real beneficiary remains unnamed.
cards.quote: Benami, literally anonymous, is a term used in Hindi and several other Indian languages for transactions made in the name of a fictitious or relatively insignificant person, whereas the real beneficiary remains unnamed.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who was a lathyal?
cards.back: Lathyal, literally one who wields the lathi or stick, functioned as a strongman of the zamindar.
cards.quote: Lathyal, literally one who wields the lathi or stick, functioned as a strongman of the zamindar.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was the Fifth Report, and when was it submitted to the British Parliament?
cards.back: Many of the changes we are discussing were documented in detail in a report that was submitted to the British Parliament in 1813. It was the fifth of a series of reports on the administration and activities of the East India Company in India.
cards.quote: Many of the changes we are discussing were documented in detail in a report that was submitted to the British Parliament in 1813. It was the fifth of a series of reports on the administration and activities of the East India Company in India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did the British Parliament pass a series of Acts on India in the late eighteenth century?
cards.back: The British Parliament passed a series of Acts in the late eighteenth century to regulate and control Company rule in India.
cards.quote: The British Parliament passed a series of Acts in the late eighteenth century to regulate and control Company rule in India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which body produced the Fifth Report, and what did it become the basis of?
cards.back: The Fifth Report was one such report produced by a Select Committee. It became the basis of intense parliamentary debates on the nature of the East India Company's rule in India.
cards.quote: The Fifth Report was one such report produced by a Select Committee. It became the basis of intense parliamentary debates on the nature of the East India Company's rule in India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How should official reports like the Fifth Report be read?
cards.back: But official reports like this have to be read carefully. We need to know who wrote the reports and why they were written.
cards.quote: But official reports like this have to be read carefully. We need to know who wrote the reports and why they were written.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did recent researches find wrong with the Fifth Report's account of the zamindars?
cards.back: the Fifth Report exaggerated the collapse of traditional zamindari power, as also overestimated the scale on which zamindars were losing their land.
cards.quote: They indicate that, intent on criticising the maladministration of the company, the Fifth Report exaggerated the collapse of traditional zamindari power, as also overestimated the scale on which zamindars were losing their land.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who was Francis Buchanan?
cards.back: Francis Buchanan was a physician who came to India and served in the Bengal Medical Service (from 1794 to 1815). For a few years he was surgeon to the Governor-General of India, Lord Wellesley.
cards.quote: Francis Buchanan was a physician who came to India and served in the Bengal Medical Service (from 1794 to 1815). For a few years he was surgeon to the Governor-General of India, Lord Wellesley.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who were the Paharias?
cards.back: They lived around the Rajmahal hills, subsisting on forest produce and practising shifting cultivation.
cards.quote: They lived around the Rajmahal hills, subsisting on forest produce and practising shifting cultivation.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Steps in the Paharias' shifting cultivation, in order.
cards.back:
They cleared patches of forest by cutting bushes and burning the undergrowth.
On these patches, enriched by the potash from the ash, the Paharias grew a variety of pulses and millets for consumption.
They scratched the ground lightly with hoes, cultivated the cleared land for a few years, then left it fallow so that it could recover its fertility, and moved to a new area.
cards.quote: They cleared patches of forest by cutting bushes and burning the undergrowth. On these patches, enriched by the potash from the ash, the Paharias grew a variety of pulses and millets for consumption. They scratched the ground lightly with hoes, cultivated the cleared land for a few years, then left it fallow so that it could recover its fertility, and moved to a new area.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the Paharias collect from the forests, and for what use?
cards.back:
mahua (a flower) for food
silk cocoons and resin for sale
wood for charcoal production
cards.quote: From the forests they collected mahua (a flower) for food, silk cocoons and resin for sale, and wood for charcoal production.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Name the ways of life that tied the Paharias to the forest.
cards.back:
hunters
shifting cultivators
food gatherers
charcoal producers
silkworm rearers
cards.quote: The life of the Paharias – as hunters, shifting cultivators, food gatherers, charcoal producers, silkworm rearers – was thus intimately connected to the forest.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What role did the chiefs of the Paharias play for their group?
cards.back: Their chiefs maintained the unity of the group, settled disputes, and led the tribe in battles with other tribes and plainspeople.
cards.quote: Their chiefs maintained the unity of the group, settled disputes, and led the tribe in battles with other tribes and plainspeople.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did the Paharias raid the plains? Name the three reasons.
cards.back:
necessary for survival, particularly in years of scarcity
a way of asserting power over settled communities
a means of negotiating political relations with outsiders
cards.quote: These raids were necessary for survival, particularly in years of scarcity; they were a way of asserting power over settled communities; and they were a means of negotiating political relations with outsiders.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: The zamindars on the plains had to often purchase peace by paying a regular ____ to the hill chiefs.
cards.back: The zamindars on the plains had to often purchase peace by paying a regular tribute to the hill chiefs.
cards.quote: The zamindars on the plains had to often purchase peace by paying a regular tribute to the hill chiefs.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did traders pay the hill folk, and what did the Paharia chiefs give in return?
cards.back: Traders similarly gave a small amount to the hill folk for permission to use the passes controlled by them. Once the toll was paid, the Paharia chiefs protected the traders, ensuring that their goods were not plundered by anyone.
cards.quote: Traders similarly gave a small amount to the hill folk for permission to use the passes controlled by them. Once the toll was paid, the Paharia chiefs protected the traders, ensuring that their goods were not plundered by anyone.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When and why did the negotiated peace with the Paharias break down?
cards.back: This negotiated peace was somewhat fragile. It broke down in the last decades of the eighteenth century when the frontiers of settled agriculture were being aggressively extended in eastern India.
cards.quote: This negotiated peace was somewhat fragile. It broke down in the last decades of the eighteenth century when the frontiers of settled agriculture were being aggressively extended in eastern India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did the British think settled agriculture was necessary? Name the three reasons.
cards.back:
to enlarge the sources of land revenue
produce crops for export
establish the basis of a settled, ordered society
cards.quote: To the British, extension of settled agriculture was necessary to enlarge the sources of land revenue, produce crops for export, and establish the basis of a settled, ordered society.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What policies did the British follow towards the Paharias in the 1770s and 1780s?
cards.back: In the 1770s the British embarked on a brutal policy of extermination, hunting the Paharias down and killing them. Then, by the 1780s, Augustus Cleveland, the Collector of Bhagalpur, proposed a policy of pacification.
cards.quote: In the 1770s the British embarked on a brutal policy of extermination, hunting the Paharias down and killing them. Then, by the 1780s, Augustus Cleveland, the Collector of Bhagalpur, proposed a policy of pacification.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Paharia chiefs were given an ____ and made responsible for the proper conduct of their men.
cards.back: Paharia chiefs were given an annual allowance and made responsible for the proper conduct of their men.
cards.quote: Paharia chiefs were given an annual allowance and made responsible for the proper conduct of their men.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What happened to the Paharia chiefs who accepted the allowances?
cards.back: Many Paharia chiefs refused the allowances. Those who accepted, most often lost authority within the community. Being in the pay of the colonial government, they came to be perceived as subordinate employees or stipendiary chiefs.
cards.quote: Many Paharia chiefs refused the allowances. Those who accepted, most often lost authority within the community. Being in the pay of the colonial government, they came to be perceived as subordinate employees or stipendiary chiefs.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the arrival of Santhal settlers affect the Paharias?
cards.back: Santhals were pouring into the area, clearing forests, cutting down timber, ploughing land and growing rice and cotton. As the lower hills were taken over by Santhal settlers, the Paharias receded deeper into the Rajmahal hills.
cards.quote: Santhals were pouring into the area, clearing forests, cutting down timber, ploughing land and growing rice and cotton. As the lower hills were taken over by Santhal settlers, the Paharias receded deeper into the Rajmahal hills.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: If Paharia life was symbolised by the ____, which they used for shifting cultivation, the settlers came to represent the power of the ____.
cards.back: If Paharia life was symbolised by the hoe, which they used for shifting cultivation, the settlers came to represent the power of the plough.
cards.quote: If Paharia life was symbolised by the hoe, which they used for shifting cultivation, the settlers came to represent the power of the plough.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who had extended the frontiers of cultivation near Ganjuria Pahar, as Buchanan found?
cards.back: On enquiry he discovered that the frontiers of cultivation here had been extended by the Santhals. They had moved into this area around 1800, displaced the hill folk who lived on these lower slopes, cleared the forests and settled the land.
cards.quote: On enquiry he discovered that the frontiers of cultivation here had been extended by the Santhals. They had moved into this area around 1800, displaced the hill folk who lived on these lower slopes, cleared the forests and settled the land.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When did the Santhals begin to come into Bengal, and who invited them?
cards.back: The Santhals had begun to come into Bengal around the 1780s. Zamindars hired them to reclaim land and expand cultivation, and British officials invited them to settle in the Jangal Mahals.
cards.quote: The Santhals had begun to come into Bengal around the 1780s. Zamindars hired them to reclaim land and expand cultivation, and British officials invited them to settle in the Jangal Mahals.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did the British turn to the Santhals after failing with the Paharias?
cards.back: Having failed to subdue the Paharias and transform them into settled agriculturists, the British turned to the Santhals. The Paharias refused to cut forests, resisted touching the plough, and continued to be turbulent. The Santhals, by contrast, appeared to be ideal settlers, clearing forests and ploughing the land with vigour.
cards.quote: Having failed to subdue the Paharias and transform them into settled agriculturists, the British turned to the Santhals. The Paharias refused to cut forests, resisted touching the plough, and continued to be turbulent. The Santhals, by contrast, appeared to be ideal settlers, clearing forests and ploughing the land with vigour.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was Damin-i-Koh, and when was it demarcated?
cards.back: The Santhals were given land and persuaded to settle in the foothills of Rajmahal. By 1832 a large area of land was demarcated as Damin-i-Koh. This was declared to be the land of the Santhals.
cards.quote: The Santhals were given land and persuaded to settle in the foothills of Rajmahal. By 1832 a large area of land was demarcated as Damin-i-Koh. This was declared to be the land of the Santhals.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: The land grant to the Santhals stipulated that at least ____ of the area was to be cleared and cultivated within the first ____.
cards.back: The land grant to the Santhals stipulated that at least one-tenth of the area was to be cleared and cultivated within the first ten years.
cards.quote: The land grant to the Santhals stipulated that at least one-tenth of the area was to be cleared and cultivated within the first ten years.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the number of Santhal villages and the Santhal population grow between 1838 and 1851?
cards.back: From 40 Santhal villages in the area in 1838, as many as 1,473 villages had come up by 1851. Over the same period, the Santhal population increased from a mere 3,000 to over 82,000.
cards.quote: From 40 Santhal villages in the area in 1838, as many as 1,473 villages had come up by 1851. Over the same period, the Santhal population increased from a mere 3,000 to over 82,000.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How do Santhal myths and songs represent the Santhal past?
cards.back: Santhal myths and songs of the nineteenth century refer very frequently to a long history of travel: they represent the Santhal past as one of continuous mobility, a tireless search for a place to settle.
cards.quote: Santhal myths and songs of the nineteenth century refer very frequently to a long history of travel: they represent the Santhal past as one of continuous mobility, a tireless search for a place to settle.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Paharias vs Santhals: how each fared after Damin-i-Koh (Paharias first, then Santhals).
cards.back:
When the most fertile soils became inaccessible to them, being part of the Damin, the Paharias could not effectively sustain their mode of cultivation.
The Santhals, by contrast, gave up their earlier life of mobility and settled down, cultivating a range of commercial crops for the market, and dealing with traders and moneylenders.
cards.quote: Shifting agriculture depended on the ability to move to newer and newer land and utilisation of the natural fertility of the soil. When the most fertile soils became inaccessible to them, being part of the Damin, the Paharias could not effectively sustain their mode of cultivation. When the forests of the region were cleared for cultivation the hunters amongst them also faced problems. The Santhals, by contrast, gave up their earlier life of mobility and settled down, cultivating a range of commercial crops for the market, and dealing with traders and moneylenders.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why was Santhal land slipping away from them? Name the three pressures.
cards.back:
The state was levying heavy taxes on the land that the Santhals had cleared
moneylenders (dikus) were charging them high rates of interest and taking over the land when debts remained unpaid
zamindars were asserting control over the Damin area
cards.quote: The Santhals, however, soon found that the land they had brought under cultivation was slipping away from their hands. The state was levying heavy taxes on the land that the Santhals had cleared, moneylenders (dikus) were charging them high rates of interest and taking over the land when debts remained unpaid, and zamindars were asserting control over the Damin area.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Against whom did the Santhals rebel by the 1850s, and why?
cards.back: By the 1850s, the Santhals felt that the time had come to rebel against zamindars, moneylenders and the colonial state, in order to create an ideal world for themselves where they would rule.
cards.quote: By the 1850s, the Santhals felt that the time had come to rebel against zamindars, moneylenders and the colonial state, in order to create an ideal world for themselves where they would rule.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When and how was the Santhal Pargana created, and why?
cards.back: It was after the Santhal Revolt (1855-56) that the Santhal Pargana was created, carving out 5,500 square miles from the districts of Bhagalpur and Birbhum. The colonial state hoped that by creating a new territory for the Santhals and imposing some special laws within it, the Santhals could be conciliated.
cards.quote: It was after the Santhal Revolt (1855-56) that the Santhal Pargana was created, carving out 5,500 square miles from the districts of Bhagalpur and Birbhum. The colonial state hoped that by creating a new territory for the Santhals and imposing some special laws within it, the Santhals could be conciliated.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Besides what the landscape looked like, what did Buchanan describe?
cards.back: When Buchanan wrote about a landscape, he most often described not just what he saw, what the landscape was like, but also how it could be transformed and made more productive – what crops could be cultivated, which trees cut down, and which ones grown.
cards.quote: When Buchanan wrote about a landscape, he most often described not just what he saw, what the landscape was like, but also how it could be transformed and made more productive – what crops could be cultivated, which trees cut down, and which ones grown.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What shaped Buchanan’s assessment of what was necessary for the Rajmahal landscape?
cards.back: his vision and his priorities were different from those of the local inhabitants: his assessment of what was necessary was shaped by the commercial concerns of the Company and modern Western notions of what constituted progress.
cards.quote: his vision and his priorities were different from those of the local inhabitants: his assessment of what was necessary was shaped by the commercial concerns of the Company and modern Western notions of what constituted progress.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Being critical of the lifestyles of forest dwellers, what did Buchanan feel had to be done to forests?
cards.back: He was inevitably critical of the lifestyles of forest dwellers and felt that forests had to be turned into agricultural lands.
cards.quote: He was inevitably critical of the lifestyles of forest dwellers and felt that forests had to be turned into agricultural lands.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Where did the 1875 Deccan revolt begin?
cards.back: The movement began at Supa, a large village in Poona (present-day Pune) district. It was a market centre where many shopkeepers and moneylenders lived.
cards.quote: The movement began at Supa, a large village in Poona (present-day Pune) district. It was a market centre where many shopkeepers and moneylenders lived.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What happened at Supa on 12 May 1875?
cards.back: On 12 May 1875, ryots from surrounding rural areas gathered and attacked the shopkeepers, demanding their bahi khatas (account books) and debt bonds. They burnt the khatas, looted grain shops, and in some cases set fire to the houses of sahukars.
cards.quote: On 12 May 1875, ryots from surrounding rural areas gathered and attacked the shopkeepers, demanding their bahi khatas (account books) and debt bonds. They burnt the khatas, looted grain shops, and in some cases set fire to the houses of sahukars.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Everywhere the pattern was the same: sahukars were attacked, ____ burnt and ____ destroyed.
cards.back: Everywhere the pattern was the same: sahukars were attacked, account books burnt and debt bonds destroyed.
cards.quote: Everywhere the pattern was the same: sahukars were attacked, account books burnt and debt bonds destroyed.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did British officials react to the spread of the Deccan revolt?
cards.back: As the revolt spread, British officials saw the spectre of 1857 (see Chapter 11). Police posts were established in villages to frighten rebellious peasants into submission. Troops were quickly called in; 951 people were arrested, and many convicted.
cards.quote: As the revolt spread, British officials saw the spectre of 1857 (see Chapter 11). Police posts were established in villages to frighten rebellious peasants into submission. Troops were quickly called in; 951 people were arrested, and many convicted.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who was a sahukar?
cards.back: A sahukar was someone who acted as both a moneylender and a trader.
cards.quote: A sahukar was someone who acted as both a moneylender and a trader.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: The Permanent Settlement was rarely extended to any region beyond ____.
cards.back: The Permanent Settlement was rarely extended to any region beyond Bengal.
cards.quote: The Permanent Settlement was rarely extended to any region beyond Bengal.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why was the Permanent Settlement rarely extended beyond Bengal (first reason)?
cards.back: One reason was that after 1810, agricultural prices rose, increasing the value of harvest produce, and enlarging the income of the Bengal zamindars. Since the revenue demand was fixed under the Permanent Settlement, the colonial state could not claim any share of this enhanced income.
cards.quote: One reason was that after 1810, agricultural prices rose, increasing the value of harvest produce, and enlarging the income of the Bengal zamindars. Since the revenue demand was fixed under the Permanent Settlement, the colonial state could not claim any share of this enhanced income.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What kind of revenue settlements were made in territories annexed in the nineteenth century?
cards.back:
Temporary revenue settlements
Keen on expanding its financial resources, the colonial government had to think of ways to maximise its land revenue. So in territories annexed in the nineteenth century, temporary revenue settlements were made.
cards.quote: Keen on expanding its financial resources, the colonial government had to think of ways to maximise its land revenue. So in territories annexed in the nineteenth century, temporary revenue settlements were made.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Whose economic ideas shaped the early revenue settlement in Maharashtra in the 1820s?
cards.back: By the 1820s, the economist David Ricardo was a celebrated figure in England. Colonial officials had learnt Ricardian ideas during their college years. In Maharashtra when British officials set about formulating the terms of the early settlement in the 1820s, they operated with some of these ideas.
cards.quote: By the 1820s, the economist David Ricardo was a celebrated figure in England. Colonial officials had learnt Ricardian ideas during their college years. In Maharashtra when British officials set about formulating the terms of the early settlement in the 1820s, they operated with some of these ideas.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did Ricardian ideas say about the landowner’s claim and the surplus?
cards.back: According to Ricardian ideas, a landowner should have a claim only to the “average rent” that prevailed at a given time. When the land yielded more than this “average rent”, the landowner had a surplus that the state needed to tax.
cards.quote: According to Ricardian ideas, a landowner should have a claim only to the “average rent” that prevailed at a given time. When the land yielded more than this “average rent”, the landowner had a surplus that the state needed to tax.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What is a rentier?
cards.back: Rentier is a term used to designate people who live on rental income from property.
cards.quote: Rentier is a term used to designate people who live on rental income from property.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the ryotwari settlement of the Bombay Deccan work?
cards.back: Unlike the Bengal system, the revenue was directly settled with the ryot. The average income from different types of soil was estimated, the revenue-paying capacity of the ryot was assessed and a proportion of it fixed as the share of the state. The lands were resurveyed every 30 years and the revenue rates increased. Therefore the revenue demand was no longer permanent.
cards.quote: Unlike the Bengal system, the revenue was directly settled with the ryot. The average income from different types of soil was estimated, the revenue-paying capacity of the ryot was assessed and a proportion of it fixed as the share of the state. The lands were resurveyed every 30 years and the revenue rates increased. Therefore the revenue demand was no longer permanent.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What happened after the first revenue settlement in the Bombay Deccan in the 1820s?
cards.back: The first revenue settlement in the Bombay Deccan was made in the 1820s. The revenue that was demanded was so high that in many places peasants deserted their villages and migrated to new regions.
cards.quote: The first revenue settlement in the Bombay Deccan was made in the 1820s. The revenue that was demanded was so high that in many places peasants deserted their villages and migrated to new regions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When someone failed to pay, his ____ were seized and a ____ was imposed on the whole village.
cards.back: When someone failed to pay, his crops were seized and a fine was imposed on the whole village.
cards.quote: When someone failed to pay, his crops were seized and a fine was imposed on the whole village.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Prices of agricultural products fell sharply after ____ and did not recover for over a decade and a half.
cards.back: Prices of agricultural products fell sharply after 1832 and did not recover for over a decade and a half.
cards.quote: Prices of agricultural products fell sharply after 1832 and did not recover for over a decade and a half.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was the toll of the 1832-34 famine in the Deccan?
cards.back: At the same time the countryside was devastated by a famine that struck in the years 1832-34. One-third of the cattle of the Deccan were killed, and half the human population died.
cards.quote: At the same time the countryside was devastated by a famine that struck in the years 1832-34. One-third of the cattle of the Deccan were killed, and half the human population died.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Inevitably, they borrowed. Revenue could rarely be paid without a loan from a ____.
cards.back: Inevitably, they borrowed. Revenue could rarely be paid without a loan from a moneylender.
cards.quote: Inevitably, they borrowed. Revenue could rarely be paid without a loan from a moneylender.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: By the 1840s, officials were finding evidence of alarming levels of peasant ____ everywhere.
cards.back: By the 1840s, officials were finding evidence of alarming levels of peasant indebtedness everywhere.
cards.quote: By the 1840s, officials were finding evidence of alarming levels of peasant indebtedness everywhere.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the revenue demand and agricultural prices change after the mid-1840s?
cards.back: So the revenue demand was moderated to encourage peasants to expand cultivation. After 1845 agricultural prices recovered steadily.
cards.quote: So the revenue demand was moderated to encourage peasants to expand cultivation. After 1845 agricultural prices recovered steadily.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Before the 1860s, ____ of raw cotton imports into Britain came from America.
cards.back: Before the 1860s, three-fourths of raw cotton imports into Britain came from America.
cards.quote: Before the 1860s, three-fourths of raw cotton imports into Britain came from America.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why was India seen as a source of cotton for Lancashire? Name its three advantages.
cards.back:
suitable soil
a climate favourable to cotton cultivation
cheap labour
cards.quote: India was seen as a country that could supply cotton to Lancashire if the American supply dried up. It possessed suitable soil, a climate favourable to cotton cultivation, and cheap labour.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the American Civil War affect raw cotton imports into Britain from America?
cards.back: When the American Civil War broke out in 1861, a wave of panic spread through cotton circles in Britain. Raw cotton imports from America fell to less than three per cent of the normal: from over 2,000,000 bales (of 400 lbs each) in 1861 to 55,000 bales in 1862.
cards.quote: When the American Civil War broke out in 1861, a wave of panic spread through cotton circles in Britain. Raw cotton imports from America fell to less than three per cent of the normal: from over 2,000,000 bales (of 400 lbs each) in 1861 to 55,000 bales in 1862.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How much advance were Deccan ryots given for every acre they planted with cotton?
cards.back: The ryots in the Deccan villages suddenly found access to seemingly limitless credit. They were being given Rs 100 as advance for every acre they planted with cotton. Sahukars were more than willing to extend long-term loans.
cards.quote: The ryots in the Deccan villages suddenly found access to seemingly limitless credit. They were being given Rs 100 as advance for every acre they planted with cotton. Sahukars were more than willing to extend long-term loans.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What happened to cotton acreage in the Bombay Deccan between 1860 and 1864?
cards.back: Between 1860 and 1864 cotton acreage doubled. By 1862 over 90 per cent of cotton imports into Britain were coming from India.
cards.quote: Between 1860 and 1864 cotton acreage doubled. By 1862 over 90 per cent of cotton imports into Britain were coming from India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did cotton expansion mean for the large majority of cotton producers in the Bombay Deccan?
cards.back: But these boom years did not bring prosperity to all cotton producers. Some rich peasants did gain, but for the large majority, cotton expansion meant heavier debt.
cards.quote: But these boom years did not bring prosperity to all cotton producers. Some rich peasants did gain, but for the large majority, cotton expansion meant heavier debt.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What happened to Indian cotton exports to Britain as the American Civil War ended?
cards.back: As the Civil War ended, cotton production in America revived and Indian cotton exports to Britain steadily declined.
cards.quote: As the Civil War ended, cotton production in America revived and Indian cotton exports to Britain steadily declined.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: After the first Bombay Deccan revenue settlement, by how much did the new settlement raise the demand?
cards.back: Now it was time for the next. And in the new settlement, the demand was increased dramatically: from 50 to 100 per cent.
cards.quote: Now it was time for the next. And in the new settlement, the demand was increased dramatically: from 50 to 100 per cent.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What customary norm limited the interest a moneylender could charge, and what happened to it?
cards.back: One general norm was that the interest charged could not be more than the principal. This was meant to limit the moneylender’s exactions and defined what could be counted as “fair interest”. Under colonial rule this norm broke down.
cards.quote: One general norm was that the interest charged could not be more than the principal. This was meant to limit the moneylender’s exactions and defined what could be counted as “fair interest”. Under colonial rule this norm broke down.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How much interest did a moneylender charge on a Rs 100 loan in one Deccan Riots Commission case?
cards.back: In one of the many cases investigated by the Deccan Riots Commission, the moneylender had charged over Rs 2,000 as interest on a loan of Rs 100.
cards.quote: In one of the many cases investigated by the Deccan Riots Commission, the moneylender had charged over Rs 2,000 as interest on a loan of Rs 100.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was the deed of hire a debt-ridden peasant had to sign?
cards.back: So he took land on rent and animals on hire. He now had to pay for the animals which had originally belonged to him. He had to sign a deed of hire stating very clearly that these animals and carts did not belong to him. In cases of conflict, these deeds could be enforced through the court.
cards.quote: So he took land on rent and animals on hire. He now had to pay for the animals which had originally belonged to him. He had to sign a deed of hire stating very clearly that these animals and carts did not belong to him. In cases of conflict, these deeds could be enforced through the court.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the Limitation Law of 1859 say, and what was it meant to check?
cards.back: In 1859 the British passed a Limitation Law that stated that the loan bonds signed between moneylenders and ryots would have validity for only three years. This law was meant to check the accumulation of interest over time.
cards.quote: In 1859 the British passed a Limitation Law that stated that the loan bonds signed between moneylenders and ryots would have validity for only three years. This law was meant to check the accumulation of interest over time.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did moneylenders turn the three-year Limitation Law around?
cards.back: forcing the ryot to sign a new bond every three years. When a new bond was signed, the unpaid balance – that is, the original loan and the accumulated interest – was entered as the principal on which a new set of interest charges was calculated.
cards.quote: forcing the ryot to sign a new bond every three years. When a new bond was signed, the unpaid balance – that is, the original loan and the accumulated interest – was entered as the principal on which a new set of interest charges was calculated.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Name the means moneylenders used to short-change the ryot.
cards.back:
refused to give receipts when loans were repaid
entered fictitious figures in bonds
acquired the peasants’ harvest at low prices
ultimately took over peasants’ property
cards.quote: they refused to give receipts when loans were repaid, entered fictitious figures in bonds, acquired the peasants’ harvest at low prices, and ultimately took over peasants’ property.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the British believe about how the terms of transactions had to be stated?
cards.back: The British, however, were suspicious of transactions based on informal understanding, as was common in the past. The terms of transactions, they believed, had to be clearly, unambiguously and categorically stated in contracts, deeds and bonds, and regulated by law.
cards.quote: The British, however, were suspicious of transactions based on informal understanding, as was common in the past. The terms of transactions, they believed, had to be clearly, unambiguously and categorically stated in contracts, deeds and bonds, and regulated by law.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Over time, what did Deccan peasants come to associate the misery of their lives with?
cards.back: Over time, peasants came to associate the misery of their lives with the new regime of bonds and deeds.
cards.quote: Over time, peasants came to associate the misery of their lives with the new regime of bonds and deeds.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why was the Deccan Riots Commission set up, and when did its report reach Parliament?
cards.back: When the revolt spread in the Deccan, the Government of Bombay was initially unwilling to see it as anything serious. But the Government of India, worried by the memory of 1857, pressurised the Government of Bombay to set up a commission of enquiry to investigate into the causes of the riots. The commission produced a report that was presented to the British Parliament in 1878.
cards.quote: When the revolt spread in the Deccan, the Government of Bombay was initially unwilling to see it as anything serious. But the Government of India, worried by the memory of 1857, pressurised the Government of Bombay to set up a commission of enquiry to investigate into the causes of the riots. The commission produced a report that was presented to the British Parliament in 1878.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the Deccan Riots Commission conclude about the cause of peasant anger?
cards.back: The Deccan Riots Commission, for instance, was specifically asked to judge whether the level of government revenue demand was the cause of the revolt. And after presenting all the evidence, the commission reported that the government demand was not the cause of peasant anger. It was the moneylenders who were to blame.
cards.quote: The Deccan Riots Commission, for instance, was specifically asked to judge whether the level of government revenue demand was the cause of the revolt. And after presenting all the evidence, the commission reported that the government demand was not the cause of peasant anger. It was the moneylenders who were to blame.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What persistent reluctance of the colonial government did the “blame the moneylenders” argument show?
cards.back: This shows that there was a persistent reluctance on the part of the colonial government to admit that popular discontent was ever on account of government action.
cards.quote: It was the moneylenders who were to blame. This argument is found very frequently in colonial records. This shows that there was a persistent reluctance on the part of the colonial government to admit that popular discontent was ever on account of government action.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How should official reports be used as sources for history?
cards.back: Official reports, thus, are invaluable sources for the reconstruction of history. But they have to be always read with care and juxtaposed with evidence culled from newspapers, unofficial accounts, legal records and, where possible, oral sources.
cards.quote: Official reports, thus, are invaluable sources for the reconstruction of history. But they have to be always read with care and juxtaposed with evidence culled from newspapers, unofficial accounts, legal records and, where possible, oral sources.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline of the chapter: what happened in 1765?
cards.back: English East India Company acquires Diwani of Bengal
cards.quote: English East India Company acquires Diwani of Bengal

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline of the chapter: what happened in 1773?
cards.back: Regulating Act passed by the British Parliament to regulate the activities of the East India Company
cards.quote: Regulating Act passed by the British Parliament to regulate the activities of the East India Company

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline of the chapter: what happened in 1793?
cards.back: Permanent Settlement in Bengal
cards.quote: Permanent Settlement in Bengal

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline of the chapter: what happened in 1800s?
cards.back: Santhals begin to come to the Rajmahal hills and settle there
cards.quote: Santhals begin to come to the Rajmahal hills and settle there

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: According to the chapter timeline, in which decade did agricultural prices begin to fall?
cards.back: 1820s Agricultural prices begin to fall
cards.quote: 1820s Agricultural prices begin to fall

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline of the chapter: what happened in 1840s-50s?
cards.back: A slow process of agrarian expansion in the Bombay Deccan
cards.quote: A slow process of agrarian expansion in the Bombay Deccan

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: According to the chapter timeline, in which year did the cotton boom begin?
cards.back: 1861 Cotton boom begins
cards.quote: 1861 Cotton boom begins

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline of the chapter: what happened in 1875?
cards.back: Ryots in Deccan villages rebel
cards.quote: Ryots in Deccan villages rebel

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When did the Indian Constitution come into effect, and what is its distinction?
cards.back: The Indian Constitution, which came into effect on 26 January 1950, has the dubious distinction of being the longest in the world.
cards.quote: The Indian Constitution, which came into effect on 26 January 1950, has the dubious distinction of being the longest in the world.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Between which months and years was the Constitution of India framed?
cards.back: The Constitution of India was framed between December 1946 and November 1949.
cards.quote: The Constitution of India was framed between December 1946 and November 1949.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: At Independence, India was not merely large and diverse, but also ____.
cards.back: At Independence, India was not merely large and diverse, but also deeply divided.
cards.quote: At Independence, India was not merely large and diverse, but also deeply divided.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How many sessions did the Constituent Assembly hold, and over how many days did its sittings spread?
cards.back: held eleven sessions, with sittings spread over 165 days.
cards.quote: held eleven sessions, with sittings spread over 165 days.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What had happened to India on 15 August 1947?
cards.back: On 15 August 1947, India had been made free, but it had also been divided.
cards.quote: On 15 August 1947, India had been made free, but it had also been divided.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which upsurge of spring 1946 evoked popular sympathy just before the Constitution was made?
cards.back: An even more recent upsurge had also evoked much popular sympathy – this was the rising of the ratings of the Royal Indian Navy in Bombay and other cities in the spring of 1946.
cards.quote: An even more recent upsurge had also evoked much popular sympathy – this was the rising of the ratings of the Royal Indian Navy in Bombay and other cities in the spring of 1946.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: One striking feature of these popular upsurges was the degree of ____ they manifested.
cards.back: One striking feature of these popular upsurges was the degree of Hindu-Muslim unity they manifested.
cards.quote: One striking feature of these popular upsurges was the degree of Hindu-Muslim unity they manifested.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: The ____ of August 1946 began a year of almost continuous rioting across northern and eastern India (see Chapter 11).
cards.back: The Great Calcutta Killings of August 1946 began a year of almost continuous rioting across northern and eastern India (see Chapter 11).
cards.quote: The Great Calcutta Killings of August 1946 began a year of almost continuous rioting across northern and eastern India (see Chapter 11).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What share of the subcontinent was under nawabs and maharajas during the Raj, and what was their status?
cards.back: During the period of the Raj, approximately one-third of the area of the subcontinent was under the control of nawabs and maharajas who owed allegiance to the British Crown, but were otherwise left mostly free to rule – or misrule – their territory as they wished.
cards.quote: During the period of the Raj, approximately one-third of the area of the subcontinent was under the control of nawabs and maharajas who owed allegiance to the British Crown, but were otherwise left mostly free to rule – or misrule – their territory as they wished.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When the British left India, the constitutional status of these princes remained ____.
cards.back: When the British left India, the constitutional status of these princes remained ambiguous.
cards.quote: When the British left India, the constitutional status of these princes remained ambiguous.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Long years ago we made a ____, and now the time comes when we shall redeem our pledge, not wholly or in full measure, but very substantially.
cards.back: Long years ago we made a tryst with destiny, and now the time comes when we shall redeem our pledge, not wholly or in full measure, but very substantially.
cards.quote: Long years ago we made a tryst with destiny, and now the time comes when we shall redeem our pledge, not wholly or in full measure, but very substantially.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.note: Nehru’s speech in the Constituent Assembly at midnight on 14 August 1947 (Fig. 12.3).

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Was the Constituent Assembly elected on the basis of universal franchise?
cards.back: The members of the Constituent Assembly were not elected on the basis of universal franchise.
cards.quote: The members of the Constituent Assembly were not elected on the basis of universal franchise.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.1 The making of the Constituent Assembly

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How were the representatives to the Constituent Assembly chosen?
cards.back: In the winter of 1945-46 provincial elections were held in India. The Provincial Legislatures then chose the representatives to the Constituent Assembly.
cards.quote: In the winter of 1945-46 provincial elections were held in India. The Provincial Legislatures then chose the representatives to the Constituent Assembly.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.1 The making of the Constituent Assembly

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which party dominated the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: The Constituent Assembly that came into being was dominated by one party: the Congress.
cards.quote: The Constituent Assembly that came into being was dominated by one party: the Congress.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.1 The making of the Constituent Assembly

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which seats did the Congress and the Muslim League win in the provincial elections?
cards.back: Congress swept the general seats in the provincial elections, and the Muslim League captured most of the reserved Muslim seats.
cards.quote: Congress swept the general seats in the provincial elections, and the Muslim League captured most of the reserved Muslim seats.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.1 The making of the Constituent Assembly

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the Muslim League do about the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: But the League chose to boycott the Constituent Assembly, pressing its demand for Pakistan with a separate constitution.
cards.quote: But the League chose to boycott the Constituent Assembly, pressing its demand for Pakistan with a separate constitution.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.1 The making of the Constituent Assembly

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why were the Socialists initially unwilling to join the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: The Socialists too were initially unwilling to join, for they believed the Constituent Assembly was a creation of the British, and therefore incapable of being truly autonomous.
cards.quote: The Socialists too were initially unwilling to join, for they believed the Constituent Assembly was a creation of the British, and therefore incapable of being truly autonomous.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.1 The making of the Constituent Assembly

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What share of the members of the Constituent Assembly were also members of the Congress?
cards.back: In effect, therefore, 82 per cent of the members of the Constituent Assembly were also members of the Congress.
cards.quote: In effect, therefore, 82 per cent of the members of the Constituent Assembly were also members of the Congress.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.1 The making of the Constituent Assembly

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: The Congress however was not a party with ____.
cards.back: The Congress however was not a party with one voice.
cards.quote: The Congress however was not a party with one voice.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.1 The making of the Constituent Assembly

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What two differences of opinion divided Congress members in the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: Some members were inspired by socialism while others were defenders of landlordism. Some were close to communal parties while others were assertively secular.
cards.quote: Some members were inspired by socialism while others were defenders of landlordism. Some were close to communal parties while others were assertively secular.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.1 The making of the Constituent Assembly

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did public opinion influence the discussions within the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: The discussions within the Constituent Assembly were also influenced by the opinions expressed by the public. As the deliberations continued, the arguments were reported in newspapers, and the proposals were publicly debated.
cards.quote: The discussions within the Constituent Assembly were also influenced by the opinions expressed by the public. As the deliberations continued, the arguments were reported in newspapers, and the proposals were publicly debated.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.1 The making of the Constituent Assembly

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was the public asked to do to create a sense of collective participation?
cards.back: In order to create a sense of collective participation the public was also asked to send in their views on what needed to be done.
cards.quote: In order to create a sense of collective participation the public was also asked to send in their views on what needed to be done.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.1 The making of the Constituent Assembly

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did linguistic minorities, religious minorities and dalits demand in the public discussions?
cards.back:
Many of the linguistic minorities wanted the protection of their mother tongue
religious minorities asked for special safeguards
dalits demanded an end to all caste oppression and reservation of seats in government bodies
cards.quote: Many of the linguistic minorities wanted the protection of their mother tongue, religious minorities asked for special safeguards, while dalits demanded an end to all caste oppression and reservation of seats in government bodies.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.1 The making of the Constituent Assembly

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who was the president of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: Bhimrao Ambedkar
cards.quote: Drafting Committee Bhimrao Ambedkar

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: Important Committees of the Constituent Assembly and Presidents

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who was the president of the Steering Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: Rajendra Prasad
cards.quote: Steering Committee Rajendra Prasad

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: Important Committees of the Constituent Assembly and Presidents

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who was the president of the Flag Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: J. B. Kripalani
cards.quote: Flag Committee J. B. Kripalani

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: Important Committees of the Constituent Assembly and Presidents

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who was the president of the Advisory Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
cards.quote: Advisory Committee Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: Important Committees of the Constituent Assembly and Presidents

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who was the president of the Union Power Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru
cards.quote: Union Power Committee Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: Important Committees of the Constituent Assembly and Presidents

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How many members did the Constituent Assembly have, and how many played particularly important roles?
cards.back: The Constituent Assembly had 300 members. Of these, six members played particularly important roles.
cards.quote: The Constituent Assembly had 300 members. Of these, six members played particularly important roles.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which three Congress representatives were among the six dominant members of the Assembly?
cards.back: Three were representatives of the Congress, namely, Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabh Bhai Patel and Rajendra Prasad.
cards.quote: Three were representatives of the Congress, namely, Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabh Bhai Patel and Rajendra Prasad.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which two crucial resolutions did Nehru move in the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: It was Nehru who moved the crucial “Objectives Resolution”, as well as the resolution proposing that the National Flag of India be a “horizontal tricolour of saffron, white and dark green in equal proportion”, with a wheel in navy blue at the centre.
cards.quote: It was Nehru who moved the crucial “Objectives Resolution”, as well as the resolution proposing that the National Flag of India be a “horizontal tricolour of saffron, white and dark green in equal proportion”, with a wheel in navy blue at the centre.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What role did Patel play in the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: Patel, on the other hand, worked mostly behind the scenes, playing a key role in the drafting of several reports, and working to reconcile opposing points of view.
cards.quote: Patel, on the other hand, worked mostly behind the scenes, playing a key role in the drafting of several reports, and working to reconcile opposing points of view.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was Rajendra Prasad’s role in the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: Rajendra Prasad’s role was as President of the Assembly, where he had to steer the discussion along constructive lines while making sure all members had a chance to speak.
cards.quote: Rajendra Prasad’s role was as President of the Assembly, where he had to steer the discussion along constructive lines while making sure all members had a chance to speak.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did B. R. Ambedkar, once a political opponent of the Congress, come to chair the Drafting Committee?
cards.back: During the period of British rule, Ambedkar had been a political opponent of the Congress; but, on the advice of Mahatma Gandhi, he was asked at Independence to join the Union Cabinet as law minister. In this capacity, he served as Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution.
cards.quote: During the period of British rule, Ambedkar had been a political opponent of the Congress; but, on the advice of Mahatma Gandhi, he was asked at Independence to join the Union Cabinet as law minister. In this capacity, he served as Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which two lawyers served with Ambedkar and gave crucial inputs in drafting the Constitution?
cards.back: Serving with him were two other lawyers, K.M. Munshi from Gujarat and Alladi Krishnaswamy Aiyar from Madras, both of whom gave crucial inputs in the drafting of the Constitution.
cards.quote: Serving with him were two other lawyers, K.M. Munshi from Gujarat and Alladi Krishnaswamy Aiyar from Madras, both of whom gave crucial inputs in the drafting of the Constitution.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who was B. N. Rau, and what did he prepare?
cards.back: One was B. N. Rau, Constitutional Advisor to the Government of India, who prepared a series of background papers based on a close study of the political systems obtaining in other countries.
cards.quote: One was B. N. Rau, Constitutional Advisor to the Government of India, who prepared a series of background papers based on a close study of the political systems obtaining in other countries.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who was the Chief Draughtsman of the Constituent Assembly, and what could he do?
cards.back: The other was the Chief Draughtsman, S. N. Mukherjee, who had the ability to put complex proposals in clear legal language.
cards.quote: The other was the Chief Draughtsman, S. N. Mukherjee, who had the ability to put complex proposals in clear legal language.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who guided the Draft Constitution through the Assembly, and how long did it take?
cards.back: Ambedkar himself had the responsibility of guiding the Draft Constitution through the Assembly. This took three years in all, with the printed record of the discussions taking up eleven bulky volumes.
cards.quote: Ambedkar himself had the responsibility of guiding the Draft Constitution through the Assembly. This took three years in all, with the printed record of the discussions taking up eleven bulky volumes.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When did Jawaharlal Nehru introduce the “Objectives Resolution” in the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: On 13 December 1946, Jawaharlal Nehru introduced the “Objectives Resolution” in the Constituent Assembly.
cards.quote: On 13 December 1946, Jawaharlal Nehru introduced the “Objectives Resolution” in the Constituent Assembly.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was the Objectives Resolution (13 December 1946)?
cards.back: It was a momentous resolution that outlined the defining ideals of the Constitution of Independent India, and provided the framework within which the work of constitution-making was to proceed.
cards.quote: It was a momentous resolution that outlined the defining ideals of the Constitution of Independent India, and provided the framework within which the work of constitution-making was to proceed.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the Objectives Resolution proclaim and guarantee? (three points)
cards.back:
proclaimed India to be an “Independent Sovereign Republic”
guaranteed its citizens justice, equality and freedom
assured that “adequate safeguards shall be provided for minorities, backward and tribal areas, and Depressed and Other Backward Classes
cards.quote: It proclaimed India to be an “Independent Sovereign Republic”, guaranteed its citizens justice, equality and freedom, and assured that “adequate safeguards shall be provided for minorities, backward and tribal areas, and Depressed and Other Backward Classes

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: We say that it is our firm and solemn resolve to have an ____.
cards.back: We say that it is our firm and solemn resolve to have an independent sovereign republic.
cards.quote: We say that it is our firm and solemn resolve to have an independent sovereign republic.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.note: Nehru’s speech of 13 December 1946 (Source 1).

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: We are not going just to ____, I hope, a certain democratic procedure or an institution of a so-called democratic country. We may improve upon it.
cards.back: We are not going just to copy, I hope, a certain democratic procedure or an institution of a so-called democratic country. We may improve upon it.
cards.quote: We are not going just to copy, I hope, a certain democratic procedure or an institution of a so-called democratic country. We may improve upon it.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.note: Nehru, 13 December 1946 (Source 1): India will not merely copy other democracies.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did Nehru say the word “democratic” was left out of the Objectives Resolution?
cards.back: we thought it is obvious that the word “republic” contains that word and we did not want to use unnecessary words and redundant words
cards.quote: we thought it is obvious that the word “republic” contains that word and we did not want to use unnecessary words and redundant words

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.note: Nehru, Source 1: the Resolution gave the content of democracy, including economic democracy.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was Nehru doing by referring to the American and French Revolutions?
cards.back: In returning to the past and referring to the American and French Revolutions, Nehru was locating the history of constitution-making in India within a longer history of struggle for liberty and freedom.
cards.quote: In returning to the past and referring to the American and French Revolutions, Nehru was locating the history of constitution-making in India within a longer history of struggle for liberty and freedom.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Did Nehru suggest the ideas of earlier revolutions could be mechanically borrowed for India?
cards.back: But Nehru was not suggesting that those events were to provide any blueprint for the present; or that the ideas of those revolutions could be mechanically borrowed and applied in India.
cards.quote: But Nehru was not suggesting that those events were to provide any blueprint for the present; or that the ideas of those revolutions could be mechanically borrowed and applied in India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What would be the objective of the Indian Constitution, as NCERT reads Nehru’s speech?
cards.back: The objective of the Indian Constitution would be to fuse the liberal ideas of democracy with the socialist idea of economic justice, and re-adapt and re-work all these ideas within the Indian context.
cards.quote: The objective of the Indian Constitution would be to fuse the liberal ideas of democracy with the socialist idea of economic justice, and re-adapt and re-work all these ideas within the Indian context.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: The system of government established in India, he declared, had to “fit in with the ____ and be acceptable to them”.
cards.back: The system of government established in India, he declared, had to “fit in with the temper of our people and be acceptable to them”.
cards.quote: The system of government established in India, he declared, had to “fit in with the temper of our people and be acceptable to them”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which Communist member saw the dark hand of British imperialism over the Assembly’s deliberations?
cards.back: A Communist member, Somnath Lahiri saw the dark hand of British imperialism hanging over the deliberations of the Constituent Assembly.
cards.quote: A Communist member, Somnath Lahiri saw the dark hand of British imperialism hanging over the deliberations of the Constituent Assembly.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Under whose direction could the Nehru-headed interim administration operate in winter 1946-47?
cards.back: An interim administration headed by Jawaharlal Nehru was in place, but it could only operate under the directions of the Viceroy and the British Government in London.
cards.quote: An interim administration headed by Jawaharlal Nehru was in place, but it could only operate under the directions of the Viceroy and the British Government in London.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who said the Constituent Assembly was “working the British plans as the British should like it to be worked out”?
cards.back: Lahiri exhorted his colleagues to realise that the Constituent Assembly was British-made and was “working the British plans as the British should like it to be worked out”.
cards.quote: Lahiri exhorted his colleagues to realise that the Constituent Assembly was British-made and was “working the British plans as the British should like it to be worked out”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Governments do not come into being by State Papers. Governments are, in fact the expression of the ____.
cards.back: Governments do not come into being by State Papers. Governments are, in fact the expression of the will of the people.
cards.quote: Governments do not come into being by State Papers. Governments are, in fact the expression of the will of the people.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.note: Nehru’s reply to the charge that the Assembly was British-made.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which Acts gradually enlarged the space for Indian participation in provincial governments?
cards.back: A number of Acts were passed (1909, 1919 and 1935), gradually enlarging the space for Indian participation in provincial governments.
cards.quote: A number of Acts were passed (1909, 1919 and 1935), gradually enlarging the space for Indian participation in provincial governments.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When was the provincial executive made partly, and then almost entirely, responsible to the legislature?
cards.back: The executive was made partly responsible to the provincial legislature in 1919, and almost entirely so under the Government of India Act of 1935.
cards.quote: The executive was made partly responsible to the provincial legislature in 1919, and almost entirely so under the Government of India Act of 1935.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: In the 1937 elections under the 1935 Act, in how many provinces did the Congress come to power?
cards.back: When elections were held in 1937, under the 1935 Act, the Congress came to power in eight out of the 11 provinces.
cards.quote: When elections were held in 1937, under the 1935 Act, the Congress came to power in eight out of the 11 provinces.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How much of the adult population could vote even in 1935?
cards.back: The electorate that elected the provincial bodies had expanded over the years, but even in 1935 it remained limited to no more than 10 to 15 per cent of the adult population: there was no universal adult franchise.
