cards.quote: The electorate that elected the provincial bodies had expanded over the years, but even in 1935 it remained limited to no more than 10 to 15 per cent of the adult population: there was no universal adult franchise.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: To whom were the legislatures elected under the 1935 Act responsible?
cards.back: The legislatures elected under the 1935 Act operated within the framework of colonial rule, and were responsible to the Governor appointed by the British.
cards.quote: The legislatures elected under the 1935 Act operated within the framework of colonial rule, and were responsible to the Governor appointed by the British.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was the vision Nehru outlined on 13 December 1946?
cards.back: The vision that Nehru was trying to outline on 13 December 1946 was of the Constitution of an independent, sovereign Republic of India.
cards.quote: The vision that Nehru was trying to outline on 13 December 1946 was of the Constitution of an independent, sovereign Republic of India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who made a powerful plea on 27 August 1947 for continuing separate electorates?
cards.back: On 27 August 1947, B. Pocker Bahadur from Madras made a powerful plea for continuing separate electorates.
cards.quote: On 27 August 1947, B. Pocker Bahadur from Madras made a powerful plea for continuing separate electorates.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did Bahadur say separate electorates were needed?
cards.back: Only separate electorates would ensure that Muslims had a meaningful voice in the governance of the country.
cards.quote: Only separate electorates would ensure that Muslims had a meaningful voice in the governance of the country.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did most nationalists see separate electorates?
cards.back: Most nationalists saw separate electorates as a measure deliberately introduced by the British to divide the people.
cards.quote: Most nationalists saw separate electorates as a measure deliberately introduced by the British to divide the people.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who told Bahadur that “The English played their game under the cover of safeguards”?
cards.back: “The English played their game under the cover of safeguards,” R.V. Dhulekar told Bahadur.
cards.quote: “The English played their game under the cover of safeguards,” R.V. Dhulekar told Bahadur.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What made nationalists fervently opposed to separate electorates?
cards.back: Partition had made nationalists fervently opposed to the idea of separate electorates.
cards.quote: Partition had made nationalists fervently opposed to the idea of separate electorates.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who called separate electorates a “poison that has entered the body politic of our country”?
cards.back: Separate electorates was a “poison that has entered the body politic of our country”, declared Sardar Patel.
cards.quote: Separate electorates was a “poison that has entered the body politic of our country”, declared Sardar Patel.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: The British element is gone, but they have left the ____ behind.
cards.back: The British element is gone, but they have left the mischief behind.
cards.quote: The British element is gone, but they have left the mischief behind.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.note: Sardar Patel, Source 3, on separate electorates.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who argued that separate electorates were harmful for the nation and also for the minorities?
cards.back: Countering the demand for separate electorates, Govind Ballabh Pant declared that it was not only harmful for the nation but also for the minorities.
cards.quote: Countering the demand for separate electorates, Govind Ballabh Pant declared that it was not only harmful for the nation but also for the minorities.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did Pant call separate electorates a suicidal demand?
cards.back: It was a suicidal demand, he argued, that would permanently isolate the minorities, make them vulnerable, and deprive them of any effective say within the government.
cards.quote: It was a suicidal demand, he argued, that would permanently isolate the minorities, make them vulnerable, and deprive them of any effective say within the government.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: There cannot be any ____. All loyalties must exclusively be centred round the State.
cards.back: There cannot be any divided loyalty. All loyalties must exclusively be centred round the State.
cards.quote: There cannot be any divided loyalty. All loyalties must exclusively be centred round the State.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.note: G. B. Pant, Source 5: what a loyal citizen of the State owes.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who deplored “thinking always in terms of communities and never in terms of citizens”?
cards.back: “There is the unwholesome and to some extent degrading habit of thinking always in terms of communities and never in terms of citizens,” said Pant.
cards.quote: “There is the unwholesome and to some extent degrading habit of thinking always in terms of communities and never in terms of citizens,” said Pant.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Let us remember that it is the citizen that must count. It is the citizen that forms the base as well as the summit of the ____.
cards.back: Let us remember that it is the citizen that must count. It is the citizen that forms the base as well as the summit of the social pyramid.
cards.quote: Let us remember that it is the citizen that must count. It is the citizen that forms the base as well as the summit of the social pyramid.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.note: G. B. Pant on the citizen.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What could communities be recognised as, and what must members of all communities do politically?
cards.back: Communities could be recognised as cultural entities and assured cultural rights. Politically, however, members of all communities had to act as equal members of one State, or else there would be divided loyalties.
cards.quote: Communities could be recognised as cultural entities and assured cultural rights. Politically, however, members of all communities had to act as equal members of one State, or else there would be divided loyalties.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which Muslim member felt separate electorates were self-destructive?
cards.back: Not all Muslims supported the demand for separate electorates. Begum Aizaas Rasul, for instance, felt that separate electorates were self-destructive since they isolated the minorities from the majority.
cards.quote: Not all Muslims supported the demand for separate electorates. Begum Aizaas Rasul, for instance, felt that separate electorates were self-destructive since they isolated the minorities from the majority.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did most Muslim members of the Assembly agree by 1949?
cards.back: By 1949, most Muslim members of the Constituent Assembly were agreed that separate electorates were against the interests of the minorities.
cards.quote: By 1949, most Muslim members of the Constituent Assembly were agreed that separate electorates were against the interests of the minorities.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who urged that the term “minorities” be read in economic terms?
cards.back: While welcoming the Objectives Resolution, N.G. Ranga, a socialist who had been a leader of the peasant movement, urged that the term minorities be interpreted in economic terms.
cards.quote: While welcoming the Objectives Resolution, N.G. Ranga, a socialist who had been a leader of the peasant movement, urged that the term minorities be interpreted in economic terms.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.2 “We will need much more than this Resolution”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who were the real minorities for Ranga?
cards.back: The real minorities for Ranga were the poor and the downtrodden.
cards.quote: The real minorities for Ranga were the poor and the downtrodden.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.2 “We will need much more than this Resolution”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who said, “They need props. They need a ladder”?
cards.back: “They need props. They need a ladder,” said Ranga.
cards.quote: “They need props. They need a ladder,” said Ranga.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.2 “We will need much more than this Resolution”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: No, the real minorities are the ____ of this country.
cards.back: No, the real minorities are the masses of this country.
cards.quote: No, the real minorities are the masses of this country.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.2 “We will need much more than this Resolution”

cards.note: N. G. Ranga, Source 6.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which gifted orator was among the tribal representatives in the Assembly?
cards.back: One of the groups mentioned by Ranga, the tribals, had among its representatives to the Assembly the gifted orator Jaipal Singh.
cards.quote: One of the groups mentioned by Ranga, the tribals, had among its representatives to the Assembly the gifted orator Jaipal Singh.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.2 “We will need much more than this Resolution”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did Jaipal Singh argue about tribes and protection?
cards.back: Tribes were not a numerical minority, he argued, but they needed protection.
cards.quote: Tribes were not a numerical minority, he argued, but they needed protection.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.2 “We will need much more than this Resolution”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did Jaipal Singh feel was essential for tribals, though he did not ask for separate electorates?
cards.back: Singh was not asking for separate electorates, but he felt that reservation of seats in the legislature was essential to allow tribals to represent themselves.
cards.quote: Singh was not asking for separate electorates, but he felt that reservation of seats in the legislature was essential to allow tribals to represent themselves.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.2 “We will need much more than this Resolution”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What had Ambedkar demanded for the Depressed Castes, and why did Gandhi oppose it?
cards.back: During the national movement Ambedkar had demanded separate electorates for the Depressed Castes, and Mahatma Gandhi had opposed it, arguing that this would permanently segregate them from the rest of society.
cards.quote: During the national movement Ambedkar had demanded separate electorates for the Depressed Castes, and Mahatma Gandhi had opposed it, arguing that this would permanently segregate them from the rest of society.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.3 “We were suppressed for thousands of years”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who said, “We have been suffering, but we are prepared to suffer no more”?
cards.back: “We have been suffering, but we are prepared to suffer no more,” said J. Nagappa from Madras.
cards.quote: “We have been suffering, but we are prepared to suffer no more,” said J. Nagappa from Madras.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.3 “We were suppressed for thousands of years”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What share of the population did the Depressed Castes form, according to Nagappa?
cards.back: Nagappa pointed out that numerically the Depressed Castes were not a minority: they formed between 20 and 25 per cent of the total population.
cards.quote: Nagappa pointed out that numerically the Depressed Castes were not a minority: they formed between 20 and 25 per cent of the total population.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.3 “We were suppressed for thousands of years”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did Nagappa say caused the suffering of the Depressed Castes?
cards.back: Their suffering was due to their systematic marginalisation, not their numerical insignificance.
cards.quote: Their suffering was due to their systematic marginalisation, not their numerical insignificance.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.3 “We were suppressed for thousands of years”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who said: 'What we want is not all kinds of safeguards. It is the moral safeguard which gives protection to the underdogs'?
cards.back: Dakshayani Velayudhan from Madras, argued: What we want is not all kinds of safeguards. It is the moral safeguard which gives protection to the underdogs of this country
cards.quote: Dakshayani Velayudhan from Madras, argued: What we want is not all kinds of safeguards. It is the moral safeguard which gives protection to the underdogs of this country

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.3 “We were suppressed for thousands of years”

cards.note: Dakshayani Velayudhan of Madras, in the Constituent Assembly.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did Ambedkar do after the Partition violence about separate electorates?
cards.back: After the Partition violence, Ambedkar too no longer argued for separate electorates.
cards.quote: After the Partition violence, Ambedkar too no longer argued for separate electorates.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.3 “We were suppressed for thousands of years”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the Constituent Assembly finally recommend for the Depressed Castes? (three points)
cards.back:
untouchability be abolished
Hindu temples be thrown open to all castes
seats in legislatures and jobs in government offices be reserved for the lowest castes
cards.quote: The Constituent Assembly finally recommended that untouchability be abolished, Hindu temples be thrown open to all castes, and seats in legislatures and jobs in government offices be reserved for the lowest castes.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.3 “We were suppressed for thousands of years”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: We have never asked for ____. What we have asked for is social justice, economic justice, and political justice.
cards.back: We have never asked for privileges. What we have asked for is social justice, economic justice, and political justice.
cards.quote: We have never asked for privileges. What we have asked for is social justice, economic justice, and political justice.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.3 “We were suppressed for thousands of years”

cards.note: Hansa Mehta of Bombay, Source 8, on justice for women.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did Hansa Mehta of Bombay demand for women?
cards.back: Hansa Mehta of Bombay demanded justice for women, not reserved seats, or separate electorates.
cards.quote: Hansa Mehta of Bombay demanded justice for women, not reserved seats, or separate electorates.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 3.3 “We were suppressed for thousands of years”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What kind of central authority did Nehru say it would be injurious to provide for?
cards.back:
A weak central authority
it would be injurious to the interests of the country to provide for a weak central authority which would be incapable of ensuring peace
cards.quote: it would be injurious to the interests of the country to provide for a weak central authority which would be incapable of ensuring peace

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.note: Nehru’s letter to the President of the Constituent Assembly, arguing for a strong Centre after Partition.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What three lists of subjects did the Draft Constitution provide for?
cards.back: The Draft Constitution provided for three lists of subjects: Union, State, and Concurrent.
cards.quote: The Draft Constitution provided for three lists of subjects: Union, State, and Concurrent.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who controlled the first, second and third lists of subjects?
cards.back: The subjects in the first list were to be the preserve of the Central Government, while those in the second list were vested with the states. As for the third list, here Centre and state shared responsibility.
cards.quote: The subjects in the first list were to be the preserve of the Central Government, while those in the second list were vested with the states. As for the third list, here Centre and state shared responsibility.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the Draft Constitution’s lists compare with other federations?
cards.back: However, many more items were placed under exclusive Union control than in other federations, and more placed on the Concurrent list too than desired by the provinces.
cards.quote: However, many more items were placed under exclusive Union control than in other federations, and more placed on the Concurrent list too than desired by the provinces.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Besides, ____ gave the Centre the powers to take over a state administration on the recommendation of the Governor.
cards.back: Besides, Article 356 gave the Centre the powers to take over a state administration on the recommendation of the Governor.
cards.quote: Besides, Article 356 gave the Centre the powers to take over a state administration on the recommendation of the Governor.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How were taxes divided under the Constitution’s fiscal federalism? (three arrangements)
cards.back:
In the case of some taxes (for instance, customs duties and Company taxes) the Centre retained all the proceeds
in other cases (such as income tax and excise duties) it shared them with the states
in still other cases (for instance, estate duties) it assigned them wholly to the states
cards.quote: In the case of some taxes (for instance, customs duties and Company taxes) the Centre retained all the proceeds; in other cases (such as income tax and excise duties) it shared them with the states; in still other cases (for instance, estate duties) it assigned them wholly to the states.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which taxes could the states levy and collect on their own?
cards.back: The states, meanwhile, could levy and collect certain taxes on their own: these included land and property taxes, sales tax, and the hugely profitable tax on bottled liquor.
cards.quote: The states, meanwhile, could levy and collect certain taxes on their own: these included land and property taxes, sales tax, and the hugely profitable tax on bottled liquor.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who most eloquently defended the rights of the states?
cards.back: The rights of the states were most eloquently defended by K. Santhanam from Madras.
cards.quote: The rights of the states were most eloquently defended by K. Santhanam from Madras.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did Santhanam feel a reallocation of powers was necessary?
cards.back: A reallocation of powers was necessary, he felt, to strengthen not only the states but also the Centre.
cards.quote: A reallocation of powers was necessary, he felt, to strengthen not only the states but also the Centre.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did Santhanam say a Centre with more powers would not be strong?
cards.back: If the Centre was overburdened with responsibilities, it could not function effectively.
cards.quote: If the Centre was overburdened with responsibilities, it could not function effectively.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did Santhanam say the fiscal provisions would affect the provinces?
cards.back: The fiscal provisions would impoverish the provinces since most taxes, except land revenue, had been made the preserve of the Centre.
cards.quote: The fiscal provisions would impoverish the provinces since most taxes, except land revenue, had been made the preserve of the Centre.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did Santhanam predict would happen in a few years?
cards.back: In a few years, he said, all the provinces would rise in “revolt against the Centre”.
cards.quote: In a few years, he said, all the provinces would rise in “revolt against the Centre”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did a member from Orissa warn?
cards.back: A member from Orissa warned that “the Centre is likely to break” since powers had been excessively centralised under the Constitution.
cards.quote: A member from Orissa warned that “the Centre is likely to break” since powers had been excessively centralised under the Constitution.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who wanted “a strong and united Centre … much stronger than the Centre we had created under the Government of India Act of 1935”?
cards.back: Ambedkar had declared that he wanted “a strong and united Centre (hear, hear) much stronger than the Centre we had created under the Government of India Act of 1935”.
cards.quote: Ambedkar had declared that he wanted “a strong and united Centre (hear, hear) much stronger than the Centre we had created under the Government of India Act of 1935”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 4.2 “What we want today is a strong Government”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who declared that “the Centre should be made as strong as possible”?
cards.back: Reacting to the demands for giving power to the provinces, Gopalaswami Ayyangar declared that “the Centre should be made as strong as possible”.
cards.quote: Reacting to the demands for giving power to the provinces, Gopalaswami Ayyangar declared that “the Centre should be made as strong as possible”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 4.2 “What we want today is a strong Government”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did Balakrishna Sharma say only a strong centre could do? (four things)
cards.back:
plan for the well-being of the country
mobilise the available economic resources
establish a proper administration
defend the country against foreign aggression
cards.quote: One member from the United Provinces, Balakrishna Sharma, reasoned at length that only a strong centre could plan for the well-being of the country, mobilise the available economic resources, establish a proper administration, and defend the country against foreign aggression.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 4.2 “What we want today is a strong Government”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did many members say the powers of the Centre had to be greatly strengthened?
cards.back: Reminding the members of the riots and violence that was ripping the nation apart, many members had repeatedly stated that the powers of the Centre had to be greatly strengthened to enable it to stop the communal frenzy.
cards.quote: Reminding the members of the riots and violence that was ripping the nation apart, many members had repeatedly stated that the powers of the Centre had to be greatly strengthened to enable it to stop the communal frenzy.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 4.2 “What we want today is a strong Government”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did most nationalists change their position on provincial autonomy after Partition?
cards.back: After Partition most nationalists changed their position because they felt that the earlier political pressures for a decentralised structure were no longer there.
cards.quote: After Partition most nationalists changed their position because they felt that the earlier political pressures for a decentralised structure were no longer there.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 4.2 “What we want today is a strong Government”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What system was already in place, imposed by the colonial government?
cards.back: There was already a unitary system in place, imposed by the colonial government.
cards.quote: There was already a unitary system in place, imposed by the colonial government.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 4.2 “What we want today is a strong Government”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What further pushed the Constitution towards centralisation?
cards.back: The violence of the times gave a further push to centralisation, now seen as necessary both to forestall chaos and to plan for the country’s economic development.
cards.quote: The violence of the times gave a further push to centralisation, now seen as necessary both to forestall chaos and to plan for the country’s economic development.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 4.2 “What we want today is a strong Government”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What bias did the Constitution show in the distribution of powers?
cards.back: The Constitution thus showed a distinct bias towards the rights of the Union of India over those of its constituent states.
cards.quote: The Constitution thus showed a distinct bias towards the rights of the Union of India over those of its constituent states.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 4.2 “What we want today is a strong Government”

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: According to Gandhi in October 1947, Hindustani should be neither Sanskritised Hindi nor Persianised Urdu but what?
cards.back:
A happy combination of both
This Hindustani should be neither Sanskritised Hindi nor Persianised Urdu but a happy combination of both.
cards.quote: This Hindustani should be neither Sanskritised Hindi nor Persianised Urdu but a happy combination of both.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.note: Mahatma Gandhi, Harijan Sevak, 12 October 1947 (Source 10).

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: To confine oneself to Hindi or Urdu would be a ____ and the spirit of patriotism.
cards.back: To confine oneself to Hindi or Urdu would be a crime against intelligence and the spirit of patriotism.
cards.quote: To confine oneself to Hindi or Urdu would be a crime against intelligence and the spirit of patriotism.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.note: Mahatma Gandhi, Source 10.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which language had the Congress accepted by the 1930s as the national language?
cards.back: By the 1930s, the Congress had accepted that Hindustani ought to be the national language.
cards.quote: By the 1930s, the Congress had accepted that Hindustani ought to be the national language.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was Hindustani?
cards.back: Hindustani – a blend of Hindi and Urdu – was a popular language of a large section of the people of India, and it was a composite language enriched by the interaction of diverse cultures.
cards.quote: Hindustani – a blend of Hindi and Urdu – was a popular language of a large section of the people of India, and it was a composite language enriched by the interaction of diverse cultures.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did Gandhi think Hindustani would be the ideal language of communication?
cards.back: This multi-cultural language, Mahatma Gandhi thought, would be the ideal language of communication between diverse communities: it could unify Hindus and Muslims, and people of the north and the south.
cards.quote: This multi-cultural language, Mahatma Gandhi thought, would be the ideal language of communication between diverse communities: it could unify Hindus and Muslims, and people of the north and the south.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What happened to Hindi and Urdu as communal conflicts deepened?
cards.back: As communal conflicts deepened, Hindi and Urdu also started growing apart.
cards.quote: As communal conflicts deepened, Hindi and Urdu also started growing apart.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How were Hindi and Urdu changing from the end of the nineteenth century?
cards.back: On the one hand, there was a move to Sanskritise Hindi, purging it of all words of Persian and Arabic origin. On the other hand, Urdu was being increasingly Persianised.
cards.quote: On the one hand, there was a move to Sanskritise Hindi, purging it of all words of Persian and Arabic origin. On the other hand, Urdu was being increasingly Persianised.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who made an aggressive plea that Hindi be used as the language of constitution-making?
cards.back: In one of the earliest sessions of the Constituent Assembly, R. V. Dhulekar, a Congressman from the United Provinces, made an aggressive plea that Hindi be used as the language of constitution-making.
cards.quote: In one of the earliest sessions of the Constituent Assembly, R. V. Dhulekar, a Congressman from the United Provinces, made an aggressive plea that Hindi be used as the language of constitution-making.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who retorted that people who did not know Hindustani were “not worthy to be members of this Assembly”?
cards.back: When told that not everyone in the Assembly knew the language, Dhulekar retorted: “People who are present in this House to fashion a constitution for India and do not know Hindustani are not worthy to be members of this Assembly. They better leave.”
cards.quote: When told that not everyone in the Assembly knew the language, Dhulekar retorted: “People who are present in this House to fashion a constitution for India and do not know Hindustani are not worthy to be members of this Assembly. They better leave.”

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was the Language Committee’s compromise formula? (three points)
cards.back:
Hindi in the Devanagari script would be the official language, but the transition to Hindi would be gradual
For the first fifteen years, English would continue to be used for all official purposes
Each province was to be allowed to choose one of the regional languages for official work within the province
cards.quote: It had decided, but not yet formally declared, that Hindi in the Devanagari script would be the official language, but the transition to Hindi would be gradual. For the first fifteen years, English would continue to be used for all official purposes. Each province was to be allowed to choose one of the regional languages for official work within the province.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: For the first ____, English would continue to be used for all official purposes.
cards.back: For the first fifteen years, English would continue to be used for all official purposes.
cards.quote: For the first fifteen years, English would continue to be used for all official purposes.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did Dhulekar want Hindi to be declared?
cards.back: He wanted Hindi to be declared not an Official Language, but a National Language.
cards.quote: He wanted Hindi to be declared not an Official Language, but a National Language.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did Durgabai inform the House about the south?
cards.back: Durgabai informed the House that the opposition in the south against Hindi was very strong
cards.quote: Durgabai informed the House that the opposition in the south against Hindi was very strong

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did Durgabai feel about moves that eroded the composite character of Hindustani?
cards.back: Any move that eroded the inclusive and composite character of Hindustani, she felt, was bound to create anxieties and fears amongst different language groups.
cards.quote: Any move that eroded the inclusive and composite character of Hindustani, she felt, was bound to create anxieties and fears amongst different language groups.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Many of its provisions were arrived at through a process of ____, by forging a middle ground between two opposed positions.
cards.back: Many of its provisions were arrived at through a process of give-and-take, by forging a middle ground between two opposed positions.
cards.quote: Many of its provisions were arrived at through a process of give-and-take, by forging a middle ground between two opposed positions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: On which central feature of the Constitution was there substantial agreement?
cards.back: However, on one central feature of the Constitution there was substantial agreement. This was on the granting of the vote to every adult Indian.
cards.quote: However, on one central feature of the Constitution there was substantial agreement. This was on the granting of the vote to every adult Indian.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why was universal adult franchise an unprecedented act of faith?
cards.back: This was an unprecedented act of faith, for in other democracies the vote had been granted slowly, and in stages.
cards.quote: This was an unprecedented act of faith, for in other democracies the vote had been granted slowly, and in stages.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: In the United States and United Kingdom, who was first granted the vote, and then who?
cards.back: In countries such as the United States and the United Kingdom, only men of property were first granted the vote; then, men with education were also allowed into the charmed circle.
cards.quote: In countries such as the United States and the United Kingdom, only men of property were first granted the vote; then, men with education were also allowed into the charmed circle.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was the second important feature of the Constitution?
cards.back: A second important feature of the Constitution was its emphasis on secularism.
cards.quote: A second important feature of the Constitution was its emphasis on secularism.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Was secularism proclaimed in the Preamble, and how were its features spelled out?
cards.back: There was no ringing pronouncement of secularism in the Preamble, but operationally, its key features as understood in Indian contexts were spelled out in an exemplary manner.
cards.quote: There was no ringing pronouncement of secularism in the Preamble, but operationally, its key features as understood in Indian contexts were spelled out in an exemplary manner.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Through which Fundamental Rights were the key features of secularism spelled out? (three)
cards.back:
“freedom of religion” (Articles 25-28)
“cultural and educational rights” (Articles 29, 30)
“rights to equality” (Articles 14, 16, 17)

cards.quote: The State also sought to distance itself from religious communities, banning compulsory religious instructions in State-run schools and colleges, and declaring religious discrimination in employment to be illegal.

cards.quote: However, a certain legal space was created for social reform within communities, a space that was used to ban untouchability and introduce changes in personal and family laws.

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

early states
cities
the growing use of iron
the development of coinage

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.back: Early Buddhist and Jaina texts (see also Chapter 4) mention, amongst other things, sixteen states known as mahajanapadas.

Magadha
Koshala
Kuru

Gandhara

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What were the mahajanapadas not ruled by kings called, and how was power held in them?
cards.back: While most mahajanapadas were ruled by kings, some, known as ganas or sanghas, were oligarchies (p. 30), where power was shared by a number of men, often collectively called rajas.
cards.quote: While most mahajanapadas were ruled by kings, some, known as ganas or sanghas, were oligarchies (p. 30), where power was shared by a number of men, often collectively called rajas.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What are inscriptions?
cards.back: Inscriptions are writings engraved on hard surfaces such as stone, metal or pottery.
cards.quote: Inscriptions are writings engraved on hard surfaces such as stone, metal or pottery.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What do inscriptions usually record?
cards.back: They usually record the achievements, activities or ideas of those who commissioned them and include the exploits of kings, or donations made by women and men to religious institutions.
cards.quote: They usually record the achievements, activities or ideas of those who commissioned them and include the exploits of kings, or donations made by women and men to religious institutions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Others are dated on the basis of ____ or styles of writing, with a fair amount of precision.
cards.back: Others are dated on the basis of palaeography or styles of writing, with a fair amount of precision.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The earliest inscriptions were in ____, a name for languages used by ordinary people.

cards.quote: The earliest inscriptions were in Prakrit, a name for languages used by ordinary people.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Name the other languages, besides Prakrit, used to write inscriptions and texts.

Pali
Tamil
Sanskrit
cards.quote: You will also find terms in languages such as Pali, Tamil and Sanskrit, which too were used to write inscriptions and texts.

cards.front: ____ means the land where a jana (a people, clan or tribe) sets its foot or settles.

cards.quote: Oligarchy refers to a form of government where power is exercised by a group of men.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Brahmanas began composing Sanskrit texts known as the ____.
cards.back: Brahmanas began composing Sanskrit texts known as the Dharmasutras.
cards.quote: Brahmanas began composing Sanskrit texts known as the Dharmasutras.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who were rulers ideally expected to be, according to the Dharmasutras?
cards.back: These laid down norms for rulers (as well as for other social categories), who were ideally expected to be Kshatriyas (see also Chapter 3).
cards.quote: These laid down norms for rulers (as well as for other social categories), who were ideally expected to be Kshatriyas (see also Chapter 3).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.back: Rulers were advised to collect taxes and tribute from cultivators, traders and artisans.
cards.quote: Rulers were advised to collect taxes and tribute from cultivators, traders and artisans.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What did some states acquire, and what did others continue to depend on?
cards.back: Gradually, some states acquired standing armies and maintained regular bureaucracies. Others continued to depend on militia, recruited, more often than not, from the peasantry.
cards.quote: Gradually, some states acquired standing armies and maintained regular bureaucracies. Others continued to depend on militia, recruited, more often than not, from the peasantry.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which mahajanapada became the most powerful between the sixth and fourth centuries BCE?
cards.back: Between the sixth and the fourth centuries BCE, Magadha (in present-day Bihar) became the most powerful mahajanapada.
cards.quote: Between the sixth and the fourth centuries BCE, Magadha (in present-day Bihar) became the most powerful mahajanapada.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Name the reasons modern historians give for the growth of Magadha's power.
cards.back:
Magadha was a region where agriculture was especially productive.
Besides, iron mines (in present-day Jharkhand) were accessible and provided resources for tools and weapons.
Elephants, an important component of the army, were found in forests in the region.
Also, the Ganga and its tributaries provided a means of cheap and convenient communication.
cards.quote: Magadha was a region where agriculture was especially productive. Besides, iron mines (in present-day Jharkhand) were accessible and provided resources for tools and weapons. Elephants, an important component of the army, were found in forests in the region. Also, the Ganga and its tributaries provided a means of cheap and convenient communication.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: To what did early Buddhist and Jaina writers attribute Magadha's power?
cards.back: However, early Buddhist and Jaina writers who wrote about Magadha attributed its power to the policies of individuals: ruthlessly ambitious kings of whom Bimbisara, Ajatasattu and Mahapadma Nanda are the best known, and their ministers, who helped implement their policies.
cards.quote: However, early Buddhist and Jaina writers who wrote about Magadha attributed its power to the policies of individuals: ruthlessly ambitious kings of whom Bimbisara, Ajatasattu and Mahapadma Nanda are the best known, and their ministers, who helped implement their policies.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What was the Prakrit name of present-day Rajgir, the initial capital of Magadha?
cards.back: Initially, Rajagaha (the Prakrit name for present-day Rajgir in Bihar) was the capital of Magadha.
cards.quote: Initially, Rajagaha (the Prakrit name for present-day Rajgir in Bihar) was the capital of Magadha.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What does the old name Rajagaha mean?
cards.back: Interestingly, the old name means "house of the king".
cards.quote: Interestingly, the old name means "house of the king".

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which scripts were used for Prakrit inscriptions, and where was Kharosthi used?
cards.back: Most Prakrit inscriptions were written in the Brahmi script; however, some, in the northwest, were written in Kharosthi.
cards.quote: Most Prakrit inscriptions were written in the Brahmi script; however, some, in the northwest, were written in Kharosthi.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The growth of Magadha culminated in the emergence of the ____.
cards.back: The growth of Magadha culminated in the emergence of the Mauryan Empire.
cards.quote: The growth of Magadha culminated in the emergence of the Mauryan Empire.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who founded the Mauryan Empire (c. 321 BCE), and how far did his control extend?
cards.back: Chandragupta Maurya, who founded the empire (c. 321 BCE), extended control as far northwest as Afghanistan and Baluchistan
cards.quote: Chandragupta Maurya, who founded the empire (c. 321 BCE), extended control as far northwest as Afghanistan and Baluchistan

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which Mauryan ruler conquered Kalinga (present-day coastal Orissa)?
cards.back: his grandson Asoka, arguably the most famous ruler of early India, conquered Kalinga (present-day coastal Orissa).
cards.quote: his grandson Asoka, arguably the most famous ruler of early India, conquered Kalinga (present-day coastal Orissa).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Name the sources historians use to reconstruct Mauryan history.
cards.back:
archaeological finds, especially sculpture
the account of Megasthenes
the Arthashastra
later Buddhist, Jaina and Puranic literature
the inscriptions of Asoka (c. 272/268-231 BCE) on rocks and pillars
cards.quote: These include archaeological finds, especially sculpture. Also valuable are contemporary works, such as the account of Megasthenes (a Greek ambassador to the court of Chandragupta Maurya), which survives in fragments. Another source that is often used is the Arthashastra, parts of which were probably composed by Kautilya or Chanakya, traditionally believed to be the minister of Chandragupta. Besides, the Mauryas are mentioned in later Buddhist, Jaina and Puranic literature, as well as in Sanskrit literary works. While these are useful, the inscriptions of Asoka (c. 272/268-231 BCE) on rocks and pillars are often regarded as amongst the most valuable sources.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who is believed to have composed parts of the Arthashastra?
cards.back: the Arthashastra, parts of which were probably composed by Kautilya or Chanakya, traditionally believed to be the minister of Chandragupta
cards.quote: the Arthashastra, parts of which were probably composed by Kautilya or Chanakya, traditionally believed to be the minister of Chandragupta

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who was the first ruler to inscribe his messages to subjects and officials on stone surfaces?
cards.back: Asoka was the first ruler who inscribed his messages to his subjects and officials on stone surfaces
cards.quote: Asoka was the first ruler who inscribed his messages to his subjects and officials on stone surfaces

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What did Asoka's dhamma include?
cards.back:
respect towards elders
generosity towards Brahmanas and those who renounced worldly life
treating slaves and servants kindly
respect for religions and traditions other than one's own
cards.quote: He used the inscriptions to proclaim what he understood to be dhamma. This included respect towards elders, generosity towards Brahmanas and those who renounced worldly life, treating slaves and servants kindly, and respect for religions and traditions other than one's own.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Name the five major political centres of the Mauryan Empire.
cards.back:
the capital Pataliputra
Taxila
Ujjayini
Tosali
Suvarnagiri
cards.quote: the capital Pataliputra and the provincial centres of Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri, all mentioned in Asokan inscriptions.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In the Mauryan empire, where was administrative control likely to have been strongest?
cards.back:
In areas around the capital and the provincial centres
It is likely that administrative control was strongest in areas around the capital and the provincial centres.
cards.quote: It is likely that administrative control was strongest in areas around the capital and the provincial centres.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why were Taxila, Ujjayini and Suvarnagiri carefully chosen as provincial centres?
cards.back: These centres were carefully chosen, both Taxila and Ujjayini being situated on important long-distance trade routes, while Suvarnagiri (literally, the golden mountain) was possibly important for tapping the gold mines of Karnataka.
cards.quote: These centres were carefully chosen, both Taxila and Ujjayini being situated on important long-distance trade routes, while Suvarnagiri (literally, the golden mountain) was possibly important for tapping the gold mines of Karnataka.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: According to Megasthenes, which occupations connected with land did officers superintend?
cards.back: They collect the taxes, and superintend the occupations connected with land; as those of the woodcutters, the carpenters, the blacksmiths, and the miners.
cards.quote: They collect the taxes, and superintend the occupations connected with land; as those of the woodcutters, the carpenters, the blacksmiths, and the miners.

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I

one looked after the navy
the second managed transport and provisions
the third was responsible for foot-soldiers
the fourth for horses
the fifth for chariots
the sixth for elephants

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How did twentieth-century nationalist leaders regard Asoka?
cards.back: So it is not surprising that nationalist leaders in the twentieth century regarded him as an inspiring figure.
cards.quote: So it is not surprising that nationalist leaders in the twentieth century regarded him as an inspiring figure.

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I

About 150 years

cards.quote: It lasted for about 150 years, which is not a very long time in the vast span of the history of the subcontinent.

The Sangam texts

cards.front: According to Greek sources, how large was the Mauryan standing army?

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which rulers (c. first century BCE-first century CE) ruled from Central Asia to northwest India?
cards.back: the Kushanas (c. first century BCE-first century CE), who ruled over a vast kingdom extending from Central Asia to northwest India
cards.quote: the Kushanas (c. first century BCE-first century CE), who ruled over a vast kingdom extending from Central Asia to northwest India

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In what are the notions of kingship that the Kushanas wished to project perhaps best evidenced?
cards.back: The notions of kingship they wished to project are perhaps best evidenced in their coins and sculpture.
cards.quote: The notions of kingship they wished to project are perhaps best evidenced in their coins and sculpture.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Where were colossal statues of Kushana rulers found installed in a shrine?
cards.back: Colossal statues of Kushana rulers have been found installed in a shrine at Mat near Mathura (Uttar Pradesh).
cards.quote: Colossal statues of Kushana rulers have been found installed in a shrine at Mat near Mathura (Uttar Pradesh).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Many Kushana rulers also adopted the title ____, or "son of god", possibly inspired by Chinese rulers who called themselves sons of heaven.
cards.back: Many Kushana rulers also adopted the title devaputra, or "son of god", possibly inspired by Chinese rulers who called themselves sons of heaven.
cards.quote: Many Kushana rulers also adopted the title devaputra, or "son of god", possibly inspired by Chinese rulers who called themselves sons of heaven.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who were samantas?
cards.back: samantas, men who maintained themselves through local resources including control over land. They offered homage and provided military support to rulers.
cards.quote: samantas, men who maintained themselves through local resources including control over land. They offered homage and provided military support to rulers.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which men, offering homage and military support to rulers in fourth-century states, could become kings if powerful?
cards.back: They offered homage and provided military support to rulers. Powerful samantas could become kings: conversely, weak rulers might find themselves being reduced to positions of subordination.
cards.quote: They offered homage and provided military support to rulers. Powerful samantas could become kings: conversely, weak rulers might find themselves being reduced to positions of subordination.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: ____, composed in praise of kings in particular, and patrons in general, by poets.
cards.back: prashastis, composed in praise of kings in particular, and patrons in general, by poets.
cards.quote: prashastis, composed in praise of kings in particular, and patrons in general, by poets.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who composed the Prayaga Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription), and for which ruler?
cards.back: The Prayaga Prashasti (also known as the Allahabad Pillar Inscription) composed in Sanskrit by Harishena, the court poet of Samudragupta, arguably the most powerful of the Gupta rulers (c. fourth century CE), is a case in point.
cards.quote: The Prayaga Prashasti (also known as the Allahabad Pillar Inscription) composed in Sanskrit by Harishena, the court poet of Samudragupta, arguably the most powerful of the Gupta rulers (c. fourth century CE), is a case in point.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The Sudarshana lake inscription (c. second century CE) records the achievements of which ruler?
cards.back: We know about it from a rock inscription (c. second century CE) in Sanskrit, composed to record the achievements of the Shaka ruler Rudradaman.
cards.quote: We know about it from a rock inscription (c. second century CE) in Sanskrit, composed to record the achievements of the Shaka ruler Rudradaman.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who built the Sudarshana lake, and during whose rule?
cards.back: The inscription mentions that the lake, with embankments and water channels, was built by a local governor during the rule of the Mauryas.
cards.quote: The inscription mentions that the lake, with embankments and water channels, was built by a local governor during the rule of the Mauryas.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How did Rudradaman claim to have repaired the Sudarshana lake?
cards.back: Rudradaman, who was then ruling in the area, claimed to have got the lake repaired using his own resources, without imposing any tax on his subjects.
cards.quote: Rudradaman, who was then ruling in the area, claimed to have got the lake repaired using his own resources, without imposing any tax on his subjects.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: ____ is used for paddy cultivation in areas where water is plentiful.
cards.back: Transplantation is used for paddy cultivation in areas where water is plentiful.
cards.quote: Transplantation is used for paddy cultivation in areas where water is plentiful.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How does transplantation of paddy work, and what does it ensure?
cards.back: Here, seeds are first broadcast; when the saplings have grown they are transplanted in waterlogged fields. This ensures a higher ratio of survival of saplings and higher yields.
cards.quote: Here, seeds are first broadcast; when the saplings have grown they are transplanted in waterlogged fields. This ensures a higher ratio of survival of saplings and higher yields.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which anthologies of stories do historians examine to learn what subjects thought of kings?
cards.back: Nevertheless, historians have tried to solve this problem by examining stories contained in anthologies such as the Jatakas and the Panchatantra.
cards.quote: Nevertheless, historians have tried to solve this problem by examining stories contained in anthologies such as the Jatakas and the Panchatantra.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The Jatakas were written in ____ around the middle of the first millennium CE.
cards.back: The Jatakas were written in Pali around the middle of the first millennium CE.
cards.quote: The Jatakas were written in Pali around the middle of the first millennium CE.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In the Gandatindu Jataka, what did subjects complain about when the king went in disguise?
cards.back: complaining that they were attacked by robbers at night and by tax collectors during the day.
cards.quote: complaining that they were attacked by robbers at night and by tax collectors during the day.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In the Gandatindu Jataka, how did people escape their situation?
cards.back: To escape from this situation, people abandoned their village and went to live in the forest.
cards.quote: To escape from this situation, people abandoned their village and went to live in the forest.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why was the relationship between a king and the rural population often strained?
cards.back: kings frequently tried to fill their coffers by demanding high taxes, and peasants particularly found such demands oppressive.
cards.quote: kings frequently tried to fill their coffers by demanding high taxes, and peasants particularly found such demands oppressive.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which strategy to increase production spread in the Ganga and Kaveri valleys from c. sixth century BCE?
cards.back: One such strategy was the shift to plough agriculture, which spread in fertile alluvial river valleys such as those of the Ganga and the Kaveri from c. sixth century BCE.
cards.quote: One such strategy was the shift to plough agriculture, which spread in fertile alluvial river valleys such as those of the Ganga and the Kaveri from c. sixth century BCE.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Where was the iron-tipped ploughshare used to turn the alluvial soil?
cards.back: The iron-tipped ploughshare was used to turn the alluvial soil in areas which had high rainfall.
cards.quote: The iron-tipped ploughshare was used to turn the alluvial soil in areas which had high rainfall.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What dramatically increased paddy production in parts of the Ganga valley?
cards.back: Moreover, in some parts of the Ganga valley, production of paddy was dramatically increased by the introduction of transplantation, although this meant back-breaking work for the producer.
cards.quote: Moreover, in some parts of the Ganga valley, production of paddy was dramatically increased by the introduction of transplantation, although this meant back-breaking work for the producer.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which areas did not adopt the iron ploughshare till the twentieth century?
cards.back: areas which were semi-arid, such as parts of Punjab and Rajasthan did not adopt it till the twentieth century,
cards.quote: areas which were semi-arid, such as parts of Punjab and Rajasthan did not adopt it till the twentieth century,

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which agriculture, much better suited to the terrain, was practised in the hilly tracts of the northeastern and central subcontinent?
cards.back:
Hoe agriculture
those living in hilly tracts in the northeastern and central parts of the subcontinent practised hoe agriculture, which was much better suited to the terrain.
cards.quote: those living in hilly tracts in the northeastern and central parts of the subcontinent practised hoe agriculture, which was much better suited to the terrain.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Through what means was irrigation commonly practised to increase production?
cards.back: Another strategy adopted to increase agricultural production was the use of irrigation, through wells and tanks, and less commonly, canals.
cards.quote: Another strategy adopted to increase agricultural production was the use of irrigation, through wells and tanks, and less commonly, canals.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who organised irrigation works, and who recorded them in inscriptions?
cards.back: Communities as well as individuals organised the construction of irrigation works. The latter, usually powerful men including kings, often recorded such activities in inscriptions.
cards.quote: Communities as well as individuals organised the construction of irrigation works. The latter, usually powerful men including kings, often recorded such activities in inscriptions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Name the categories of people engaged in agriculture mentioned in Buddhist stories.
cards.back:
landless agricultural labourers
small peasants
large landholders
cards.quote: stories, especially within the Buddhist tradition, refer to landless agricultural labourers, small peasants, as well as large landholders.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Buddhist stories name landless labourers, small peasants and large landholders. Which Pali term covers the second and third?
cards.back: landless agricultural labourers, small peasants, as well as large landholders. The term gahapati was often used in Pali texts to designate the second and third categories.
cards.quote: stories, especially within the Buddhist tradition, refer to landless agricultural labourers, small peasants, as well as large landholders. The term gahapati was often used in Pali texts to designate the second and third categories.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What was a gahapati?
cards.back: A gahapati was the owner, master or head of a household, who exercised control over the women, children, slaves and workers who shared a common residence.
cards.quote: A gahapati was the owner, master or head of a household, who exercised control over the women, children, slaves and workers who shared a common residence.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: For whom was the term gahapati sometimes used as a marker of status?
cards.back: Sometimes the term was used as a marker of status for men belonging to the urban elite, including wealthy merchants.
cards.quote: Sometimes the term was used as a marker of status for men belonging to the urban elite, including wealthy merchants.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who emerged as powerful figures in villages and controlled other cultivators?
cards.back: The large landholders, as well as the village headman (whose position was often hereditary), emerged as powerful figures, and often exercised control over other cultivators.
cards.quote: The large landholders, as well as the village headman (whose position was often hereditary), emerged as powerful figures, and often exercised control over other cultivators.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Types of village people in Sangam texts (Tamil term and meaning).
cards.back:
large landowners or vellalar
ploughmen or uzhavar
slaves or adimai
cards.quote: large landowners or vellalar, ploughmen or uzhavar and slaves or adimai.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: On what were the differences in rural society (large landholders, cultivators, slaves) likely based?
cards.back:
Differential access to land, labour and some of the new technologies
It is likely that these differences were based on differential access to land, labour and some of the new technologies.
cards.quote: It is likely that these differences were based on differential access to land, labour and some of the new technologies.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is the Manusmrti, and when was it compiled?
cards.back: The Manusmrti is one of the best-known legal texts of early India, written in Sanskrit and compiled between c. second century BCE and c. second century CE.
cards.quote: The Manusmrti is one of the best-known legal texts of early India, written in Sanskrit and compiled between c. second century BCE and c. second century CE.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who composed the Harshacharita, and whose biography is it?
cards.back: The Harshacharita is a biography of Harshavardhana, the ruler of Kanauj (see Map 3), composed in Sanskrit by his court poet, Banabhatta (c. seventh century CE).
cards.quote: The Harshacharita is a biography of Harshavardhana, the ruler of Kanauj (see Map 3), composed in Sanskrit by his court poet, Banabhatta (c. seventh century CE).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: From the early centuries of the Common Era, we find ____ being made, many of which were recorded in inscriptions.
cards.back: From the early centuries of the Common Era, we find grants of land being made, many of which were recorded in inscriptions.
cards.quote: From the early centuries of the Common Era, we find grants of land being made, many of which were recorded in inscriptions.

source.section: Land grants and new rural elites

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: On what were most land grants recorded?
cards.back: Some of these inscriptions were on stone, but most were on copper plates (Fig. 2.13) which were probably given as a record of the transaction to those who received the land.
cards.quote: Some of these inscriptions were on stone, but most were on copper plates (Fig. 2.13) which were probably given as a record of the transaction to those who received the land.

source.section: Land grants and new rural elites

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: To whom were the surviving land grants generally made?
cards.back: The records that have survived are generally about grants to religious institutions or to Brahmanas.
cards.quote: The records that have survived are generally about grants to religious institutions or to Brahmanas.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Land grants and new rural elites

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who was Prabhavati Gupta, and into which family was she married?
cards.back: Prabhavati Gupta was the daughter of one of the most important rulers in early Indian history, Chandragupta II (c. 375-415 CE). She was married into another important ruling family, that of the Vakatakas, who were powerful in the Deccan (see Map 3).
cards.quote: Prabhavati Gupta was the daughter of one of the most important rulers in early Indian history, Chandragupta II (c. 375-415 CE). She was married into another important ruling family, that of the Vakatakas, who were powerful in the Deccan (see Map 3).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Land grants and new rural elites

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What do legal texts say about women's access to land, and what does Prabhavati's inscription show?
cards.back: According to Sanskrit legal texts, women were not supposed to have independent access to resources such as land. However, the inscription indicates that Prabhavati had access to land, which she then granted.
cards.quote: According to Sanskrit legal texts, women were not supposed to have independent access to resources such as land. However, the inscription indicates that Prabhavati had access to land, which she then granted.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Land grants and new rural elites

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why might Prabhavati have had access to land?
cards.back: This may have been because she was a queen (one of the few known from early Indian history), and her situation was therefore exceptional. It is also possible that the provisions of legal texts were not uniformly implemented.
cards.quote: This may have been because she was a queen (one of the few known from early Indian history), and her situation was therefore exceptional. It is also possible that the provisions of legal texts were not uniformly implemented.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Land grants and new rural elites

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: One view on land grants: what strategy were they part of?
cards.back: Some feel that land grants were part of a strategy adopted by ruling lineages to extend agriculture to new areas.
cards.quote: Some feel that land grants were part of a strategy adopted by ruling lineages to extend agriculture to new areas.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Land grants and new rural elites

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What was an agrahara?
cards.back: An agrahara was land granted to a Brahmana, who was usually exempted from paying land revenue and other dues to the king, and was often given the right to collect these dues from the local people.
cards.quote: An agrahara was land granted to a Brahmana, who was usually exempted from paying land revenue and other dues to the king, and was often given the right to collect these dues from the local people.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Land grants and new rural elites

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Name the groups often beyond the reach of officials or samantas.
cards.back:
pastoralists
fisherfolk and hunter-gatherers
mobile or semi-sedentary artisans
shifting cultivators
cards.quote: However, there were people who were often beyond the reach of officials or samantas: pastoralists, fisherfolk and hunter-gatherers, mobile or semi-sedentary artisans and shifting cultivators.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: Land grants and new rural elites

cards.back: Pataliputra, for instance, began as a village known as Pataligrama.
cards.quote: Pataliputra, for instance, began as a village known as Pataligrama.

cards.back: By the fourth century BCE, it was the capital of the Mauryan Empire and one of the largest cities in Asia.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which Chinese pilgrim found Pataliputra in ruins in the seventh century CE?
cards.back: When the Chinese pilgrim Xuan Zang visited the city in the seventh century CE, he found it in ruins, and with a very small population.
cards.quote: When the Chinese pilgrim Xuan Zang visited the city in the seventh century CE, he found it in ruins, and with a very small population.

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Types of towns by route location, with NCERT's example of each.

yet others, such as Puhar, were near the coast, from where sea routes began

cards.back: fine pottery bowls and dishes, with a glossy finish, known as Northern Black Polished Ware, probably used by rich people

washing folk
weavers
scribes
carpenters
potters
goldsmiths
blacksmiths
officials
religious teachers
merchants
