cards.front: Why are newspapers an important source for the study of the national movement?
cards.back: One more important source is contemporary newspapers, published in English as well as in the different Indian languages, which tracked Mahatma Gandhi’s movements and reported on his activities, and also represented what ordinary Indians thought of him.
cards.quote: One more important source is contemporary newspapers, published in English as well as in the different Indian languages, which tracked Mahatma Gandhi’s movements and reported on his activities, and also represented what ordinary Indians thought of him.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why should newspaper accounts not be seen as unprejudiced?
cards.back: Newspaper accounts, however, should not be seen as unprejudiced. They were published by people who had their own political opinions and world views. These ideas shaped what was published and the way events were reported.
cards.quote: Newspaper accounts, however, should not be seen as unprejudiced. They were published by people who had their own political opinions and world views. These ideas shaped what was published and the way events were reported.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 1919: which two events are listed?
cards.back: Rowlatt Satyagraha (March-April) Jallianwala Bagh massacre (April)
cards.quote: Rowlatt Satyagraha (March-April) Jallianwala Bagh massacre (April)

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 1928: which peasant movement is listed?
cards.back: Peasant movement in Bardoli
cards.quote: Peasant movement in Bardoli

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 1930: which events are listed?
cards.back: Civil Disobedience Movement begins; Dandi March (March-April)
cards.quote: Civil Disobedience Movement begins; Dandi March (March-April)

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 1931: which two events are listed?
cards.back: Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March); Second Round Table Conference (December)
cards.quote: Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March); Second Round Table Conference (December)

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 1946: what did Mahatma Gandhi do?
cards.back: Mahatma Gandhi visits Noakhali and other riot-torn areas to stop communal violence
cards.quote: Mahatma Gandhi visits Noakhali and other riot-torn areas to stop communal violence

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What share of India’s population lived in villages in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries?
cards.back: During the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries about 85 per cent of the population of India lived in its villages.
cards.quote: During the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries about 85 per cent of the population of India lived in its villages.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Define rural society.
cards.back: Both peasants and landed elites were involved in agricultural production and claimed rights to a share of the produce. This created relationships of cooperation, competition and conflict among them. The sum of these agrarian relationships made up rural society.
cards.quote: Both peasants and landed elites were involved in agricultural production and claimed rights to a share of the produce. This created relationships of cooperation, competition and conflict among them. The sum of these agrarian relationships made up rural society.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Most important among these was the Mughal state, which derived the bulk of its income from ____.
cards.back: Most important among these was the Mughal state, which derived the bulk of its income from agricultural production.
cards.quote: Most important among these was the Mughal state, which derived the bulk of its income from agricultural production.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who were the agents of the Mughal state in the rural world, and what did they seek to do?
cards.back: Agents of the state – revenue assessors, collectors, record keepers – sought to control rural society so as to ensure that cultivation took place and the state got its regular share of taxes from the produce.
cards.quote: Agents of the state – revenue assessors, collectors, record keepers – sought to control rural society so as to ensure that cultivation took place and the state got its regular share of taxes from the produce.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Since many crops were grown for sale, which three things entered the villages and linked them with the towns?
cards.back: Since many crops were grown for sale, trade, money and markets entered the villages and linked the agricultural areas with the towns.
cards.quote: Since many crops were grown for sale, trade, money and markets entered the villages and linked the agricultural areas with the towns.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The basic unit of agricultural society was the ____, inhabited by peasants
cards.back: The basic unit of agricultural society was the village, inhabited by peasants
cards.quote: The basic unit of agricultural society was the village, inhabited by peasants

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who authored the Ain-i Akbari?
cards.back: One of the most important chronicles was the Ain-i Akbari (in short the Ain, see also Section 8) authored by Akbar’s court historian Abu’l Fazl.
cards.quote: One of the most important chronicles was the Ain-i Akbari (in short the Ain, see also Section 8) authored by Akbar’s court historian Abu’l Fazl.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The central purpose of the Ain was to present a vision of Akbar’s empire where ____ was provided by a strong ruling class.
cards.back: The central purpose of the Ain was to present a vision of Akbar’s empire where social harmony was provided by a strong ruling class.
cards.quote: The central purpose of the Ain was to present a vision of Akbar’s empire where social harmony was provided by a strong ruling class.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Any revolt or assertion of autonomous power against the Mughal state was, in the eyes of the author of the Ain, ____.
cards.back: Any revolt or assertion of autonomous power against the Mughal state was, in the eyes of the author of the Ain, predestined to fail.
cards.quote: Any revolt or assertion of autonomous power against the Mughal state was, in the eyes of the author of the Ain, predestined to fail.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How does NCERT describe whatever we learn from the Ain about peasants?
cards.back:
A view from the top
In other words, whatever we learn from the Ain about peasants remains a view from the top.
cards.quote: In other words, whatever we learn from the Ain about peasants remains a view from the top.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The term which Indo-Persian sources of the Mughal period most frequently used to denote a peasant was ____ (plural, riaya) or ____.
cards.back: The term which Indo-Persian sources of the Mughal period most frequently used to denote a peasant was raiyat (plural, riaya) or muzarian.
cards.quote: The term which Indo-Persian sources of the Mughal period most frequently used to denote a peasant was raiyat (plural, riaya) or muzarian.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Besides raiyat and muzarian, which other terms for a peasant occur in the sources?
cards.back: In addition, we also encounter the terms kisan or asami.
cards.quote: In addition, we also encounter the terms kisan or asami.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the two kinds of peasants mentioned in seventeenth-century sources.
cards.back:
khud-kashta
pahi-kashta
cards.quote: Sources of the seventeenth century refer to two kinds of peasants – khud-kashta and pahi-kashta.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why did people become pahi-kashta?
cards.back: People became pahi-kashta either out of choice – for example, when terms of revenue in a distant village were more favourable – or out of compulsion – for example, forced by economic distress after a famine.
cards.quote: People became pahi-kashta either out of choice – for example, when terms of revenue in a distant village were more favourable – or out of compulsion – for example, forced by economic distress after a famine.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Seldom did the average peasant of north India possess more than ____; most possessed even less.
cards.back: Seldom did the average peasant of north India possess more than a pair of bullocks and two ploughs; most possessed even less.
cards.quote: Seldom did the average peasant of north India possess more than a pair of bullocks and two ploughs; most possessed even less.
blanks: a pair of bullocks and two ploughs

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Cultivation was based on the principle of ____.
cards.back: Cultivation was based on the principle of individual ownership.
cards.quote: Cultivation was based on the principle of individual ownership.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the three factors that accounted for the constant expansion of agriculture.
cards.back:
abundance of land
available labour
mobility of peasants
cards.quote: The abundance of land, available labour and the mobility of peasants were three factors that accounted for the constant expansion of agriculture.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Areas which received ____ or more of rainfall a year were generally rice-producing zones
cards.back: Areas which received 40 inches or more of rainfall a year were generally rice-producing zones
cards.quote: Areas which received 40 inches or more of rainfall a year were generally rice-producing zones

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Where did tobacco arrive first in India, and when did it spread to northern India?
cards.back: This plant, which arrived first in the Deccan, spread to northern India in the early years of the seventeenth century.
cards.quote: This plant, which arrived first in the Deccan, spread to northern India in the early years of the seventeenth century.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Akbar and his nobles came across tobacco for the first time in ____.
cards.back: Akbar and his nobles came across tobacco for the first time in 1604.
cards.quote: Akbar and his nobles came across tobacco for the first time in 1604.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which Mughal emperor banned tobacco, concerned about its addiction?
cards.back: Jahangir was so concerned about its addiction that he banned it.
cards.quote: Jahangir was so concerned about its addiction that he banned it.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: By how much did India’s population increase between 1600 and 1800?
cards.back: India’s population increased, according to calculations by economic historians, by about 50 million people between 1600 and 1800, which is an increase of about 33 per cent over 200 years.
cards.quote: India’s population increased, according to calculations by economic historians, by about 50 million people between 1600 and 1800, which is an increase of about 33 per cent over 200 years.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What irrigation work did the state undertake in northern India?
cards.back: Irrigation projects received state support as well. For example, in northern India the state undertook digging of new canals (nahr, nala) and also repaired old ones like the shahnahr in the Punjab during Shah Jahan’s reign.
cards.quote: Irrigation projects received state support as well. For example, in northern India the state undertook digging of new canals (nahr, nala) and also repaired old ones like the shahnahr in the Punjab during Shah Jahan’s reign.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why did the light wooden plough preserve moisture in the hot months?
cards.back: One example was the wooden plough, which was light and easily assembled with an iron tip or coulter. It therefore did not make deep furrows, which preserved the moisture better during the intensely hot months.
cards.quote: One example was the wooden plough, which was light and easily assembled with an iron tip or coulter. It therefore did not make deep furrows, which preserved the moisture better during the intensely hot months.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: A drill, pulled by a pair of giant oxen, was used to plant seeds, but ____ of seed was the most prevalent method.
cards.back: A drill, pulled by a pair of giant oxen, was used to plant seeds, but broadcasting of seed was the most prevalent method.
cards.quote: A drill, pulled by a pair of giant oxen, was used to plant seeds, but broadcasting of seed was the most prevalent method.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the two major seasonal cycles of agriculture.
cards.back:
kharif (autumn)
rabi (spring)
cards.quote: Agriculture was organised around two major seasonal cycles, the kharif (autumn) and the rabi (spring).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What term does NCERT give for most regions producing a minimum of two crops a year (kharif and rabi)?
cards.back:
Do-fasla
Agriculture was organised around two major seasonal cycles, the kharif (autumn) and the rabi (spring). This would mean that most regions, except those terrains that were the most arid or inhospitable, produced a minimum of two crops a year (do-fasla), whereas some, where rainfall or irrigation assured a continuous supply of water, even gave three crops.
cards.quote: Agriculture was organised around two major seasonal cycles, the kharif (autumn) and the rabi (spring). This would mean that most regions, except those terrains that were the most arid or inhospitable, produced a minimum of two crops a year (do-fasla), whereas some, where rainfall or irrigation assured a continuous supply of water, even gave three crops.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: We often come across the term ____ (literally, perfect crops) in our sources.
cards.back: We often come across the term jins-i kamil (literally, perfect crops) in our sources.
cards.quote: We often come across the term jins-i kamil (literally, perfect crops) in our sources.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The Mughal state also encouraged peasants to cultivate such crops as they brought in ____.
cards.back: The Mughal state also encouraged peasants to cultivate such crops as they brought in more revenue.
cards.quote: The Mughal state also encouraged peasants to cultivate such crops as they brought in more revenue.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which crops were jins-i kamil par excellence?
cards.back: Crops such as cotton and sugarcane were jins-i kamil par excellence.
cards.quote: Crops such as cotton and sugarcane were jins-i kamil par excellence.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Where was cotton grown, and for what was Bengal famous?
cards.back: Cotton was grown over a great swathe of territory spread over central India and the Deccan plateau, whereas Bengal was famous for its sugar.
cards.quote: Cotton was grown over a great swathe of territory spread over central India and the Deccan plateau, whereas Bengal was famous for its sugar.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Cash crops like mustard and lentils show which two kinds of production were intertwined in a peasant’s holding?
cards.back: Such cash crops would also include various sorts of oilseeds (for example, mustard) and lentils. This shows how subsistence and commercial production were closely intertwined in an average peasant’s holding.
cards.quote: Such cash crops would also include various sorts of oilseeds (for example, mustard) and lentils. This shows how subsistence and commercial production were closely intertwined in an average peasant’s holding.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did maize reach India, and where was it a major crop by the seventeenth century?
cards.back: Maize (makka), for example, was introduced into India via Africa and Spain and by the seventeenth century it was being listed as one of the major crops of western India.
cards.quote: Maize (makka), for example, was introduced into India via Africa and Spain and by the seventeenth century it was being listed as one of the major crops of western India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the five vegetables and fruits introduced into India from the New World in the seventeenth century.
cards.back:
tomatoes, potatoes and chillies
the pineapple and the papaya
cards.quote: Vegetables like tomatoes, potatoes and chillies were introduced from the New World at this time, as were fruits like the pineapple and the papaya.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the three constituents of the village community.
cards.back:
the cultivators
the panchayat
the village headman (muqaddam or mandal)
cards.quote: There were three constituents of this community – the cultivators, the panchayat, and the village headman (muqaddam or mandal).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Among those who tilled the land, there was a sizeable number who worked as menials or agricultural labourers (____).
cards.back: Among those who tilled the land, there was a sizeable number who worked as menials or agricultural labourers (majur).
cards.quote: Among those who tilled the land, there was a sizeable number who worked as menials or agricultural labourers (majur).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Despite the abundance of cultivable land, certain caste groups were assigned ____ and thus relegated to poverty.
cards.back: Despite the abundance of cultivable land, certain caste groups were assigned menial tasks and thus relegated to poverty.
cards.quote: Despite the abundance of cultivable land, certain caste groups were assigned menial tasks and thus relegated to poverty.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who were the halalkhoran and the mallahzadas?
cards.back: In Muslim communities menials like the halalkhoran (scavengers) were housed outside the boundaries of the village; similarly the mallahzadas (literally, sons of boatmen) in Bihar were comparable to slaves.
cards.quote: In Muslim communities menials like the halalkhoran (scavengers) were housed outside the boundaries of the village; similarly the mallahzadas (literally, sons of boatmen) in Bihar were comparable to slaves.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which castes rose in the hierarchy because of cattle rearing and horticulture?
cards.back: Castes such as the Ahirs, Gujars and Malis rose in the hierarchy because of the profitability of cattle rearing and horticulture.
cards.quote: Castes such as the Ahirs, Gujars and Malis rose in the hierarchy because of the profitability of cattle rearing and horticulture.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which eastern pastoral and fishing castes acquired the status of peasants?
cards.back: In the eastern regions, intermediate pastoral and fishing castes like the Sadgops and Kaivartas acquired the status of peasants.
cards.quote: In the eastern regions, intermediate pastoral and fishing castes like the Sadgops and Kaivartas acquired the status of peasants.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was the village panchayat?
cards.back: The village panchayat was an assembly of elders, usually important people of the village with hereditary rights over their property.
cards.quote: The village panchayat was an assembly of elders, usually important people of the village with hereditary rights over their property.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: An ____, the panchayat represented various castes and communities in the village
cards.back: An oligarchy, the panchayat represented various castes and communities in the village
cards.quote: An oligarchy, the panchayat represented various castes and communities in the village

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The decisions made by these panchayats were ____ on the members.
cards.back: The decisions made by these panchayats were binding on the members.
cards.quote: The decisions made by these panchayats were binding on the members.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The panchayat was headed by a headman known as ____ or ____.
cards.back: The panchayat was headed by a headman known as muqaddam or mandal.
cards.quote: The panchayat was headed by a headman known as muqaddam or mandal.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How was the headman chosen, and how long did he hold office?
cards.back: Some sources suggest that the headman was chosen through the consensus of the village elders, and that this choice had to be ratified by the zamindar. Headmen held office as long as they enjoyed the confidence of the village elders, failing which they could be dismissed by them.
cards.quote: Some sources suggest that the headman was chosen through the consensus of the village elders, and that this choice had to be ratified by the zamindar. Headmen held office as long as they enjoyed the confidence of the village elders, failing which they could be dismissed by them.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was the chief function of the headman?
cards.back: The chief function of the headman was to supervise the preparation of village accounts, assisted by the accountant or patwari of the panchayat.
cards.quote: The chief function of the headman was to supervise the preparation of village accounts, assisted by the accountant or patwari of the panchayat.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Of what were the mandals principally accused?
cards.back: The mandals often misused their positions. They were principally accused of defrauding village accounts in connivance with the patwari, and for underassessing the revenue they owed from their own lands in order to pass the additional burden on to the smaller cultivator.
cards.quote: The mandals often misused their positions. They were principally accused of defrauding village accounts in connivance with the patwari, and for underassessing the revenue they owed from their own lands in order to pass the additional burden on to the smaller cultivator.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did the panchayat get its funds, and what were they used for?
cards.back: The panchayat derived its funds from contributions made by individuals to a common financial pool. These funds were used for defraying the costs of entertaining revenue officials who visited the village from time to time.
cards.quote: The panchayat derived its funds from contributions made by individuals to a common financial pool. These funds were used for defraying the costs of entertaining revenue officials who visited the village from time to time.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: One important function of the panchayat was to ensure that ____ among the various communities inhabiting the village were upheld.
cards.back: One important function of the panchayat was to ensure that caste boundaries among the various communities inhabiting the village were upheld.
cards.quote: One important function of the panchayat was to ensure that caste boundaries among the various communities inhabiting the village were upheld.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What punishments could panchayats inflict?
cards.back: Panchayats also had the authority to levy fines and inflict more serious forms of punishment like expulsion from the community.
cards.quote: Panchayats also had the authority to levy fines and inflict more serious forms of punishment like expulsion from the community.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In addition to the village panchayat each caste or jati in the village had its own ____.
cards.back: In addition to the village panchayat each caste or jati in the village had its own jati panchayat.
cards.quote: In addition to the village panchayat each caste or jati in the village had its own jati panchayat.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did jati panchayats do in Rajasthan?
cards.back: In Rajasthan jati panchayats arbitrated civil disputes between members of different castes.
cards.quote: In Rajasthan jati panchayats arbitrated civil disputes between members of different castes.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What does NCERT call the demand for unpaid labour imposed by the “superior” castes or officials of the state?
cards.back:
Begar
Archival records from western India — notably Rajasthan and Maharashtra — contain petitions presented to the panchayat complaining about extortionate taxation or the demand for unpaid labour (begar) imposed by the “superior” castes or officials of the state.
cards.quote: Archival records from western India — notably Rajasthan and Maharashtra — contain petitions presented to the panchayat complaining about extortionate taxation or the demand for unpaid labour (begar) imposed by the “superior” castes or officials of the state.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In the eyes of the petitioners the right to the basic minimum for survival was ____.
cards.back: In the eyes of the petitioners the right to the basic minimum for survival was sanctioned by custom.
cards.quote: In the eyes of the petitioners the right to the basic minimum for survival was sanctioned by custom.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did petitioners regard the village panchayat?
cards.back: They regarded the village panchayat as the court of appeal that would ensure that the state carried out its moral obligations and guaranteed justice.
cards.quote: They regarded the village panchayat as the court of appeal that would ensure that the state carried out its moral obligations and guaranteed justice.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did peasants do when the panchayat’s compromise on excessive revenue demands failed?
cards.back: In cases of excessive revenue demands, the panchayat often suggested compromise. In cases where reconciliation failed, peasants took recourse to more drastic forms of resistance, such as deserting the village.
cards.quote: In cases of excessive revenue demands, the panchayat often suggested compromise. In cases where reconciliation failed, peasants took recourse to more drastic forms of resistance, such as deserting the village.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What share of village households were artisans, according to Marathi documents and early British surveys?
cards.back: Marathi documents and village surveys made in the early years of British rule have revealed the existence of substantial numbers of artisans, sometimes as high as 25 per cent of the total households in the villages.
cards.quote: Marathi documents and village surveys made in the early years of British rule have revealed the existence of substantial numbers of artisans, sometimes as high as 25 per cent of the total households in the villages.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How were village artisans most commonly compensated?
cards.back: The most common way of doing so was by giving them a share of the harvest, or an allotment of land, perhaps cultivable wastes, which was likely to be decided by the panchayat.
cards.quote: The most common way of doing so was by giving them a share of the harvest, or an allotment of land, perhaps cultivable wastes, which was likely to be decided by the panchayat.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In Maharashtra such lands became the artisans’ ____ or ____ – their hereditary holding.
cards.back: In Maharashtra such lands became the artisans’ miras or watan – their hereditary holding.
cards.quote: In Maharashtra such lands became the artisans’ miras or watan – their hereditary holding.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: By what name was the Bengal zamindars’ practice of paying artisans an allowance and diet money later described?
cards.back:
The jajmani system
For example, eighteenth-century records tell us of zamindars in Bengal who remunerated blacksmiths, carpenters, even goldsmiths for their work by paying them “a small daily allowance and diet money”. This later came to be described as the jajmani system, though the term was not in vogue in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
cards.quote: For example, eighteenth-century records tell us of zamindars in Bengal who remunerated blacksmiths, carpenters, even goldsmiths for their work by paying them “a small daily allowance and diet money”. This later came to be described as the jajmani system, though the term was not in vogue in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why was the village not a “little republic” of equals, despite what some British officials saw?
cards.back: Some British officials in the nineteenth century saw the village as a “little republic” made up of fraternal partners sharing resources and labour in a collective. However, this was not a sign of rural egalitarianism. There was individual ownership of assets and deep inequities based on caste and gender distinctions.
cards.quote: Some British officials in the nineteenth century saw the village as a “little republic” made up of fraternal partners sharing resources and labour in a collective. However, this was not a sign of rural egalitarianism. There was individual ownership of assets and deep inequities based on caste and gender distinctions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: A group of ____ decided the affairs of the village, exploited the weaker sections and had the authority to dispense justice.
cards.back: A group of powerful individuals decided the affairs of the village, exploited the weaker sections and had the authority to dispense justice.
cards.quote: A group of powerful individuals decided the affairs of the village, exploited the weaker sections and had the authority to dispense justice.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: More importantly, a ____ had already developed through trade between villages and towns.
cards.back: More importantly, a cash nexus had already developed through trade between villages and towns.
cards.quote: More importantly, a cash nexus had already developed through trade between villages and towns.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In what form was revenue assessed and collected in the Mughal heartland?
cards.back: In the Mughal heartland too, revenue was assessed and collected in cash.
cards.quote: In the Mughal heartland too, revenue was assessed and collected in cash.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which French traveller found it remarkable that almost every Indian village had a moneychanger called a Shroff?
cards.back: The seventeenth-century French traveller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier found it remarkable that in “India a village must be very small indeed if it has not a moneychanger called a Shroff.
cards.quote: The seventeenth-century French traveller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier found it remarkable that in “India a village must be very small indeed if it has not a moneychanger called a Shroff.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Men vs women: which agricultural tasks did each perform?
cards.back: Men tilled and ploughed, while women sowed, weeded, threshed and winnowed the harvest.
cards.quote: Men tilled and ploughed, while women sowed, weeded, threshed and winnowed the harvest.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What restrictions applied to menstruating women in western India and Bengal?
cards.back: Menstruating women, for instance, were not allowed to touch the plough or the potter’s wheel in western India, or enter the groves where betel-leaves (paan) were grown in Bengal.
cards.quote: Menstruating women, for instance, were not allowed to touch the plough or the potter’s wheel in western India, or enter the groves where betel-leaves (paan) were grown in Bengal.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which artisanal tasks depended on female labour?
cards.back: Artisanal tasks such as spinning yarn, sifting and kneading clay for pottery, and embroidery were among the many aspects of production dependent on female labour.
cards.quote: Artisanal tasks such as spinning yarn, sifting and kneading clay for pottery, and embroidery were among the many aspects of production dependent on female labour.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The more ____ the product, the greater the demand on women’s labour to produce it.
cards.back: The more commercialised the product, the greater the demand on women’s labour to produce it.
cards.quote: The more commercialised the product, the greater the demand on women’s labour to produce it.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why were women an important resource in agrarian society?
cards.back: Women were considered an important resource in agrarian society also because they were child bearers in a society dependent on labour.
cards.quote: Women were considered an important resource in agrarian society also because they were child bearers in a society dependent on labour.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What payment did marriages in many rural communities require, and was remarriage legitimate?
cards.back: Marriages in many rural communities required the payment of bride-price rather than dowry to the bride’s family. Remarriage was considered legitimate both among divorced and widowed women.
cards.quote: Marriages in many rural communities required the payment of bride-price rather than dowry to the bride’s family. Remarriage was considered legitimate both among divorced and widowed women.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did women petition the village panchayat about?
cards.back: Wives protested against the infidelity of their husbands or the neglect of the wife and children by the male head of the household, the grihasthi.
cards.quote: Wives protested against the infidelity of their husbands or the neglect of the wife and children by the male head of the household, the grihasthi.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Amongst the landed gentry, women had the right to ____.
cards.back: Amongst the landed gentry, women had the right to inherit property.
cards.quote: Amongst the landed gentry, women had the right to inherit property.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which famous eighteenth-century zamindari had a woman at the helm?
cards.back: In fact, one of the biggest and most famous of the eighteenth-century zamindaris, that of Rajshahi, had a woman at the helm.
cards.quote: In fact, one of the biggest and most famous of the eighteenth-century zamindaris, that of Rajshahi, had a woman at the helm.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What are the terms for dense forest and for scrubland in NCERT’s account of forests in rural India?
cards.back:
Dense forest: jangal; scrubland: kharbandi
Apart from the intensively cultivated provinces in northern and north-western India, huge swathes of forests — dense forest (jangal) or scrubland (kharbandi) — existed all over eastern India, central India, northern India (including the Terai on the Indo-Nepal border), Jharkhand, and in peninsular India down the Western Ghats and the Deccan plateau.
cards.quote: Apart from the intensively cultivated provinces in northern and north-western India, huge swathes of forests — dense forest (jangal) or scrubland (kharbandi) — existed all over eastern India, central India, northern India (including the Terai on the Indo-Nepal border), Jharkhand, and in peninsular India down the Western Ghats and the Deccan plateau.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What average forest cover do informed conjectures suggest for all India in the sixteenth-seventeenth centuries?
cards.back:
40 per cent
Though it is nearly impossible to set an all-India average of the forest cover for this period, informed conjectures based on contemporary sources suggest an average of 40 per cent.
cards.quote: Though it is nearly impossible to set an all-India average of the forest cover for this period, informed conjectures based on contemporary sources suggest an average of 40 per cent.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Forest dwellers were termed ____ in contemporary texts.
cards.back: Forest dwellers were termed jangli in contemporary texts.
cards.quote: Forest dwellers were termed jangli in contemporary texts.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the three livelihoods of those termed jangli.
cards.back:
gathering of forest produce
hunting
shifting agriculture
cards.quote: Rather, the term described those whose livelihood came from the gathering of forest produce, hunting and shifting agriculture.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: For the state, the forest was a subversive place – a place of refuge (____) for troublemakers.
cards.back: For the state, the forest was a subversive place – a place of refuge (mawas) for troublemakers.
cards.quote: For the state, the forest was a subversive place – a place of refuge (mawas) for troublemakers.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did the peshkash levied from forest people often include?
cards.back: So the peshkash levied from forest people often included a supply of elephants.
cards.quote: So the peshkash levied from forest people often included a supply of elephants.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was peshkash?
cards.back: Peshkash was a form of tribute collected by the Mughal state.
cards.quote: Peshkash was a form of tribute collected by the Mughal state.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was a pargana?
cards.back: Pargana was an administrative subdivision of a Mughal province.
cards.quote: Pargana was an administrative subdivision of a Mughal province.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In the Mughal political ideology, the ____ symbolised the overwhelming concern of the state to relate to all its subjects, rich and poor.
cards.back: In the Mughal political ideology, the hunt symbolised the overwhelming concern of the state to relate to all its subjects, rich and poor.
cards.quote: In the Mughal political ideology, the hunt symbolised the overwhelming concern of the state to relate to all its subjects, rich and poor.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did regular hunting expeditions enable the emperor to do, according to court historians?
cards.back: Regular hunting expeditions, so court historians tell us, enabled the emperor to travel across the extensive territories of his empire and personally attend to the grievances of its inhabitants.
cards.quote: Regular hunting expeditions, so court historians tell us, enabled the emperor to travel across the extensive territories of his empire and personally attend to the grievances of its inhabitants.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The spread of ____ was an important external factor that impinged on the lives of those who lived in the forests.
cards.back: The spread of commercial agriculture was an important external factor that impinged on the lives of those who lived in the forests.
cards.quote: The spread of commercial agriculture was an important external factor that impinged on the lives of those who lived in the forests.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which forest product became a major item of overseas export in the seventeenth century?
cards.back: Forest products – like honey, beeswax and gum lac – were in great demand. Some, such as gum lac, became major items of overseas export from India in the seventeenth century.
cards.quote: Forest products – like honey, beeswax and gum lac – were in great demand. Some, such as gum lac, became major items of overseas export from India in the seventeenth century.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did many tribal chiefs become?
cards.back: Many tribal chiefs had become zamindars, some even became kings.
cards.quote: Many tribal chiefs had become zamindars, some even became kings.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In Assam, the Ahom kings had their ____, people who were obliged to render military service in exchange for land.
cards.back: In Assam, the Ahom kings had their paiks, people who were obliged to render military service in exchange for land.
cards.quote: In Assam, the Ahom kings had their paiks, people who were obliged to render military service in exchange for land.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: By when does NCERT say the transition from a tribal to a monarchical system became fully developed?
cards.back:
By the sixteenth century
Though the transition from a tribal to a monarchical system had started much earlier, the process seems to have become fully developed only by the sixteenth century.
cards.quote: Though the transition from a tribal to a monarchical system had started much earlier, the process seems to have become fully developed only by the sixteenth century.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which kings subjugated a number of neighbouring tribes in a long sequence of wars?
cards.back: the Koch kings fought and subjugated a number of neighbouring tribes in a long sequence of wars through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
cards.quote: the Koch kings fought and subjugated a number of neighbouring tribes in a long sequence of wars through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What role have some historians suggested sufi saints (pirs) played in forested zones?
cards.back: Some historians have indeed suggested that sufi saints (pirs) played a major role in the slow acceptance of Islam among agricultural communities emerging in newly colonised places
cards.quote: Some historians have indeed suggested that sufi saints (pirs) played a major role in the slow acceptance of Islam among agricultural communities emerging in newly colonised places

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who were the zamindars?
cards.back: These were the zamindars who were landed proprietors who also enjoyed certain social and economic privileges by virtue of their superior status in rural society.
cards.quote: These were the zamindars who were landed proprietors who also enjoyed certain social and economic privileges by virtue of their superior status in rural society.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the two factors that accounted for the elevated status of zamindars.
cards.back:
Caste
they performed certain services (khidmat) for the state
cards.quote: Caste was one factor that accounted for the elevated status of zamindars; another factor was that they performed certain services (khidmat) for the state.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The zamindars held extensive personal lands termed ____, meaning property.
cards.back: The zamindars held extensive personal lands termed milkiyat, meaning property.
cards.quote: The zamindars held extensive personal lands termed milkiyat, meaning property.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How were milkiyat lands cultivated?
cards.back: Milkiyat lands were cultivated for the private use of zamindars, often with the help of hired or servile labour.
cards.quote: Milkiyat lands were cultivated for the private use of zamindars, often with the help of hired or servile labour.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What could zamindars do with their milkiyat lands?
cards.back: The zamindars could sell, bequeath or mortgage these lands at will.
cards.quote: The zamindars could sell, bequeath or mortgage these lands at will.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Besides their personal milkiyat lands, what two sources of power did zamindars have, per NCERT?
cards.back: Zamindars also derived their power from the fact that they could often collect revenue on behalf of the state, a service for which they were compensated financially. Control over military resources was another source of power.
cards.quote: Zamindars also derived their power from the fact that they could often collect revenue on behalf of the state, a service for which they were compensated financially. Control over military resources was another source of power.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Most zamindars had fortresses (____) as well as an armed contingent comprising units of cavalry, artillery and infantry.
cards.back: Most zamindars had fortresses (qilachas) as well as an armed contingent comprising units of cavalry, artillery and infantry.
cards.quote: Most zamindars had fortresses (qilachas) as well as an armed contingent comprising units of cavalry, artillery and infantry.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: If Mughal rural social relations are visualised as a pyramid, what did zamindars constitute?
cards.back:
Its very narrow apex
if we visualise social relations in the Mughal countryside as a pyramid, zamindars clearly constituted its very narrow apex.
cards.quote: Thus if we visualise social relations in the Mughal countryside as a pyramid, zamindars clearly constituted its very narrow apex.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was the imperial order that confirmed a zamindar called, per NCERT?
cards.back:
Sanad
The dispossession of weaker people by a powerful military chieftain was quite often a way of expanding a zamindari. It is, however, unlikely that the state would have allowed such a show of aggression by a zamindar unless he had been confirmed by an imperial order (sanad).
cards.quote: The dispossession of weaker people by a powerful military chieftain was quite often a way of expanding a zamindari. It is, however, unlikely that the state would have allowed such a show of aggression by a zamindar unless he had been confirmed by an imperial order (sanad).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the four slow processes of zamindari consolidation.
cards.back: More important were the slow processes of zamindari consolidation, which are also documented in sources. These involved colonisation of new lands, by transfer of rights, by order of the state and by purchase.
cards.quote: More important were the slow processes of zamindari consolidation, which are also documented in sources. These involved colonisation of new lands, by transfer of rights, by order of the state and by purchase.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which groups consolidated clan- or lineage-based zamindaris in northern India and in Bengal?
cards.back: the Rajputs and Jats adopted these strategies to consolidate their control over vast swathes of territory in northern India. Likewise, peasant-pastoralists (like the Sadgops) carved out powerful zamindaris in areas of central and southwestern Bengal.
cards.quote: the Rajputs and Jats adopted these strategies to consolidate their control over vast swathes of territory in northern India. Likewise, peasant-pastoralists (like the Sadgops) carved out powerful zamindaris in areas of central and southwestern Bengal.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did zamindars help in the colonisation of agricultural land?
cards.back: Zamindars spearheaded the colonisation of agricultural land, and helped in settling cultivators by providing them with the means of cultivation, including cash loans.
cards.quote: Zamindars spearheaded the colonisation of agricultural land, and helped in settling cultivators by providing them with the means of cultivation, including cash loans.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did the buying and selling of zamindaris accelerate?
cards.back: The buying and selling of zamindaris accelerated the process of monetisation in the countryside.
cards.quote: The buying and selling of zamindaris accelerated the process of monetisation in the countryside.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: There is evidence to show that zamindars often established markets (____) to which peasants also came to sell their produce.
cards.back: There is evidence to show that zamindars often established markets (haats) to which peasants also came to sell their produce.
cards.quote: There is evidence to show that zamindars often established markets (haats) to which peasants also came to sell their produce.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Although zamindars were an exploitative class, what three elements did their relationship with the peasantry have?
cards.back:
Reciprocity, paternalism and patronage
Although there can be little doubt that zamindars were an exploitative class, their relationship with the peasantry had an element of reciprocity, paternalism and patronage.
cards.quote: Although there can be little doubt that zamindars were an exploitative class, their relationship with the peasantry had an element of reciprocity, paternalism and patronage.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did the bhakti saints portray zamindars and moneylenders?
cards.back: First, the bhakti saints, who eloquently condemned caste-based and other forms of oppression (see also Chapter 6), did not portray the zamindars (or, interestingly, the moneylender) as exploiters or oppressors of the peasantry.
cards.quote: First, the bhakti saints, who eloquently condemned caste-based and other forms of oppression (see also Chapter 6), did not portray the zamindars (or, interestingly, the moneylender) as exploiters or oppressors of the peasantry.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Whom did peasants support in the seventeenth-century agrarian uprisings in north India?
cards.back: Second, in a large number of agrarian uprisings which erupted in north India in the seventeenth century, zamindars often received the support of the peasantry in their struggle against the state.
cards.quote: Second, in a large number of agrarian uprisings which erupted in north India in the seventeenth century, zamindars often received the support of the peasantry in their struggle against the state.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Revenue from the land was the ____ of the Mughal Empire.
cards.back: Revenue from the land was the economic mainstay of the Mughal Empire.
cards.quote: Revenue from the land was the economic mainstay of the Mughal Empire.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which office was responsible for supervising the fiscal system of the empire?
cards.back: This apparatus included the office (daftar) of the diwan who was responsible for supervising the fiscal system of the empire.
cards.quote: This apparatus included the office (daftar) of the diwan who was responsible for supervising the fiscal system of the empire.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the two stages of the land revenue arrangements.
cards.back:
assessment
actual collection
cards.quote: The land revenue arrangements consisted of two stages – first, assessment and then actual collection.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Jama vs hasil: the difference.
cards.back: The jama was the amount assessed, as opposed to hasil, the amount collected.
cards.quote: The jama was the amount assessed, as opposed to hasil, the amount collected.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Akbar decree about the mode of payment in the amil-guzar’s list of duties?
cards.back: In his list of duties of the amil-guzar or revenue collector, Akbar decreed that while he should strive to make cultivators pay in cash, the option of payment in kind was also to be kept open.
cards.quote: In his list of duties of the amil-guzar or revenue collector, Akbar decreed that while he should strive to make cultivators pay in cash, the option of payment in kind was also to be kept open.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Aurangzeb instruct his revenue officials to do in 1665?
cards.back: in 1665, Aurangzeb expressly instructed his revenue officials to prepare annual records of the number of cultivators in each village (Source 7).
cards.quote: in 1665, Aurangzeb expressly instructed his revenue officials to prepare annual records of the number of cultivators in each village (Source 7).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who was an amin?
cards.back: Amin was an official responsible for ensuring that imperial regulations were carried out in the provinces.
cards.quote: Amin was an official responsible for ensuring that imperial regulations were carried out in the provinces.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the four classes of land under Akbar, as listed in the Ain.
cards.back:
Polaj is land which is annually cultivated for each crop in succession and is never allowed to lie fallow.
Parauti is land left out of cultivation for a time that it may recover its strength.
Chachar is land that has lain fallow for three or four years.
Banjar is land uncultivated for five years and more.
cards.quote: Polaj is land which is annually cultivated for each crop in succession and is never allowed to lie fallow. Parauti is land left out of cultivation for a time that it may recover its strength. Chachar is land that has lain fallow for three or four years. Banjar is land uncultivated for five years and more.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Source 5: Classification of lands under Akbar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How was revenue assessed on polaj and parauti land under Akbar?
cards.back: Of the first two kinds of land, there are three classes, good, middling, and bad. They add together the produce of each sort, and the third of this represents the medium produce, one-third part of which is exacted as the Royal dues.
cards.quote: Of the first two kinds of land, there are three classes, good, middling, and bad. They add together the produce of each sort, and the third of this represents the medium produce, one-third part of which is exacted as the Royal dues.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Source 5: Classification of lands under Akbar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was the mansabdari, and what did it look after?
cards.back: The Mughal administrative system had at its apex a military-cum-bureaucratic apparatus (mansabdari) which was responsible for looking after the civil and military affairs of the state.
cards.quote: The Mughal administrative system had at its apex a military-cum-bureaucratic apparatus (mansabdari) which was responsible for looking after the civil and military affairs of the state.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How were mansabdars paid?
cards.back: Some mansabdars were paid in cash (naqdi), while the majority of them were paid through assignments of revenue (jagirs) in different regions of the empire. They were transferred periodically.
cards.quote: Some mansabdars were paid in cash (naqdi), while the majority of them were paid through assignments of revenue (jagirs) in different regions of the empire. They were transferred periodically.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: First, ____ : in the Hindi language kan signifies grain, and kut, estimates
cards.back: First, kankut : in the Hindi language kan signifies grain, and kut, estimates
cards.quote: First, kankut : in the Hindi language kan signifies grain, and kut, estimates

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is batai (bhaoli) in revenue collection?
cards.back: Secondly, batai, also called bhaoli, the crops are reaped and stacked and divided by agreement in the presence of the parties.
cards.quote: Secondly, batai, also called bhaoli, the crops are reaped and stacked and divided by agreement in the presence of the parties.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Thirdly, ____, when they divide the fields after they are sown.
cards.back: Thirdly, khet-batai, when they divide the fields after they are sown.
cards.quote: Thirdly, khet-batai, when they divide the fields after they are sown.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the large territorial empires of Asia alongside the Mughal Empire.
cards.back:
Ming (China)
Safavid (Iran)
Ottoman (Turkey)
cards.quote: These empires were the Ming (China), Safavid (Iran) and Ottoman (Turkey).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Voyages of discovery and the opening up of the ____ resulted in a massive expansion of Asia’s (particularly India’s) trade with Europe.
cards.back: Voyages of discovery and the opening up of the New World resulted in a massive expansion of Asia’s (particularly India’s) trade with Europe.
cards.quote: Voyages of discovery and the opening up of the New World resulted in a massive expansion of Asia’s (particularly India’s) trade with Europe.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did an expanding trade bring into Asia, and where did a large part of it gravitate?
cards.back: An expanding trade brought in huge amounts of silver bullion into Asia to pay for goods procured from India, and a large part of that bullion gravitated towards India.
cards.quote: An expanding trade brought in huge amounts of silver bullion into Asia to pay for goods procured from India, and a large part of that bullion gravitated towards India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What marked the period between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries in the availability of metal currency?
cards.back: As a result, the period between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries was also marked by a remarkable stability in the availability of metal currency, particularly the silver rupya in India.
cards.quote: As a result, the period between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries was also marked by a remarkable stability in the availability of metal currency, particularly the silver rupya in India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did the stability of silver facilitate?
cards.back: This facilitated an unprecedented expansion of minting of coins and the circulation of money in the economy as well as the ability of the Mughal state to extract taxes and revenue in cash.
cards.quote: This facilitated an unprecedented expansion of minting of coins and the circulation of money in the economy as well as the ability of the Mughal state to extract taxes and revenue in cash.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was the Ain-i Akbari?
cards.back: The Ain-i Akbari was the culmination of a large historical, administrative project of classification undertaken by Abu’l Fazl at the order of Emperor Akbar.
cards.quote: The Ain-i Akbari was the culmination of a large historical, administrative project of classification undertaken by Abu’l Fazl at the order of Emperor Akbar.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: 8. The Ain-i Akbari of Abu’l Fazl Allami

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: When was the Ain-i Akbari completed, and after how many revisions?
cards.back:
In 1598, after five revisions
The Ain-i Akbari was the culmination of a large historical, administrative project of classification undertaken by Abu’l Fazl at the order of Emperor Akbar. It was completed in 1598, the forty-second regnal year of the emperor, after having gone through five revisions.
cards.quote: The Ain-i Akbari was the culmination of a large historical, administrative project of classification undertaken by Abu’l Fazl at the order of Emperor Akbar. It was completed in 1598, the forty-second regnal year of the emperor, after having gone through five revisions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: 8. The Ain-i Akbari of Abu’l Fazl Allami

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was the Ain-i Akbari, the third book of the Akbar Nama, organised as?
cards.back: The Ain-i Akbari, the third book, was organised as a compendium of imperial regulations and a gazetteer of the empire.
cards.quote: The Ain-i Akbari, the third book, was organised as a compendium of imperial regulations and a gazetteer of the empire.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: 8. The Ain-i Akbari of Abu’l Fazl Allami

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How many books (daftars) make up the Ain, and how many describe the administration?
cards.back: The Ain is made up of five books (daftars), of which the first three books describe the administration.
cards.quote: The Ain is made up of five books (daftars), of which the first three books describe the administration.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: 8. The Ain-i Akbari of Abu’l Fazl Allami

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What does the first book of the Ain, manzil-abadi, concern?
cards.back: The first book, called manzil-abadi, concerns the imperial household and its maintenance.
cards.quote: The first book, called manzil-abadi, concerns the imperial household and its maintenance.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: 8. The Ain-i Akbari of Abu’l Fazl Allami

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What does the second book of the Ain, sipah-abadi, cover?
cards.back: The second book, sipah-abadi, covers the military and civil administration and the establishment of servants.
cards.quote: The second book, sipah-abadi, covers the military and civil administration and the establishment of servants.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: 8. The Ain-i Akbari of Abu’l Fazl Allami

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What does the third book of the Ain, mulk-abadi, deal with?
cards.back: The third book, mulk-abadi, is the one which deals with the fiscal side of the empire and provides rich quantitative information on revenue rates, followed by the “Account of the Twelve Provinces”.
cards.quote: The third book, mulk-abadi, is the one which deals with the fiscal side of the empire and provides rich quantitative information on revenue rates, followed by the “Account of the Twelve Provinces”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: 8. The Ain-i Akbari of Abu’l Fazl Allami

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What do the fourth and fifth books of the Ain deal with?
cards.back: The fourth and fifth books (daftars) deal with the religious, literary and cultural traditions of the people of India and also contain a collection of Akbar’s “auspicious sayings”.
cards.quote: The fourth and fifth books (daftars) deal with the religious, literary and cultural traditions of the people of India and also contain a collection of Akbar’s “auspicious sayings”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: 8. The Ain-i Akbari of Abu’l Fazl Allami

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What shows Abu’l Fazl’s search for authenticity in the Ain?
cards.back: That the manuscript was revised five times by the author would suggest a high degree of caution on the part of Abu’l Fazl and a search for authenticity.
cards.quote: That the manuscript was revised five times by the author would suggest a high degree of caution on the part of Abu’l Fazl and a search for authenticity.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: 8. The Ain-i Akbari of Abu’l Fazl Allami

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did Abu’l Fazl treat oral testimonies and numeric data?
cards.back: oral testimonies were cross-checked and verified before being incorporated as “facts” in the chronicle. In the quantitative sections, all numeric data were reproduced in words so as to minimise the chances of subsequent transcriptional errors.
cards.quote: oral testimonies were cross-checked and verified before being incorporated as “facts” in the chronicle. In the quantitative sections, all numeric data were reproduced in words so as to minimise the chances of subsequent transcriptional errors.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.back: Numerous errors in totalling have been detected.

cards.front: What is the limitation of the Ain’s quantitative data?
cards.back: Another limitation of the Ain is the somewhat skewed nature of the quantitative data. Data were not collected uniformly from all provinces.
cards.quote: Another limitation of the Ain is the somewhat skewed nature of the quantitative data. Data were not collected uniformly from all provinces.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: For which regions is caste data on zamindars not available in the Ain?
cards.back: while for many subas detailed information was compiled about the caste composition of the zamindars, such information is not available for Bengal and Orissa.
cards.quote: while for many subas detailed information was compiled about the caste composition of the zamindars, such information is not available for Bengal and Orissa.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why is the Ain’s list of prices and wages of limited relevance?
cards.back: The detailed list of prices and wages that the Ain does provide is mainly derived from data pertaining to areas in or around the imperial capital of Agra, and is therefore of limited relevance for the rest of the country.
cards.quote: The detailed list of prices and wages that the Ain does provide is mainly derived from data pertaining to areas in or around the imperial capital of Agra, and is therefore of limited relevance for the rest of the country.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: 8. The Ain-i Akbari of Abu’l Fazl Allami

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What breakthrough did Abu’l Fazl achieve in the tradition of medieval chroniclers?
cards.back: By providing fascinating glimpses into the structure and organisation of the Mughal Empire and by giving us quantitative information about its products and people, Abu’l Fazl achieved a major breakthrough in the tradition of medieval chroniclers who wrote mostly about remarkable political events – wars, conquests, political machinations, and dynastic turmoil.
cards.quote: By providing fascinating glimpses into the structure and organisation of the Mughal Empire and by giving us quantitative information about its products and people, Abu’l Fazl achieved a major breakthrough in the tradition of medieval chroniclers who wrote mostly about remarkable political events – wars, conquests, political machinations, and dynastic turmoil.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: 8. The Ain-i Akbari of Abu’l Fazl Allami

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why does the Ain constitute a benchmark for studying India at the turn of the seventeenth century?
cards.back: The Ain completely departed from this tradition as it recorded information about the empire and the people of India, and thus constitutes a benchmark for studying India at the turn of the seventeenth century.
cards.quote: The Ain completely departed from this tradition as it recorded information about the empire and the people of India, and thus constitutes a benchmark for studying India at the turn of the seventeenth century.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: 8. The Ain-i Akbari of Abu’l Fazl Allami

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: The value of the Ain’s quantitative evidence is ____ where the study of agrarian relations is concerned.
cards.back: The value of the Ain’s quantitative evidence is uncontested where the study of agrarian relations is concerned.
cards.quote: The value of the Ain’s quantitative evidence is uncontested where the study of agrarian relations is concerned.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When, and where, did the sepoys first break out in mutiny in 1857?
cards.back: Late in the afternoon of 10 May 1857, the sepoys in the cantonment of Meerut broke out in mutiny.
cards.quote: Late in the afternoon of 10 May 1857, the sepoys in the cantonment of Meerut broke out in mutiny.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When did the Meerut sepoys arrive at the gates of the Red Fort?
cards.back: The sepoys arrived at the gates of the Red Fort early in the morning on 11 May.
cards.quote: The sepoys arrived at the gates of the Red Fort early in the morning on 11 May.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
