cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the sepoys tell Bahadur Shah about why they had come from Meerut?
cards.back: We have come from Meerut after killing all the Englishmen there, because they asked us to bite bullets that were coated with the fat of cows and pigs with our teeth. This has corrupted the faith of Hindus and Muslims alike.
cards.quote: We have come from Meerut after killing all the Englishmen there, because they asked us to bite bullets that were coated with the fat of cows and pigs with our teeth. This has corrupted the faith of Hindus and Muslims alike.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: The revolt thus acquired a kind of ____ because it could now be carried on in the name of the Mughal emperor.
cards.back: The revolt thus acquired a kind of legitimacy because it could now be carried on in the name of the Mughal emperor.
cards.quote: The revolt thus acquired a kind of legitimacy because it could now be carried on in the name of the Mughal emperor.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: After Delhi fell and Bahadur Shah blessed the rebellion, what happened in the Gangetic valley?
cards.back: Cantonment after cantonment in the Gangetic valley and some to the west of Delhi rose in mutiny.
cards.quote: Cantonment after cantonment in the Gangetic valley and some to the west of Delhi rose in mutiny.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the mutiny begin in a cantonment? Steps, in order.
cards.back:
The sepoys began their action with a signal: in many places it was the firing of the evening gun or the sounding of the bugle.
They first seized the bell of arms and plundered the treasury.
They then attacked government buildings – the jail, treasury, telegraph office, record room, bungalows – burning all records.
cards.quote: The sepoys began their action with a signal: in many places it was the firing of the evening gun or the sounding of the bugle. They first seized the bell of arms and plundered the treasury. They then attacked government buildings – the jail, treasury, telegraph office, record room, bungalows – burning all records.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: In which languages were proclamations put up in the cities, and what did they call for?
cards.back: Proclamations in Hindi, Urdu and Persian were put up in the cities calling upon the population, both Hindus and Muslims, to unite, rise and exterminate the firangis.
cards.quote: Proclamations in Hindi, Urdu and Persian were put up in the cities calling upon the population, both Hindus and Muslims, to unite, rise and exterminate the firangis.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What is a bell of arms?
cards.back: Bell of arms is a storeroom in which weapons are kept.
cards.quote: Bell of arms is a storeroom in which weapons are kept.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What does the term firangi mean?
cards.back: Firangi, a term of Persian origin, possibly derived from Frank (from which France gets its name), is used in Urdu and Hindi, often in a derogatory sense, to designate foreigners.
cards.quote: Firangi, a term of Persian origin, possibly derived from Frank (from which France gets its name), is used in Urdu and Hindi, often in a derogatory sense, to designate foreigners.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: In which major towns did moneylenders and the rich become objects of rebel wrath?
cards.back: In major towns like Lucknow, Kanpur and Bareilly, moneylenders and the rich also became the objects of rebel wrath.
cards.quote: In major towns like Lucknow, Kanpur and Bareilly, moneylenders and the rich also became the objects of rebel wrath.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: After the sepoys' mutiny quickly became a rebellion, defiance of what was general?
cards.back: There was a general defiance of all kinds of authority and hierarchy.
cards.quote: The mutiny in the sepoy ranks quickly became a rebellion. There was a general defiance of all kinds of authority and hierarchy.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did one British officer describe the collapse of British rule in May and June 1857?
cards.back: British rule, as one British officer noted, “collapsed like a house made of cards”.
cards.quote: British rule, as one British officer noted, “collapsed like a house made of cards”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What explained the similarity in the pattern of the 1857 revolt in different places?
cards.back:
Its planning and coordination
The reason for the similarity in the pattern of the revolt in different places lay partly in its planning and coordination. It is clear that there was communication between the sepoy lines of various cantonments.
cards.quote: The reason for the similarity in the pattern of the revolt in different places lay partly in its planning and coordination. It is clear that there was communication between the sepoy lines of various cantonments.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the 7th Awadh Irregular Cavalry write to the 48th Native Infantry after refusing the new cartridges?
cards.back: After the 7th Awadh Irregular Cavalry had refused to accept the new cartridges in early May, they wrote to the 48th Native Infantry that “they had acted for the faith and awaited the 48th’s orders”.
cards.quote: After the 7th Awadh Irregular Cavalry had refused to accept the new cartridges in early May, they wrote to the 48th Native Infantry that “they had acted for the faith and awaited the 48th’s orders”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How was the dispute over Captain Hearsey between the 41st Native Infantry and the Military Police settled?
cards.back: The Military Police refused to do either, and it was decided that the matter would be settled by a panchayat composed of native officers drawn from each regiment.
cards.quote: The Military Police refused to do either, and it was decided that the matter would be settled by a panchayat composed of native officers drawn from each regiment.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who, per NCERT, were the makers of the 1857 rebellion, deciding their own future together in their lines?
cards.back: The sepoys were the makers of their own rebellion.
cards.quote: The sepoys were the makers of their own rebellion.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Define mutiny.
cards.back: Mutiny – a collective disobedience of rules and regulations within the armed forces
cards.quote: Mutiny – a collective disobedience of rules and regulations within the armed forces

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Define revolt.
cards.back: Revolt – a rebellion of people against established authority and power.
cards.quote: Revolt – a rebellion of people against established authority and power.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Mutiny vs revolt in the context of 1857: who is meant by each?
cards.back: In the context of the revolt of 1857 the term revolt refers primarily to the uprising of the civilian population (peasants, zamindars, rajas, jagirdars) while the mutiny was of the sepoys.
cards.quote: In the context of the revolt of 1857 the term revolt refers primarily to the uprising of the civilian population (peasants, zamindars, rajas, jagirdars) while the mutiny was of the sepoys.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did Bahadur Shah first react to the sepoys’ request to lead the revolt, and why did he agree?
cards.back: Bahadur Shah’s first reaction was one of horror and rejection. It was only when some sepoys had moved into the Mughal court within the Red Fort, in defiance of normal court etiquette, that the old emperor, realising he had very few options, agreed to be the nominal leader of the rebellion.
cards.quote: Bahadur Shah’s first reaction was one of horror and rejection. It was only when some sepoys had moved into the Mughal court within the Red Fort, in defiance of normal court etiquette, that the old emperor, realising he had very few options, agreed to be the nominal leader of the rebellion.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Elsewhere, who were forced or hailed to lead the revolt in Kanpur, Jhansi, Arrah and Lucknow?
cards.back:
In Kanpur, the sepoys and the people of the town gave Nana Sahib, the successor to Peshwa Baji Rao II, no choice save to join the revolt as their leader.
In Jhansi, the rani was forced by the popular pressure around her to assume the leadership of the uprising.
So was Kunwar Singh, a local zamindar in Arrah in Bihar.
the populace in Lucknow celebrated the fall of British rule by hailing Birjis Qadr, the young son of the Nawab, as their leader.
cards.quote: In Kanpur, the sepoys and the people of the town gave Nana Sahib, the successor to Peshwa Baji Rao II, no choice save to join the revolt as their leader. In Jhansi, the rani was forced by the popular pressure around her to assume the leadership of the uprising. So was Kunwar Singh, a local zamindar in Arrah in Bihar. In Awadh, where the displacement of the popular Nawab Wajid Ali Shah and the annexation of the state were still very fresh in the memory of the people, the populace in Lucknow celebrated the fall of British rule by hailing Birjis Qadr, the young son of the Nawab, as their leader.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Where did Nana Sahib escape to at the end of 1858?
cards.back: At the end of 1858, when the rebellion collapsed, Nana Sahib escaped to Nepal.
cards.quote: At the end of 1858, when the rebellion collapsed, Nana Sahib escaped to Nepal.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who carried the message of rebellion where the leaders were not people of the court?
cards.back: Often the message of rebellion was carried by ordinary men and women and in places by religious men too.
cards.quote: Often the message of rebellion was carried by ordinary men and women and in places by religious men too.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which local leaders rose in pargana Barout and in Singhbhum?
cards.back: Shah Mal mobilised the villagers of pargana Barout in Uttar Pradesh; Gonoo, a tribal cultivator of Singhbhum in Chotanagpur, became a rebel leader of the Kol tribals of the region.
cards.quote: Shah Mal mobilised the villagers of pargana Barout in Uttar Pradesh; Gonoo, a tribal cultivator of Singhbhum in Chotanagpur, became a rebel leader of the Kol tribals of the region.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which clan did Shah Mal belong to, and what was chaurasee des?
cards.back: He belonged to a clan of Jat cultivators whose kinship ties extended over chaurasee des (eighty-four villages).
cards.quote: He belonged to a clan of Jat cultivators whose kinship ties extended over chaurasee des (eighty-four villages).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why did Shah Mal’s men destroy the bridge and dig up metalled roads?
cards.back: Shah Mal’s men attacked government buildings, destroyed the bridge over the river, and dug up metalled roads – partly to prevent government forces from coming into the area, and partly because bridges and roads were seen as symbols of British rule.
cards.quote: Shah Mal’s men attacked government buildings, destroyed the bridge over the river, and dug up metalled roads – partly to prevent government forces from coming into the area, and partly because bridges and roads were seen as symbols of British rule.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did Shah Mal do with an English officer’s bungalow?
cards.back: Locally acknowledged as the Raja, Shah Mal took over the bungalow of an English officer, turned it into a “hall of justice”, settling disputes and dispensing judgments.
cards.quote: Locally acknowledged as the Raja, Shah Mal took over the bungalow of an English officer, turned it into a “hall of justice”, settling disputes and dispensing judgments.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When was Shah Mal killed?
cards.back: Shah Mal was killed in battle in July 1857.
cards.quote: Shah Mal was killed in battle in July 1857.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why was Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah popularly called Danka Shah?
cards.back: He moved in a palanquin, with drumbeaters in front and followers at the rear. He was therefore popularly called Danka Shah – the maulvi with the drum (danka).
cards.quote: He moved in a palanquin, with drumbeaters in front and followers at the rear. He was therefore popularly called Danka Shah – the maulvi with the drum (danka).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: Two rebels of 1857: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah seen doing in 1856?
cards.back: In 1856, he was seen moving from village to village preaching jehad (religious war) against the British and urging people to rebel.
cards.quote: In 1856, he was seen moving from village to village preaching jehad (religious war) against the British and urging people to rebel.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: Two rebels of 1857: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: In which famous battle did Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah fight and defeat Henry Lawrence’s forces?
cards.back: He fought in the famous Battle of Chinhat in which the British forces under Henry Lawrence were defeated.
cards.quote: He fought in the famous Battle of Chinhat in which the British forces under Henry Lawrence were defeated.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: Two rebels of 1857: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which rifles' cartridges did the sepoys mean when they said biting the bullets would corrupt caste and religion?
cards.back: They were referring to the cartridges of the Enfield rifles which had just been given to them.
cards.quote: They were referring to the cartridges of the Enfield rifles which had just been given to them.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What rumour spread like wildfire across the sepoy lines of North India?
cards.back: the rumour that the new cartridges were greased with the fat of cows and pigs spread like wildfire across the sepoy lines of North India.
cards.quote: the rumour that the new cartridges were greased with the fat of cows and pigs spread like wildfire across the sepoy lines of North India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did rumours say the British had mixed into the flour sold in the market?
cards.back: To this end, the rumours said, the British had mixed the bone dust of cows and pigs into the flour that was sold in the market.
cards.quote: To this end, the rumours said, the British had mixed the bone dust of cows and pigs into the flour that was sold in the market.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What fear and suspicion spread among the people about British intentions in 1857?
cards.back: There was fear and suspicion that the British wanted to convert Indians to Christianity.
cards.quote: There was fear and suspicion that the British wanted to convert Indians to Christianity.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What prophecy reinforced the response to the call for action?
cards.back: The response to the call for action was reinforced by the prophecy that British rule would come to an end on the centenary of the Battle of Plassey, on 23 June 1857.
cards.quote: The response to the call for action was reinforced by the prophecy that British rule would come to an end on the centenary of the Battle of Plassey, on 23 June 1857.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How were chapattis distributed from village to village?
cards.back: Reports came from various parts of North India that chapattis were being distributed from village to village. A person would come at night and give a chapatti to the watchman of the village and ask him to make five more and distribute to the next village, and so on.
cards.quote: Reports came from various parts of North India that chapattis were being distributed from village to village. A person would come at night and give a chapatti to the watchman of the village and ask him to make five more and distribute to the next village, and so on.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Rumours circulate only when they ____ with the deeper fears and suspicions of people.
cards.back: Rumours circulate only when they resonate with the deeper fears and suspicions of people.
cards.quote: Rumours circulate only when they resonate with the deeper fears and suspicions of people.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.5 Why did people believe in the rumours?

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which Governor General led the British policy of “reforming” Indian society from the late 1820s, and how?
cards.back: from that time, under the leadership of Governor General Lord William Bentinck, the British adopted policies aimed at “reforming” Indian society by introducing Western education, Western ideas and Western institutions.
cards.quote: from that time, under the leadership of Governor General Lord William Bentinck, the British adopted policies aimed at “reforming” Indian society by introducing Western education, Western ideas and Western institutions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.5 Why did people believe in the rumours?

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which laws did the British establish to abolish customs and permit widow remarriage?
cards.back: The British established laws to abolish customs like sati (1829) and to permit the remarriage of Hindu widows.
cards.quote: The British established laws to abolish customs like sati (1829) and to permit the remarriage of Hindu widows.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.5 Why did people believe in the rumours?

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: On what pleas did the British annex Awadh, Jhansi, Satara and other states?
cards.back: On a variety of pleas, like misgovernment and the refusal to recognise adoption, the British annexed not only Awadh, but many other kingdoms and principalities like Jhansi and Satara.
cards.quote: On a variety of pleas, like misgovernment and the refusal to recognise adoption, the British annexed not only Awadh, but many other kingdoms and principalities like Jhansi and Satara.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.5 Why did people believe in the rumours?

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did it seem to the people was happening to all that they cherished and held sacred?
cards.back: It seemed to the people that all that they cherished and held sacred – from kings and socio-religious customs to patterns of landholding and revenue payment – was being destroyed and replaced by a system that was more impersonal, alien and oppressive.
cards.quote: It seemed to the people that all that they cherished and held sacred – from kings and socio-religious customs to patterns of landholding and revenue payment – was being destroyed and replaced by a system that was more impersonal, alien and oppressive.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.5 Why did people believe in the rumours?

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Whose activities aggravated the people’s perception of a destroyed way of life?
cards.back: This perception was aggravated by the activities of Christian missionaries.
cards.quote: This perception was aggravated by the activities of Christian missionaries.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 1.5 Why did people believe in the rumours?

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was a Resident?
cards.back: Resident was the designation of a representative of the Governor General who lived in a state which was not under direct British rule.
cards.quote: Resident was the designation of a representative of the Governor General who lived in a state which was not under direct British rule.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was the Subsidiary Alliance?
cards.back: Subsidiary Alliance was a system devised by Lord Wellesley in 1798.
cards.quote: Subsidiary Alliance was a system devised by Lord Wellesley in 1798.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Name the terms and conditions of the Subsidiary Alliance.
cards.back:
The British would be responsible for protecting their ally from external and internal threats to their power.
In the territory of the ally, a British armed contingent would be stationed.
The ally would have to provide the resources for maintaining this contingent.
The ally could enter into agreements with other rulers or engage in warfare only with the permission of the British.
cards.quote: (a) The British would be responsible for protecting their ally from external and internal threats to their power. (b) In the territory of the ally, a British armed contingent would be stationed. (c) The ally would have to provide the resources for maintaining this contingent. (d) The ally could enter into agreements with other rulers or engage in warfare only with the permission of the British.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did Lord Dalhousie describe Awadh in 1851, and when was it annexed?
cards.back: In 1851 Governor General Lord Dalhousie described the kingdom of Awadh as “a cherry that will drop into our mouth one day”. Five years later, in 1856, the kingdom was formally annexed to the British Empire.
cards.quote: In 1851 Governor General Lord Dalhousie described the kingdom of Awadh as “a cherry that will drop into our mouth one day”. Five years later, in 1856, the kingdom was formally annexed to the British Empire.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.1 "A cherry that will drop into our mouth one day"

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the Subsidiary Alliance of 1801 require of the Nawab of Awadh?
cards.back: The Subsidiary Alliance had been imposed on Awadh in 1801. By the terms of this alliance the Nawab had to disband his military force, allow the British to position their troops within the kingdom, and act in accordance with the advice of the British Resident who was now to be attached to the court.
cards.quote: The Subsidiary Alliance had been imposed on Awadh in 1801. By the terms of this alliance the Nawab had to disband his military force, allow the British to position their troops within the kingdom, and act in accordance with the advice of the British Resident who was now to be attached to the court.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.1 "A cherry that will drop into our mouth one day"

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why were the British interested in acquiring Awadh?
cards.back: They felt that the soil there was good for producing indigo and cotton, and the region was ideally located to be developed into the principal market of Upper India.
cards.quote: They felt that the soil there was good for producing indigo and cotton, and the region was ideally located to be developed into the principal market of Upper India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.1 "A cherry that will drop into our mouth one day"

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What process was the takeover of Awadh in 1856 expected to complete?
cards.back: The takeover of Awadh in 1856 was expected to complete a process of territorial annexation that had begun with the conquest of Bengal almost a century earlier.
cards.quote: The takeover of Awadh in 1856 was expected to complete a process of territorial annexation that had begun with the conquest of Bengal almost a century earlier.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.1 "A cherry that will drop into our mouth one day"

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Where was Nawab Wajid Ali Shah exiled, and on what plea?
cards.back: Here, Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was dethroned and exiled to Calcutta on the plea that the region was being misgoverned.
cards.quote: Here, Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was dethroned and exiled to Calcutta on the plea that the region was being misgoverned.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.2 "The life was gone out of the body"

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Was Wajid Ali Shah an unpopular ruler, as the British assumed?
cards.back: The British government also wrongly assumed that Wajid Ali Shah was an unpopular ruler. On the contrary, he was widely loved, and when he left his beloved Lucknow, there were many who followed him all the way to Kanpur singing songs of lament.
cards.quote: The British government also wrongly assumed that Wajid Ali Shah was an unpopular ruler. On the contrary, he was widely loved, and when he left his beloved Lucknow, there were many who followed him all the way to Kanpur singing songs of lament.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.2 "The life was gone out of the body"

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who lost their livelihood when the Nawab was removed and his court dissolved?
cards.back: The removal of the Nawab led to the dissolution of the court and its culture. Thus a whole range of people – musicians, dancers, poets, artisans, cooks, retainers, administrative officials and so on – lost their livelihood.
cards.quote: The removal of the Nawab led to the dissolution of the court and its culture. Thus a whole range of people – musicians, dancers, poets, artisans, cooks, retainers, administrative officials and so on – lost their livelihood.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.2 "The life was gone out of the body"

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which groups did a chain of grievances in Awadh link?
cards.back: A chain of grievances in Awadh linked prince, taluqdar, peasant and sepoy.
cards.quote: A chain of grievances in Awadh linked prince, taluqdar, peasant and sepoy.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.3 Firangi raj and the end of a world

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: In Awadh, more than anywhere else, the revolt became an expression of ____ to an alien order.
cards.back: In Awadh, more than anywhere else, the revolt became an expression of popular resistance to an alien order.
cards.quote: In Awadh, more than anywhere else, the revolt became an expression of popular resistance to an alien order.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.3 Firangi raj and the end of a world

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did taluqdars enjoy before the British came, as long as they accepted the Nawab’s suzerainty?
cards.back: Before the coming of the British, taluqdars maintained armed retainers, built forts, and enjoyed a degree of autonomy, as long as they accepted the suzerainty of the Nawab and paid the revenue of their taluqs.
cards.quote: Before the coming of the British, taluqdars maintained armed retainers, built forts, and enjoyed a degree of autonomy, as long as they accepted the suzerainty of the Nawab and paid the revenue of their taluqs.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.3 Firangi raj and the end of a world

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What happened to the taluqdars immediately after the annexation of Awadh?
cards.back: Immediately after the annexation, the taluqdars were disarmed and their forts destroyed.
cards.quote: Immediately after the annexation, the taluqdars were disarmed and their forts destroyed.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.3 Firangi raj and the end of a world

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: On what assumption was the Summary Settlement of 1856 based?
cards.back: After annexation, the first British revenue settlement, known as the Summary Settlement of 1856, was based on the assumption that the taluqdars were interlopers with no permanent stakes in land: they had established their hold over land through force and fraud.
cards.quote: After annexation, the first British revenue settlement, known as the Summary Settlement of 1856, was based on the assumption that the taluqdars were interlopers with no permanent stakes in land: they had established their hold over land through force and fraud.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.3 Firangi raj and the end of a world

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What share of Awadh villages did taluqdars hold before the British, and after the Summary Settlement?
cards.back: Figures show that in pre-British times, taluqdars had held 67 per cent of the total number of villages in Awadh; by the Summary Settlement this number had come down to 38 per cent.
cards.quote: Figures show that in pre-British times, taluqdars had held 67 per cent of the total number of villages in Awadh; by the Summary Settlement this number had come down to 38 per cent.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.3 Firangi raj and the end of a world

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: By how much did the revenue demand increase in some heavily overassessed areas of Awadh?
cards.back: Officials soon found that large areas of Awadh were actually heavily overassessed: the increase of revenue demand in some places was from 30 to 70 per cent.
cards.quote: Officials soon found that large areas of Awadh were actually heavily overassessed: the increase of revenue demand in some places was from 30 to 70 per cent.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.3 Firangi raj and the end of a world

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the dispossession of the taluqdars of Awadh mean, according to NCERT?
cards.back: The dispossession of taluqdars meant the breakdown of an entire social order. The ties of loyalty and patronage that had bound the peasant to the taluqdar were disrupted.
cards.quote: The dispossession of taluqdars meant the breakdown of an entire social order. The ties of loyalty and patronage that had bound the peasant to the taluqdar were disrupted.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.3 Firangi raj and the end of a world

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which Begum did the Awadh taluqdars loyal to the Nawab join in Lucknow to fight the British?
cards.back: Many of these taluqdars were loyal to the Nawab of Awadh, and they joined Begum Hazrat Mahal (the wife of the Nawab) in Lucknow to fight the British; some even remained with her in defeat.
cards.quote: Many of these taluqdars were loyal to the Nawab of Awadh, and they joined Begum Hazrat Mahal (the wife of the Nawab) in Lucknow to fight the British; some even remained with her in defeat.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.3 Firangi raj and the end of a world

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What had the sepoys complained of for decades?
cards.back: For decades the sepoys had complained of low levels of pay and the difficulty of getting leave.
cards.quote: For decades the sepoys had complained of low levels of pay and the difficulty of getting leave.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.3 Firangi raj and the end of a world

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did white officers relate to sepoys in the 1820s?
cards.back: In the 1820s, white officers made it a point to maintain friendly relations with the sepoys. They would take part in their leisure activities – they wrestled with them, fenced with them and went out hawking with them.
cards.quote: In the 1820s, white officers made it a point to maintain friendly relations with the sepoys. They would take part in their leisure activities – they wrestled with them, fenced with them and went out hawking with them.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.3 Firangi raj and the end of a world

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the attitude of white officers towards sepoys change from the 1840s?
cards.back: In the 1840s, this began to change. The officers developed a sense of superiority and started treating the sepoys as their racial inferiors, riding roughshod over their sensibilities.
cards.quote: In the 1840s, this began to change. The officers developed a sense of superiority and started treating the sepoys as their racial inferiors, riding roughshod over their sensibilities.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 2.3 Firangi raj and the end of a world

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who best expressed the attitude of the taluqdars, and where was he Raja?
cards.back: The attitude of the taluqdars was best expressed by Hanwant Singh, the Raja of Kalakankar, near Rae Bareli.
cards.quote: The attitude of the taluqdars was best expressed by Hanwant Singh, the Raja of Kalakankar, near Rae Bareli.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who told a British officer he had sheltered: “Sahib, your countrymen came into this country and drove out our King”?
cards.back: While taking leave of the officer, Hanwant Singh told him: Sahib, your countrymen came into this country and drove out our King.
cards.quote: While taking leave of the officer, Hanwant Singh told him: Sahib, your countrymen came into this country and drove out our King.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Where were the large majority of the sepoys of the Bengal Army recruited from?
cards.back: The large majority of the sepoys of the Bengal Army were recruited from the villages of Awadh and eastern Uttar Pradesh. Many of them were Brahmins or from the “upper” castes.
cards.quote: The large majority of the sepoys of the Bengal Army were recruited from the villages of Awadh and eastern Uttar Pradesh. Many of them were Brahmins or from the “upper” castes.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Awadh was, in fact, called the “____ of the Bengal Army”.
cards.back: Awadh was, in fact, called the “nursery of the Bengal Army”.
cards.quote: Awadh was, in fact, called the “nursery of the Bengal Army”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who joined the sepoys very swiftly when they defied their officers and took up arms?
cards.back: When the sepoys defied their superior officers and took up arms they were joined very swiftly by their brethren in the villages.
cards.quote: When the sepoys defied their superior officers and took up arms they were joined very swiftly by their brethren in the villages.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the British, as victors, treat the rebels in their records?
cards.back: As victors, the British recorded their own trials and tribulations as well as their heroism. They dismissed the rebels as a bunch of ungrateful and barbaric people.
cards.quote: As victors, the British recorded their own trials and tribulations as well as their heroism. They dismissed the rebels as a bunch of ungrateful and barbaric people.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What were ishtahars, and what did rebel leaders use them for?
cards.back: ishtahars (notifications) issued by rebel leaders to propagate their ideas and persuade people to join the revolt
cards.quote: ishtahars (notifications) issued by rebel leaders to propagate their ideas and persuade people to join the revolt

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Attempts to reconstruct what happened in 1857 are thus heavily and inevitably dependent on what the ____ wrote.
cards.back: Attempts to reconstruct what happened in 1857 are thus heavily and inevitably dependent on what the British wrote.
cards.quote: Attempts to reconstruct what happened in 1857 are thus heavily and inevitably dependent on what the British wrote.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which sections of the population did the rebel proclamations of 1857 appeal to?
cards.back: The rebel proclamations in 1857 repeatedly appealed to all sections of the population, irrespective of their caste and creed.
cards.quote: The rebel proclamations in 1857 repeatedly appealed to all sections of the population, irrespective of their caste and creed.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the ishtahars glorify?
cards.back: The ishtahars harked back to the pre-British Hindu-Muslim past and glorified the coexistence of different communities under the Mughal Empire.
cards.quote: The ishtahars harked back to the pre-British Hindu-Muslim past and glorified the coexistence of different communities under the Mughal Empire.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the proclamation issued under Bahadur Shah’s name appeal to the people to do?
cards.back: The proclamation that was issued under the name of Bahadur Shah appealed to the people to join the fight under the standards of both Muhammad and Mahavir.
cards.quote: The proclamation that was issued under the name of Bahadur Shah appealed to the people to join the fight under the standards of both Muhammad and Mahavir.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the British try to divide Hindus and Muslims in Bareilly in December 1857, and with what result?
cards.back: In Bareilly in western Uttar Pradesh, in December 1857, the British spent Rs 50,000 to incite the Hindu population against the Muslims. The attempt failed.
cards.quote: In Bareilly in western Uttar Pradesh, in December 1857, the British spent Rs 50,000 to incite the Hindu population against the Muslims. The attempt failed.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why is the Azamgarh Proclamation of 25 August 1857 important to historians?
cards.back: This is one of the main sources of our knowledge about what the rebels wanted
cards.quote: This is one of the main sources of our knowledge about what the rebels wanted

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: According to the Azamgarh Proclamation, what was ruining the people of Hindostan, Hindus and Mohammedans alike?
cards.back: the people of Hindostan, both Hindoos and Mohammedans, are being ruined under the tyranny and the oppression of the infidel and treacherous English.
cards.quote: the people of Hindostan, both Hindoos and Mohammedans, are being ruined under the tyranny and the oppression of the infidel and treacherous English.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Azamgarh Proclamation, Section I: what grievance did it state for zemindars?
cards.back: the British Government in making zemindary settlements have imposed exorbitant Jumas (revenue demand) and have disgraced and ruined several zemindars, by putting up their estates for public auction for arrears of rent
cards.quote: the British Government in making zemindary settlements have imposed exorbitant Jumas (revenue demand) and have disgraced and ruined several zemindars, by putting up their estates for public auction for arrears of rent

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Azamgarh Proclamation, Section I: what did it promise zemindars under the Badshahi Government?
cards.back: the Jumas will be light, the dignity and honour of the zemindars safe, and every zemindar will have absolute rule in his own zemindary
cards.quote: the Jumas will be light, the dignity and honour of the zemindars safe, and every zemindar will have absolute rule in his own zemindary

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Azamgarh Proclamation, Section II: what grievance did it state for merchants?
cards.back: the infidel and treacherous British Government have monopolised the trade of all the fine and valuable merchandise, such as indigo, cloth, and other articles of shipping, leaving only the trade of trifles to the people
cards.quote: the infidel and treacherous British Government have monopolised the trade of all the fine and valuable merchandise, such as indigo, cloth, and other articles of shipping, leaving only the trade of trifles to the people

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Azamgarh Proclamation, Section II: what did it promise merchants under the Badshahi Government?
cards.back: the trade of every article, without exception, both by land and water will be opened to the native merchants of India
cards.quote: the trade of every article, without exception, both by land and water will be opened to the native merchants of India

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Azamgarh Proclamation, Section III: what grievance did it state for public servants?
cards.back: under the British Government, natives employed in the civil and military services have little respect, low pay, and no manner of influence; and all the posts of dignity and emolument in both the departments are exclusively bestowed on Englishmen
cards.quote: under the British Government, natives employed in the civil and military services have little respect, low pay, and no manner of influence; and all the posts of dignity and emolument in both the departments are exclusively bestowed on Englishmen

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Azamgarh Proclamation, Section IV: how did it say European goods hurt artisans?
cards.back: the Europeans, by the introduction of English articles into India, have thrown the weavers, the cotton dressers, the carpenters, the blacksmiths, and the shoemakers, etc., out of employ, and have engrossed their occupations, so that every description of native artisan has been reduced to beggary
cards.quote: the Europeans, by the introduction of English articles into India, have thrown the weavers, the cotton dressers, the carpenters, the blacksmiths, and the shoemakers, etc., out of employ, and have engrossed their occupations, so that every description of native artisan has been reduced to beggary

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Azamgarh Proclamation, Section V: why did it say pundits and fakirs must join the war?
cards.back: the pundits and fakirs being the guardians of the Hindoo and Mohammadan religions respectively, and the Europeans being the enemies of both the religions, and as at present a war is raging against the English on account of religion, the pundits and fakirs are bound to present themselves to me
cards.quote: the pundits and fakirs being the guardians of the Hindoo and Mohammadan religions respectively, and the Europeans being the enemies of both the religions, and as at present a war is raging against the English on account of religion, the pundits and fakirs are bound to present themselves to me

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What is an arzi?
cards.back: arzis (petition or application) of rebel sepoys
cards.quote: arzis (petition or application) of rebel sepoys

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: To which regiment’s sowars were the new cartridges given, and what did they refuse?
cards.back: They gave these cartridges to the sowars (mounted soldiers) of the 3rd Light Cavalry, and ordered them to bite them; the troopers objected to it
cards.quote: They gave these cartridges to the sowars (mounted soldiers) of the 3rd Light Cavalry, and ordered them to bite them; the troopers objected to it

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What happened to 84 troopers who objected to the new cartridges, as the sepoys’ arzi records?
cards.back: loaded the guns with grape and made 84 new troopers prisoners, and put them in jail with irons on them
cards.quote: loaded the guns with grape and made 84 new troopers prisoners, and put them in jail with irons on them

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: According to the sepoys’ arzi, why had they fought the British for two years?
cards.back: we have fought for two years in order that our faith and religion may not be polluted.
cards.quote: we have fought for two years in order that our faith and religion may not be polluted.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the proclamations reject, and what did they condemn the British for?
cards.back: The proclamations completely rejected everything associated with British rule or firangi raj as they called it. They condemned the British for the annexations they had carried out and the treaties they had broken.
cards.quote: The proclamations completely rejected everything associated with British rule or firangi raj as they called it. They condemned the British for the annexations they had carried out and the treaties they had broken.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What enraged the people about British land revenue settlements and foreign commerce?
cards.back: What enraged the people was how British land revenue settlements had dispossessed landholders, both big and small, and foreign commerce had driven artisans and weavers to ruin.
cards.quote: What enraged the people was how British land revenue settlements had dispossessed landholders, both big and small, and foreign commerce had driven artisans and weavers to ruin.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What widespread fear did the proclamations express?
cards.back: The proclamations expressed the widespread fear that the British were bent on destroying the caste and religions of Hindus and Muslims and converting them to Christianity
cards.quote: The proclamations expressed the widespread fear that the British were bent on destroying the caste and religions of Hindus and Muslims and converting them to Christianity

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What were people urged to come together and fight to save?
cards.back: People were urged to come together and fight to save their livelihood, their faith, their honour, their identity – a fight which was for the “greater public good”.
cards.quote: People were urged to come together and fight to save their livelihood, their faith, their honour, their identity – a fight which was for the “greater public good”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did rebels do in villages, and what did this reflect?
cards.back: In the villages they burnt account books and ransacked moneylenders’ houses. This reflected an attempt to overturn traditional hierarchies, rebel against all oppressors.
cards.quote: In the villages they burnt account books and ransacked moneylenders’ houses. This reflected an attempt to overturn traditional hierarchies, rebel against all oppressors.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the rebels' attacks on traditional hierarchies and local elites hint at, as a vision of society?
cards.back:
A more egalitarian society
This reflected an attempt to overturn traditional hierarchies, rebel against all oppressors. It presents a glimpse of an alternative vision, perhaps of a more egalitarian society.
cards.quote: This reflected an attempt to overturn traditional hierarchies, rebel against all oppressors. It presents a glimpse of an alternative vision, perhaps of a more egalitarian society.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: In which cities did the rebels try to establish structures of authority and administration after British rule collapsed?
cards.back: Once British rule had collapsed, the rebels in places like Delhi, Lucknow and Kanpur tried to establish some kind of structure of authority and administration.
cards.quote: Once British rule had collapsed, the rebels in places like Delhi, Lucknow and Kanpur tried to establish some kind of structure of authority and administration.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which past world did the rebels harken back to in their administration?
cards.back: In all this the rebels harked back to the eighteenth-century Mughal world – a world that became a symbol of all that had been lost.
cards.quote: In all this the rebels harked back to the eighteenth-century Mughal world – a world that became a symbol of all that had been lost.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Where did resistance to the British last longest, with counter-attack plans and command hierarchies in place?
cards.back: But in Awadh, where resistance to the British lasted longest, plans of counter-attack were being drawn up by the Lucknow court and hierarchies of command were in place as late as the last months of 1857 and the early part of 1858.
cards.quote: But in Awadh, where resistance to the British lasted longest, plans of counter-attack were being drawn up by the Lucknow court and hierarchies of command were in place as late as the last months of 1857 and the early part of 1858.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the Acts of May and June 1857 do?
cards.back: By a number of Acts, passed in May and June 1857, not only was the whole of North India put under martial law but military officers and even ordinary Britons were given the power to try and punish Indians suspected of rebellion.
cards.quote: By a number of Acts, passed in May and June 1857, not only was the whole of North India put under martial law but military officers and even ordinary Britons were given the power to try and punish Indians suspected of rebellion.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was the only punishment for rebellion after the ordinary processes of law and trial were suspended?
cards.back: In other words, the ordinary processes of law and trial were suspended and it was put out that rebellion would have only one punishment – death.
cards.quote: In other words, the ordinary processes of law and trial were suspended and it was put out that rebellion would have only one punishment – death.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What was the two-pronged British attack to reconquer Delhi?
cards.back: The British thus mounted a two-pronged attack. One force moved from Calcutta into North India and the other from the Punjab – which was largely peaceful – to reconquer Delhi.
cards.quote: The British thus mounted a two-pronged attack. One force moved from Calcutta into North India and the other from the Punjab – which was largely peaceful – to reconquer Delhi.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: When did British attempts to recover Delhi begin, and when was the city finally captured?
cards.back: attempts to recover Delhi began in earnest in early June 1857 but it was only in late September that the city was finally captured.
cards.quote: attempts to recover Delhi began in earnest in early June 1857 but it was only in late September that the city was finally captured.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why were fighting and losses heavy on both sides at Delhi?
cards.back: The fighting and losses on both sides were heavy. One reason for this was the fact that rebels from all over North India had come to Delhi to defend the capital.
cards.quote: The fighting and losses on both sides were heavy. One reason for this was the fact that rebels from all over North India had come to Delhi to defend the capital.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the British reconquer the Gangetic plain, and how did the people respond?
cards.back: The forces had to reconquer the area village by village. The countryside and the people around were entirely hostile.
cards.quote: The forces had to reconquer the area village by village. The countryside and the people around were entirely hostile.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the British official Forsyth estimate about Awadh, and when was it brought under control?
cards.back: In Awadh, for example, a British official called Forsyth estimated that three-fourths of the adult male population was in rebellion. The area was brought under control only in March 1858 after protracted fighting.
cards.quote: In Awadh, for example, a British official called Forsyth estimated that three-fourths of the adult male population was in rebellion. The area was brought under control only in March 1858 after protracted fighting.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did the British try to break the united resistance of big landholders and peasants in Uttar Pradesh?
cards.back: In large parts of present-day Uttar Pradesh, where big landholders and peasants had offered united resistance, the British tried to break up the unity by promising to give back to the big landholders their estates. Rebel landholders were dispossessed and the loyal rewarded.
cards.quote: In large parts of present-day Uttar Pradesh, where big landholders and peasants had offered united resistance, the British tried to break up the unity by promising to give back to the big landholders their estates. Rebel landholders were dispossessed and the loyal rewarded.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What have historians continued to rely on to discuss rebel actions?
cards.back: But historians till now have continued to discuss rebel actions primarily through accounts written by the British.
cards.quote: But historians till now have continued to discuss rebel actions primarily through accounts written by the British.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: In what forms did colonial administrators and military men leave their versions of 1857?
cards.back:
letters and diaries
autobiographies and official histories
cards.quote: Official accounts, of course, abound: colonial administrators and military men left their versions in letters and diaries, autobiographies and official histories.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Where have British officials’ memos, notes, assessments and reports been collected?
cards.back: Many of these have now been collected in a set of volumes on mutiny records.
cards.quote: Many of these have now been collected in a set of volumes on mutiny records.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did British newspaper stories on the revolt do to public feelings?
cards.back: The stories of the revolt that were published in British newspapers and magazines narrated in gory detail the violence of the mutineers – and these stories inflamed public feelings and provoked demands of retribution and revenge.
cards.quote: The stories of the revolt that were published in British newspapers and magazines narrated in gory detail the violence of the mutineers – and these stories inflamed public feelings and provoked demands of retribution and revenge.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Name the kinds of pictorial images produced by the British and Indians on the mutiny.
cards.back:
paintings
pencil drawings
etchings
posters
cartoons
bazaar prints
cards.quote: One important record of the mutiny is the pictorial images produced by the British and Indians: paintings, pencil drawings, etchings, posters, cartoons, bazaar prints.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Which painting by Thomas Jones Barker (1859) commemorates the British heroes who saved the English?
cards.back: Some of them commemorate the British heroes who saved the English and repressed the rebels. “Relief of Lucknow”, painted by Thomas Jones Barker in 1859, is an example of this type.
cards.quote: Some of them commemorate the British heroes who saved the English and repressed the rebels. “Relief of Lucknow”, painted by Thomas Jones Barker in 1859, is an example of this type.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who collected the Christian population in Lucknow and took refuge in the Residency?
cards.back: When the rebel forces besieged Lucknow, Henry Lawrence, the Commissioner of Lucknow, collected the Christian population and took refuge in the heavily fortified Residency. Lawrence was killed but the Residency continued to be defended under the command of Colonel Inglis.
cards.quote: When the rebel forces besieged Lucknow, Henry Lawrence, the Commissioner of Lucknow, collected the Christian population and took refuge in the heavily fortified Residency. Lawrence was killed but the Residency continued to be defended under the command of Colonel Inglis.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who arrived on 25 September and reinforced the British garrisons in Lucknow?
cards.back: On 25 September James Outram and Henry Havelock arrived, cut through the rebel forces, and reinforced the British garrisons.
cards.quote: On 25 September James Outram and Henry Havelock arrived, cut through the rebel forces, and reinforced the British garrisons.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the siege of Lucknow become in British accounts?
cards.back: In British accounts the siege of Lucknow became a story of survival, heroic resistance and the ultimate triumph of British power.
cards.quote: In British accounts the siege of Lucknow became a story of survival, heroic resistance and the ultimate triumph of British power.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who stand at the centre of Barker’s “Relief of Lucknow”?
cards.back: At the centre of the canvas are the British heroes – Campbell, Outram and Havelock.
cards.quote: At the centre of the canvas are the British heroes – Campbell, Outram and Havelock.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What sense did paintings like “Relief of Lucknow” create for the British public?
cards.back: To the British public such paintings were reassuring. They created a sense that the time of trouble was past and the rebellion was over; the British were the victors.
cards.quote: To the British public such paintings were reassuring. They created a sense that the time of trouble was past and the rebellion was over; the British were the victors.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did tales of violence against women and children provoke in Britain?
cards.back: Inflamed particularly by tales of violence against women and children, there were public demands in Britain for revenge and retribution.
cards.quote: Inflamed particularly by tales of violence against women and children, there were public demands in Britain for revenge and retribution.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 5.2 English women and the honour of Britain

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who painted “In Memoriam”, and when?
cards.back: “In Memoriam” (Fig. 10.11) was painted by Joseph Noel Paton two years after the mutiny.
cards.quote: “In Memoriam” (Fig. 10.11) was painted by Joseph Noel Paton two years after the mutiny.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 5.2 English women and the honour of Britain

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How does “In Memoriam” provoke anger without showing violence?
cards.back: “In Memoriam” does not show gory violence; it only suggests it. It stirs up the spectator’s imagination, and seeks to provoke anger and fury.
cards.quote: “In Memoriam” does not show gory violence; it only suggests it. It stirs up the spectator’s imagination, and seeks to provoke anger and fury.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 5.2 English women and the honour of Britain

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What deeper religious meaning does the Miss Wheeler picture give the woman’s struggle?
cards.back: The woman’s struggle to save her honour and her life, in fact, is represented as having a deeper religious connotation: it is a battle to save the honour of Christianity. The book lying on the floor is the Bible.
cards.quote: The woman’s struggle to save her honour and her life, in fact, is represented as having a deeper religious connotation: it is a battle to save the honour of Christianity. The book lying on the floor is the Bible.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III
source.section: 5.2 English women and the honour of Britain

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What milieu did visual representations and news about the revolt create?
cards.back: Visual representations and news about the revolt created a milieu in which violent repression and vengeance were seen as both necessary and just.
cards.quote: Visual representations and news about the revolt created a milieu in which violent repression and vengeance were seen as both necessary and just.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How were rebels executed to express the urge for vengeance and retribution?
cards.back: The urge for vengeance and retribution was expressed in the brutal way in which the rebels were executed. They were blown from guns, or hanged from the gallows.
cards.quote: The urge for vengeance and retribution was expressed in the brutal way in which the rebels were executed. They were blown from guns, or hanged from the gallows.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How does the Illustrated London News image of the Peshawar execution (3 October 1857) present the scene?
cards.back: The scene of execution here appears to be a stage where a drama is being performed – an enactment of brutal power.
cards.quote: The scene of execution here appears to be a stage where a drama is being performed – an enactment of brutal power.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why had punishment to be theatrically performed in the open, according to NCERT?
cards.back: What you see is not routine punishment: it is the performance of terror. For it to instil fear among people, punishment could not be discreetly meted out in enclosed spaces. It had to be theatrically performed in the open.
cards.quote: What you see is not routine punishment: it is the performance of terror. For it to instil fear among people, punishment could not be discreetly meted out in enclosed spaces. It had to be theatrically performed in the open.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Why was Governor General Canning mocked in the British press?
cards.back: When Governor General Canning declared that a gesture of leniency and a show of mercy would help in winning back the loyalty of the sepoys, he was mocked in the British press.
cards.quote: When Governor General Canning declared that a gesture of leniency and a show of mercy would help in winning back the loyalty of the sepoys, he was mocked in the British press.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What did the national movement in the twentieth century draw inspiration from?
cards.back: The national movement in the twentieth century drew its inspiration from the events of 1857.
cards.quote: The national movement in the twentieth century drew its inspiration from the events of 1857.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How was the revolt celebrated in nationalist imagination?
cards.back: It was celebrated as the First War of Independence in which all sections of the people of India came together to fight against imperial rule.
cards.quote: It was celebrated as the First War of Independence in which all sections of the people of India came together to fight against imperial rule.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: What have art and literature, as much as history writing, helped to do?
cards.back: Art and literature, as much as the writing of history, have helped in keeping alive the memory of 1857.
cards.quote: Art and literature, as much as the writing of history, have helped in keeping alive the memory of 1857.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Who wrote the lines “Khoob lari mardani woh to Jhansi wali rani thi”?
cards.back: Children in many parts of India grow up reading the lines of Subhadra Kumari Chauhan: “Khoob lari mardani woh to Jhansi wali rani thi” (Like a man she fought, she was the Rani of Jhansi).
cards.quote: Children in many parts of India grow up reading the lines of Subhadra Kumari Chauhan: “Khoob lari mardani woh to Jhansi wali rani thi” (Like a man she fought, she was the Rani of Jhansi).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How is Rani Lakshmi Bai usually portrayed in popular prints, and what does it symbolise?
cards.back: In popular prints Rani Lakshmi Bai is usually portrayed in battle armour, with a sword in hand and riding a horse – a symbol of the determination to resist injustice and alien rule.
cards.quote: In popular prints Rani Lakshmi Bai is usually portrayed in battle armour, with a sword in hand and riding a horse – a symbol of the determination to resist injustice and alien rule.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: How did British and nationalist images each shape public attitudes?
cards.back: Fed by the images that circulated in Britain, the public sanctioned the most brutal forms of repression of the rebels. On the other hand, nationalist imageries of the revolt helped shape the nationalist imagination.
cards.quote: Fed by the images that circulated in Britain, the public sanctioned the most brutal forms of repression of the rebels. On the other hand, nationalist imageries of the revolt helped shape the nationalist imagination.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 1801: what happened?
cards.back: Subsidiary Alliance introduced by Wellesley in Awadh
cards.quote: Subsidiary Alliance introduced by Wellesley in Awadh

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 1856: what happened to the Nawab and Awadh?
cards.back: Nawab Wajid Ali Shah deposed; Awadh annexed
cards.quote: Nawab Wajid Ali Shah deposed; Awadh annexed

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 1856-57: what did the British introduce in Awadh?
cards.back: Summary revenue settlements introduced in Awadh by the British
cards.quote: Summary revenue settlements introduced in Awadh by the British

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 10 May 1857: what happened?
cards.back: Mutiny starts in Meerut
cards.quote: Mutiny starts in Meerut

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 11-12 May 1857: what happened in Delhi?
cards.back: Delhi garrisons revolt; Bahadur Shah accepts nominal leadership
cards.quote: Delhi garrisons revolt; Bahadur Shah accepts nominal leadership

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 30 May 1857: what happened?
cards.back: Rising in Lucknow
cards.quote: Rising in Lucknow

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, May-June 1857: what did the mutiny turn into?
cards.back: Mutiny turns into a general revolt of the people
cards.quote: Mutiny turns into a general revolt of the people

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 30 June 1857: what happened at Chinhat?
cards.back: British suffer defeat in the battle of Chinhat
cards.quote: British suffer defeat in the battle of Chinhat

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, 25 September 1857: who entered the Residency in Lucknow?
cards.back: British forces under Havelock and Outram enter the Residency in Lucknow
cards.quote: British forces under Havelock and Outram enter the Residency in Lucknow

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, July 1857: who was killed in battle?
cards.back: Shah Mal killed in battle
cards.quote: Shah Mal killed in battle

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part III
cards.front: Timeline, June 1858: who was killed in battle?
cards.back: Rani Jhansi killed in battle
cards.quote: Rani Jhansi killed in battle

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part III

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What sources do historians use to reconstruct the world of ideas and beliefs of c. 600 BCE-600 CE?
cards.back: The sources that historians use to reconstruct this exciting world of ideas and beliefs include Buddhist, Jaina and Brahmanical texts, as well as a large and impressive body of material remains including monuments and inscriptions.
cards.quote: The sources that historians use to reconstruct this exciting world of ideas and beliefs include Buddhist, Jaina and Brahmanical texts, as well as a large and impressive body of material remains including monuments and inscriptions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who provided money for the preservation of the ancient site at Sanchi?
cards.back: The rulers of Bhopal, Shahjehan Begum and her successor Sultan Jehan Begum, provided money for the preservation of the ancient site.
cards.quote: The rulers of Bhopal, Shahjehan Begum and her successor Sultan Jehan Begum, provided money for the preservation of the ancient site.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Thinkers who emerged in the mid-first millennium BCE, by country.
cards.back:
Zarathustra in Iran
Kong Zi in China
Socrates, Plato and Aristotle in Greece
Mahavira and Gautama Buddha, among many others, in India
cards.quote: The mid-first millennium BCE is often regarded as a turning point in world history: it saw the emergence of thinkers such as Zarathustra in Iran, Kong Zi in China, Socrates, Plato and Aristotle in Greece, and Mahavira and Gautama Buddha, among many others, in India.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which deities does the Rigveda especially praise?
cards.back: The Rigveda consists of hymns in praise of a variety of deities, especially Agni, Indra and Soma.
cards.quote: The Rigveda consists of hymns in praise of a variety of deities, especially Agni, Indra and Soma.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Between which dates was the Rigveda, the source of the early Vedic tradition, compiled?
