cards.back: There were several pre-existing traditions of thought, religious belief and practice, including the early Vedic tradition, known from the Rigveda, compiled between c.1500 and 1000 BCE.
cards.quote: There were several pre-existing traditions of thought, religious belief and practice, including the early Vedic tradition, known from the Rigveda, compiled between c.1500 and 1000 BCE.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In what kind of Sanskrit were Rigvedic verses composed, and to whom were they taught?
cards.back: Verses such as these were composed in a special kind of Sanskrit, known as Vedic Sanskrit. They were taught orally to men belonging to priestly families.
cards.quote: Verses such as these were composed in a special kind of Sanskrit, known as Vedic Sanskrit. They were taught orally to men belonging to priestly families.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: More elaborate sacrifices, such as the ____ and ____, were performed by chiefs and kings who depended on Brahmana priests to conduct the ritual.
cards.back: More elaborate sacrifices, such as the rajasuya and ashvamedha, were performed by chiefs and kings who depended on Brahmana priests to conduct the ritual.
cards.quote: More elaborate sacrifices, such as the rajasuya and ashvamedha, were performed by chiefs and kings who depended on Brahmana priests to conduct the ritual.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Who performed sacrifices at first, and who performed some of them later?
cards.back: At first, sacrifices were performed collectively. Later (c. 1000 BCE-500 BCE onwards) some were performed by the heads of households for the wellbeing of the domestic unit.
cards.quote: At first, sacrifices were performed collectively. Later (c. 1000 BCE-500 BCE onwards) some were performed by the heads of households for the wellbeing of the domestic unit.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: We get a glimpse of lively discussions and debates from Buddhist texts, which mention as many as ____ sects or schools of thought.
cards.back: We get a glimpse of lively discussions and debates from Buddhist texts, which mention as many as 64 sects or schools of thought.
cards.quote: We get a glimpse of lively discussions and debates from Buddhist texts, which mention as many as 64 sects or schools of thought.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Debates took place in the ____ — literally, a hut with a pointed roof — or in groves where travelling mendicants halted.
cards.back: Debates took place in the kutagarashala — literally, a hut with a pointed roof — or in groves where travelling mendicants halted.
cards.quote: Debates took place in the kutagarashala — literally, a hut with a pointed roof — or in groves where travelling mendicants halted.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Many of these teachers, including Mahavira and the Buddha, questioned the authority of the ____.
cards.back: Many of these teachers, including Mahavira and the Buddha, questioned the authority of the Vedas.
cards.quote: Many of these teachers, including Mahavira and the Buddha, questioned the authority of the Vedas.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Besides questioning the authority of the Vedas, what did Mahavira, the Buddha and other teachers emphasise?
cards.back: Many of these teachers, including Mahavira and the Buddha, questioned the authority of the Vedas. They also emphasised individual agency — suggesting that men and women could strive to attain liberation from the trials and tribulations of worldly existence.
cards.quote: Many of these teachers, including Mahavira and the Buddha, questioned the authority of the Vedas. They also emphasised individual agency — suggesting that men and women could strive to attain liberation from the trials and tribulations of worldly existence.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: None of the Buddha's speeches were ____ during his lifetime.
cards.back: None of the Buddha's speeches were written down during his lifetime.
cards.quote: None of the Buddha's speeches were written down during his lifetime.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: How Buddhist texts were prepared and preserved

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Where and by whom were the Buddha's teachings compiled after his death?
cards.back: After his death (c. fifth-fourth century BCE) his teachings were compiled by his disciples at a council of "elders" or senior monks at Vesali (Pali for Vaishali in present-day Bihar).
cards.quote: After his death (c. fifth-fourth century BCE) his teachings were compiled by his disciples at a council of "elders" or senior monks at Vesali (Pali for Vaishali in present-day Bihar).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: How Buddhist texts were prepared and preserved

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is the Tipitaka?
cards.back: After his death (c. fifth-fourth century BCE) his teachings were compiled by his disciples at a council of “elders” or senior monks at Vesali (Pali for Vaishali in present-day Bihar). These compilations were known as Tipitaka — literally, three baskets to hold different types of texts.
cards.quote: After his death (c. fifth-fourth century BCE) his teachings were compiled by his disciples at a council of “elders” or senior monks at Vesali (Pali for Vaishali in present-day Bihar). These compilations were known as Tipitaka — literally, three baskets to hold different types of texts.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: How Buddhist texts were prepared and preserved

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The three Pitakas of the Tipitaka and what each contains.
cards.back:
The Vinaya Pitaka included rules and regulations for those who joined the sangha or monastic order
the Buddha's teachings were included in the Sutta Pitaka
the Abhidhamma Pitaka dealt with philosophical matters
cards.quote: The Vinaya Pitaka included rules and regulations for those who joined the sangha or monastic order; the Buddha's teachings were included in the Sutta Pitaka; and the Abhidhamma Pitaka dealt with philosophical matters.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: How Buddhist texts were prepared and preserved

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which texts containing regional histories of Buddhism were written in Sri Lanka?
cards.back: As Buddhism travelled to new regions such as Sri Lanka, other texts such as the Dipavamsa (literally, the chronicle of the island) and Mahavamsa (the great chronicle) were written, containing regional histories of Buddhism.
cards.quote: As Buddhism travelled to new regions such as Sri Lanka, other texts such as the Dipavamsa (literally, the chronicle of the island) and Mahavamsa (the great chronicle) were written, containing regional histories of Buddhism.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: How Buddhist texts were prepared and preserved

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which pilgrims travelled from China to India in search of Buddhist texts?
cards.back: When Buddhism spread to East Asia, pilgrims such as Fa Xian and Xuan Zang travelled all the way from China to India in search of texts.
cards.quote: When Buddhism spread to East Asia, pilgrims such as Fa Xian and Xuan Zang travelled all the way from China to India in search of texts.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: How Buddhist texts were prepared and preserved

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Some of the oldest texts are in ____, while later compositions are in ____.
cards.back: Some of the oldest texts are in Pali, while later compositions are in Sanskrit.
cards.quote: Some of the oldest texts are in Pali, while later compositions are in Sanskrit.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: How Buddhist texts were prepared and preserved

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What does it mean that the Ajivikas are often described as fatalists?
cards.back: fatalists: those who believe that everything is predetermined.
cards.quote: fatalists: those who believe that everything is predetermined.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which tradition of early Indian thinkers is usually described as materialists?
cards.back:
Lokayatas
Lokayatas, usually described as materialists.
cards.quote: Lokayatas, usually described as materialists.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: By what name did Vardhamana, born in the sixth century BCE, come to be known?
cards.back: The basic philosophy of the Jainas was already in existence in north India before the birth of Vardhamana, who came to be known as Mahavira, in the sixth century BCE.
cards.quote: The basic philosophy of the Jainas was already in existence in north India before the birth of Vardhamana, who came to be known as Mahavira, in the sixth century BCE.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 3. Beyond Worldly Pleasures: The Message of Mahavira

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Mahavira was preceded by 23 other teachers or ____ — literally, those who guide men and women across the river of existence.
cards.back: Mahavira was preceded by 23 other teachers or tirthankaras — literally, those who guide men and women across the river of existence.
cards.quote: Mahavira was preceded by 23 other teachers or tirthankaras — literally, those who guide men and women across the river of existence.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 3. Beyond Worldly Pleasures: The Message of Mahavira

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is the most important idea in Jainism about the entire world?
cards.back: The most important idea in Jainism is that the entire world is animated: even stones, rocks and water have life.
cards.quote: The most important idea in Jainism is that the entire world is animated: even stones, rocks and water have life.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 3. Beyond Worldly Pleasures: The Message of Mahavira

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In fact the principle of ____, emphasised within Jainism, has left its mark on Indian thinking as a whole.
cards.back: In fact the principle of ahimsa, emphasised within Jainism, has left its mark on Indian thinking as a whole.
cards.quote: In fact the principle of ahimsa, emphasised within Jainism, has left its mark on Indian thinking as a whole.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 3. Beyond Worldly Pleasures: The Message of Mahavira

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: According to Jaina teachings, the cycle of birth and rebirth is shaped through ____.
cards.back: According to Jaina teachings, the cycle of birth and rebirth is shaped through karma.
cards.quote: According to Jaina teachings, the cycle of birth and rebirth is shaped through karma.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 3. Beyond Worldly Pleasures: The Message of Mahavira

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why is monastic existence a necessary condition of salvation in Jainism?
cards.back: Asceticism and penance are required to free oneself from the cycle of karma. This can be achieved only by renouncing the world; therefore, monastic existence is a necessary condition of salvation.
cards.quote: Asceticism and penance are required to free oneself from the cycle of karma. This can be achieved only by renouncing the world; therefore, monastic existence is a necessary condition of salvation.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 3. Beyond Worldly Pleasures: The Message of Mahavira

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The five vows taken by Jaina monks and nuns.
cards.back:
to abstain from killing, stealing and lying
to observe celibacy
to abstain from possessing property
cards.quote: Jaina monks and nuns took five vows: to abstain from killing, stealing and lying; to observe celibacy; and to abstain from possessing property.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 3. Beyond Worldly Pleasures: The Message of Mahavira

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In which languages did Jaina scholars produce a wealth of literature?
cards.back: Like the Buddhists, Jaina scholars produced a wealth of literature in a variety of languages — Prakrit, Sanskrit and Tamil.
cards.quote: Like the Buddhists, Jaina scholars produced a wealth of literature in a variety of languages — Prakrit, Sanskrit and Tamil.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which devotees produced some of the earliest stone sculptures associated with religious traditions?
cards.back: Some of the earliest stone sculptures associated with religious traditions were produced by devotees of the Jaina tirthankaras, and have been recovered from several sites throughout the subcontinent.
cards.quote: Some of the earliest stone sculptures associated with religious traditions were produced by devotees of the Jaina tirthankaras, and have been recovered from several sites throughout the subcontinent.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Where did the Buddha's message spread, beyond the subcontinent?
cards.back: Over the centuries, his message spread across the subcontinent and beyond — through Central Asia to China, Korea and Japan, and through Sri Lanka, across the seas to Myanmar, Thailand and Indonesia.
cards.quote: Over the centuries, his message spread across the subcontinent and beyond — through Central Asia to China, Korea and Japan, and through Sri Lanka, across the seas to Myanmar, Thailand and Indonesia.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 4. The Buddha and the Quest for Enlightenment

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is a hagiography?
cards.back: Hagiography is a biography of a saint or religious leader. Hagiographies often praise the saint's achievements, and may not always be literally accurate.
cards.quote: Hagiography is a biography of a saint or religious leader. Hagiographies often praise the saint's achievements, and may not always be literally accurate.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 4. The Buddha and the Quest for Enlightenment

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What three sights anguished Siddhartha on his first journey into the city?
cards.back: He was deeply anguished when he saw an old man, a sick man and a corpse.
cards.quote: He was deeply anguished when he saw an old man, a sick man and a corpse.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 4. The Buddha and the Quest for Enlightenment

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How did Siddhartha finally attain enlightenment after bodily mortification?
cards.back: Siddhartha explored several paths including bodily mortification which led him to a situation of near death. Abandoning these extreme methods, he meditated for several days and finally attained enlightenment.
cards.quote: Siddhartha explored several paths including bodily mortification which led him to a situation of near death. Abandoning these extreme methods, he meditated for several days and finally attained enlightenment.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 4. The Buddha and the Quest for Enlightenment

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: After this he came to be known as the Buddha or the ____.
cards.back: After this he came to be known as the Buddha or the Enlightened One.
cards.quote: After this he came to be known as the Buddha or the Enlightened One.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 4. The Buddha and the Quest for Enlightenment

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: For the rest of his life, he taught ____ or the path of righteous living.
cards.back: For the rest of his life, he taught dhamma or the path of righteous living.
cards.quote: For the rest of his life, he taught dhamma or the path of righteous living.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 4. The Buddha and the Quest for Enlightenment

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How did the Buddha try to convince people, according to some stories?
cards.back: Although some stories describe his miraculous powers, others suggest that the Buddha tried to convince people through reason and persuasion rather than through displays of supernatural power.
cards.quote: Although some stories describe his miraculous powers, others suggest that the Buddha tried to convince people through reason and persuasion rather than through displays of supernatural power.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: According to Buddhist philosophy, the world is transient (____) and constantly changing; it is also soulless (____)
cards.back: According to Buddhist philosophy, the world is transient (anicca) and constantly changing; it is also soulless (anatta)
cards.quote: According to Buddhist philosophy, the world is transient (anicca) and constantly changing; it is also soulless (anatta)

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Within this transient world, sorrow (____) is intrinsic to human existence.
cards.back: Within this transient world, sorrow (dukkha) is intrinsic to human existence.
cards.quote: Within this transient world, sorrow (dukkha) is intrinsic to human existence.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In Buddhist philosophy, which path between severe penance and self-indulgence helps people rise above worldly troubles?
cards.back: Within this transient world, sorrow (dukkha) is intrinsic to human existence. It is by following the path of moderation between severe penance and self-indulgence that human beings can rise above these worldly troubles.
cards.quote: Within this transient world, sorrow (dukkha) is intrinsic to human existence. It is by following the path of moderation between severe penance and self-indulgence that human beings can rise above these worldly troubles.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In the earliest forms of Buddhism, whether or not god existed was ____.
cards.back: In the earliest forms of Buddhism, whether or not god existed was irrelevant.
cards.quote: In the earliest forms of Buddhism, whether or not god existed was irrelevant.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The Buddha regarded the social world as the creation of ____ rather than of divine origin.
cards.back: The Buddha regarded the social world as the creation of humans rather than of divine origin.
cards.quote: The Buddha regarded the social world as the creation of humans rather than of divine origin.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is nibbana?
cards.back: The Buddha emphasised individual agency and righteous action as the means to escape from the cycle of rebirth and attain self-realisation and nibbana, literally the extinguishing of the ego and desire — and thus end the cycle of suffering for those who renounced the world.
cards.quote: The Buddha emphasised individual agency and righteous action as the means to escape from the cycle of rebirth and attain self-realisation and nibbana, literally the extinguishing of the ego and desire — and thus end the cycle of suffering for those who renounced the world.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What were the Buddha's last words to his followers, according to Buddhist tradition?
cards.back: According to Buddhist tradition, his last words to his followers were: "Be lamps unto yourselves as all of you must work out your own liberation."
cards.quote: According to Buddhist tradition, his last words to his followers were: "Be lamps unto yourselves as all of you must work out your own liberation."

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What was the sangha founded by the Buddha?
cards.back: Soon there grew a body of disciples of the Buddha and he founded a sangha, an organisation of monks who too became teachers of dhamma.
cards.quote: Soon there grew a body of disciples of the Buddha and he founded a sangha, an organisation of monks who too became teachers of dhamma.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What were the monks of the Buddha's sangha, who lived on alms, known as?
cards.back: Soon there grew a body of disciples of the Buddha and he founded a sangha, an organisation of monks who too became teachers of dhamma. These monks lived simply, possessing only the essential requisites for survival, such as a bowl to receive food once a day from the laity. As they lived on alms, they were known as bhikkhus.
cards.quote: Soon there grew a body of disciples of the Buddha and he founded a sangha, an organisation of monks who too became teachers of dhamma. These monks lived simply, possessing only the essential requisites for survival, such as a bowl to receive food once a day from the laity. As they lived on alms, they were known as bhikkhus.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Through whose mediation were women admitted into the sangha?
cards.back: Initially, only men were allowed into the sangha, but later women also came to be admitted. According to Buddhist texts, this was made possible through the mediation of Ananda, one of the Buddha's dearest disciples, who persuaded him to allow women into the sangha.
cards.quote: Initially, only men were allowed into the sangha, but later women also came to be admitted. According to Buddhist texts, this was made possible through the mediation of Ananda, one of the Buddha's dearest disciples, who persuaded him to allow women into the sangha.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The Buddha's foster mother, ____ was the first woman to be ordained as a bhikkhuni.
cards.back: The Buddha's foster mother, Mahapajapati Gotami was the first woman to be ordained as a bhikkhuni.
cards.quote: The Buddha's foster mother, Mahapajapati Gotami was the first woman to be ordained as a bhikkhuni.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Many women who entered the sangha became teachers of dhamma and went on to become ____, or respected women who had attained liberation.
cards.back: Many women who entered the sangha became teachers of dhamma and went on to become theris, or respected women who had attained liberation.
cards.quote: Many women who entered the sangha became teachers of dhamma and went on to become theris, or respected women who had attained liberation.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: From which social groups did the Buddha's followers come?
cards.back: The Buddha's followers came from many social groups. They included kings, wealthy men and gahapatis, and also humbler folk: workers, slaves and craftspeople.
cards.quote: The Buddha's followers came from many social groups. They included kings, wealthy men and gahapatis, and also humbler folk: workers, slaves and craftspeople.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Once within the sangha, all were regarded as ____, having shed their earlier social identities on becoming bhikkhus and bhikkhunis.
cards.back: Once within the sangha, all were regarded as equal, having shed their earlier social identities on becoming bhikkhus and bhikkhunis.
cards.quote: Once within the sangha, all were regarded as equal, having shed their earlier social identities on becoming bhikkhus and bhikkhunis.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: How were decisions taken within the sangha?
cards.back: The internal functioning of the sangha was based on the traditions of ganas and sanghas, where consensus was arrived at through discussions. If that failed, decisions were taken by a vote on the subject.
cards.quote: The internal functioning of the sangha was based on the traditions of ganas and sanghas, where consensus was arrived at through discussions. If that failed, decisions were taken by a vote on the subject.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What is the Therigatha?
cards.back: This unique Buddhist text, part of the Sutta Pitaka, is a collection of verses composed by bhikkhunis.
cards.quote: This unique Buddhist text, part of the Sutta Pitaka, is a collection of verses composed by bhikkhunis.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What do metta and karuna mean in Buddhist teachings?
cards.back: The importance attached to conduct and values rather than claims of superiority based on birth, the emphasis placed on metta (fellow feeling) and karuna (compassion), especially for those who were younger and weaker than oneself, were ideas that drew men and women to Buddhist teachings.
cards.quote: The importance attached to conduct and values rather than claims of superiority based on birth, the emphasis placed on metta (fellow feeling) and karuna (compassion), especially for those who were younger and weaker than oneself, were ideas that drew men and women to Buddhist teachings.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why did Buddhism grow rapidly during and after the Buddha's lifetime?
cards.back: Buddhism grew rapidly both during the lifetime of the Buddha and after his death, as it appealed to many people dissatisfied with existing religious practices and confused by the rapid social changes taking place around them.
cards.quote: Buddhism grew rapidly both during the lifetime of the Buddha and after his death, as it appealed to many people dissatisfied with existing religious practices and confused by the rapid social changes taking place around them.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What were chaityas?
cards.back: From earliest times, people tended to regard certain places as sacred. These included sites with special trees or unique rocks, or sites of awe-inspiring natural beauty. These sites, with small shrines attached to them, were sometimes described as chaityas.
cards.quote: From earliest times, people tended to regard certain places as sacred. These included sites with special trees or unique rocks, or sites of awe-inspiring natural beauty. These sites, with small shrines attached to them, were sometimes described as chaityas.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Places associated with the Buddha's life: birth, enlightenment, first sermon, nibbana.
cards.back:
where he was born (Lumbini)
where he attained enlightenment (Bodh Gaya)
where he gave his first sermon (Sarnath)
where he attained nibbana (Kusinagara)
cards.quote: where he was born (Lumbini), where he attained enlightenment (Bodh Gaya), where he gave his first sermon (Sarnath) and where he attained nibbana (Kusinagara).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What did Asoka erect at Lumbini about 200 years after the Buddha?
cards.back: We know that about 200 years after the time of the Buddha, Asoka erected a pillar at Lumbini to mark the fact that he had visited the place.
cards.quote: We know that about 200 years after the time of the Buddha, Asoka erected a pillar at Lumbini to mark the fact that he had visited the place.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Define the stupa: what does the Sanskrit word mean, and how did it originate?
cards.back: The stupa (a Sanskrit word meaning a heap) originated as a simple semi-circular mound of earth, later called anda.
cards.quote: The stupa (a Sanskrit word meaning a heap) originated as a simple semi-circular mound of earth, later called anda.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Why was the entire stupa venerated as an emblem of the Buddha and Buddhism?
cards.back: The tradition of erecting stupas may have been pre-Buddhist, but they came to be associated with Buddhism. Since they contained relics regarded as sacred, the entire stupa came to be venerated as an emblem of both the Buddha and Buddhism.
cards.quote: The tradition of erecting stupas may have been pre-Buddhist, but they came to be associated with Buddhism. Since they contained relics regarded as sacred, the entire stupa came to be venerated as an emblem of both the Buddha and Buddhism.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What does the Ashokavadana say Asoka did with the Buddha's relics?
cards.back: According to a Buddhist text known as the Ashokavadana, Asoka distributed portions of the Buddha's relics to every important town and ordered the construction of stupas over them.
cards.quote: According to a Buddhist text known as the Ashokavadana, Asoka distributed portions of the Buddha's relics to every important town and ordered the construction of stupas over them.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: By when had stupas at Bharhut, Sanchi and Sarnath been built?
cards.back: By the second century BCE a number of stupas, including those at Bharhut, Sanchi and Sarnath (Map 1), had been built.
cards.quote: By the second century BCE a number of stupas, including those at Bharhut, Sanchi and Sarnath (Map 1), had been built.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What do inscriptions on the railings and pillars of stupas record?
cards.back: Inscriptions found on the railings and pillars of stupas record donations made for building and decorating them.
cards.quote: Inscriptions found on the railings and pillars of stupas record donations made for building and decorating them.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which guild does NCERT name as having financed part of one of the gateways at Sanchi?
cards.back:
The ivory workers
others were made by guilds, such as that of the ivory workers who financed part of one of the gateways at Sanchi.
cards.quote: others were made by guilds, such as that of the ivory workers who financed part of one of the gateways at Sanchi.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: The stupa (a Sanskrit word meaning a heap) originated as a simple semi-circular mound of earth, later called ____.
cards.back: The stupa (a Sanskrit word meaning a heap) originated as a simple semi-circular mound of earth, later called anda.
cards.quote: The stupa (a Sanskrit word meaning a heap) originated as a simple semi-circular mound of earth, later called anda.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Above the anda was the ____, a balconylike structure that represented the abode of the gods.
cards.back: Above the anda was the harmika, a balconylike structure that represented the abode of the gods.
cards.quote: Above the anda was the harmika, a balconylike structure that represented the abode of the gods.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Arising from the harmika was a mast called the ____, often surmounted by a ____ or umbrella.
cards.back: Arising from the harmika was a mast called the yashti, often surmounted by a chhatri or umbrella.
cards.quote: Arising from the harmika was a mast called the yashti, often surmounted by a chhatri or umbrella.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What was richly carved in the early stupas at Sanchi and Bharhut?
cards.back: The early stupas at Sanchi and Bharhut were plain except for the stone railings, which resembled a bamboo or wooden fence, and the gateways, which were richly carved and installed at the four cardinal points.
cards.quote: The early stupas at Sanchi and Bharhut were plain except for the stone railings, which resembled a bamboo or wooden fence, and the gateways, which were richly carved and installed at the four cardinal points.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In which direction did worshippers walk around the mound of the early stupas at Sanchi and Bharhut, keeping it on their right?
cards.back:
Clockwise
walked around the mound in a clockwise direction keeping the mound on the right
cards.quote: walked around the mound in a clockwise direction keeping the mound on the right

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Where were stupa mounds elaborately carved with niches and sculptures?
cards.back: Later, the mound of the stupas came to be elaborately carved with niches and sculptures as at Amaravati, and Shahji-ki-Dheri in Peshawar (Pakistan).
cards.quote: Later, the mound of the stupas came to be elaborately carved with niches and sculptures as at Amaravati, and Shahji-ki-Dheri in Peshawar (Pakistan).

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: In ____, a local raja who wanted to build a temple stumbled upon the ruins of the stupa at Amaravati.
cards.back: In 1796, a local raja who wanted to build a temple stumbled upon the ruins of the stupa at Amaravati.
cards.quote: In 1796, a local raja who wanted to build a temple stumbled upon the ruins of the stupa at Amaravati.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 8. "Discovering" Stupas: The Fate of Amaravati and Sanchi

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: Which British official visited Amaravati and made drawings, but never published his reports?
cards.back: Some years later, a British official named Colin Mackenzie (see also Chapter 7) visited the site. Although he found several pieces of sculpture and made detailed drawings of them, these reports were never published.
cards.quote: Some years later, a British official named Colin Mackenzie (see also Chapter 7) visited the site. Although he found several pieces of sculpture and made detailed drawings of them, these reports were never published.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I
source.section: 8. "Discovering" Stupas: The Fate of Amaravati and Sanchi

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part I
cards.front: What were the Elliot marbles?
cards.back: In 1854, Walter Elliot, the commissioner of Guntur (Andhra Pradesh), visited Amaravati and collected several sculpture panels and took them away to Madras. (These came to be called the Elliot marbles after him.)

beginning with a question
following this up with a description based on Sanskritic traditions
concluding with a comparison with other cultures

cards.front: What is the origin of the term “Hindu”?

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did the Turks call the people east of the Indus, their land and their language?

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was Ibn Battuta’s book of travels called, and what did it describe?

cards.front: When did Ibn Battuta set off for India, and where had he travelled before?

cards.front: Why did Ibn Battuta set off for Delhi?
cards.back: He had heard about Muhammad bin Tughlaq, the Sultan of Delhi, and lured by his reputation as a generous patron of arts and letters, set off for Delhi, passing through Multan and Uch.
cards.quote: He had heard about Muhammad bin Tughlaq, the Sultan of Delhi, and lured by his reputation as a generous patron of arts and letters, set off for Delhi, passing through Multan and Uch.

cards.back: The Sultan was impressed by his scholarship, and appointed him the qazi or judge of Delhi.
cards.quote: The Sultan was impressed by his scholarship, and appointed him the qazi or judge of Delhi.

cards.quote: Once the misunderstanding between him and the Sultan was cleared, he was restored to imperial service, and was ordered in 1342 to proceed to China as the Sultan’s envoy to the Mongol ruler.

cards.back: From Malabar he went to the Maldives, where he stayed for eighteen months as the qazi, but eventually decided to proceed to Sri Lanka.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the three “barriers” to understanding identified by Al-Biruni.
cards.back:
The first amongst these was language.
The second barrier he identified was the difference in religious beliefs and practices.
The self-absorption and consequent insularity of the local population according to him, constituted the third barrier.
cards.quote: The first amongst these was language. According to him, Sanskrit was so different from Arabic and Persian that ideas and concepts could not be easily translated from one language into another. The second barrier he identified was the difference in religious beliefs and practices. The self-absorption and consequent insularity of the local population according to him, constituted the third barrier.

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: On whose works did Al-Biruni depend almost exclusively?
cards.back: Al-Biruni depended almost exclusively on the works of Brahmanas, often citing passages from the Vedas, the Puranas, the Bhagavad Gita, the works of Patanjali, the Manusmriti, etc., to provide an understanding of Indian society.
cards.quote: Al-Biruni depended almost exclusively on the works of Brahmanas, often citing passages from the Vedas, the Puranas, the Bhagavad Gita, the works of Patanjali, the Manusmriti, etc., to provide an understanding of Indian society.

peasants and artisans

cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did most bazaars have, and what spaces were marked in some?
cards.back: Most bazaars had a mosque and a temple, and in some of them at least, spaces were marked for public performances by dancers, musicians and singers.
cards.quote: Most bazaars had a mosque and a temple, and in some of them at least, spaces were marked for public performances by dancers, musicians and singers.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Ibn Battuta and the Excitement of the Unfamiliar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How have historians used Ibn Battuta’s account to explain the wealth of towns?
cards.back: While Ibn Battuta was not particularly concerned with explaining the prosperity of towns, historians have used his account to suggest that towns derived a significant portion of their wealth through the appropriation of surplus from villages.
cards.quote: While Ibn Battuta was not particularly concerned with explaining the prosperity of towns, historians have used his account to suggest that towns derived a significant portion of their wealth through the appropriation of surplus from villages.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Ibn Battuta and the Excitement of the Unfamiliar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why did Ibn Battuta find Indian agriculture very productive?
cards.back: Ibn Battuta found Indian agriculture very productive because of the fertility of the soil, which allowed farmers to cultivate two crops a year.
cards.quote: Ibn Battuta found Indian agriculture very productive because of the fertility of the soil, which allowed farmers to cultivate two crops a year.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Ibn Battuta and the Excitement of the Unfamiliar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Ibn Battuta note about the subcontinent’s place in trade?
cards.back: He also noted that the subcontinent was well integrated with inter-Asian networks of trade and commerce, with Indian manufactures being in great demand in both West Asia and Southeast Asia, fetching huge profits for artisans and merchants.
cards.quote: He also noted that the subcontinent was well integrated with inter-Asian networks of trade and commerce, with Indian manufactures being in great demand in both West Asia and Southeast Asia, fetching huge profits for artisans and merchants.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Ibn Battuta and the Excitement of the Unfamiliar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which Indian textiles were in great demand?
cards.back: Indian textiles, particularly cotton cloth, fine muslins, silks, brocade and satin, were in great demand.
cards.quote: Indian textiles, particularly cotton cloth, fine muslins, silks, brocade and satin, were in great demand.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Ibn Battuta and the Excitement of the Unfamiliar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was the market place for male and female singers in Daulatabad called?
cards.back: In Daulatabad there is a market place for male and female singers, which is known as Tarababad.
cards.quote: In Daulatabad there is a market place for male and female singers, which is known as Tarababad.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Ibn Battuta and the Excitement of the Unfamiliar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did the state encourage merchants, according to NCERT?
cards.back: The state evidently took special measures to encourage merchants. Almost all trade routes were well supplied with inns and guest houses.
cards.quote: The state evidently took special measures to encourage merchants. Almost all trade routes were well supplied with inns and guest houses.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Ibn Battuta and the Excitement of the Unfamiliar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What amazed Ibn Battuta about the postal system?
cards.back: Ibn Battuta was also amazed by the efficiency of the postal system which allowed merchants to not only send information and remit credit across long distances, but also to dispatch goods required at short notice.
cards.quote: Ibn Battuta was also amazed by the efficiency of the postal system which allowed merchants to not only send information and remit credit across long distances, but also to dispatch goods required at short notice.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Ibn Battuta and the Excitement of the Unfamiliar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How fast did spies’ news reach the Sultan through the postal system?
cards.back: The postal system was so efficient that while it took fifty days to reach Delhi from Sind, the news reports of spies would reach the Sultan through the postal system in just five days.
cards.quote: The postal system was so efficient that while it took fifty days to reach Delhi from Sind, the news reports of spies would reach the Sultan through the postal system in just five days.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Ibn Battuta and the Excitement of the Unfamiliar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Types of postal system in India, as described by Ibn Battuta.
cards.back: In India the postal system is of two kinds. The horse-post, called uluq, is run by royal horses stationed at a distance of every four miles. The foot-post has three stations per mile; it is called dawa, that is one-third of a mile
cards.quote: In India the postal system is of two kinds. The horse-post, called uluq, is run by royal horses stationed at a distance of every four miles. The foot-post has three stations per mile; it is called dawa, that is one-third of a mile

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Ibn Battuta and the Excitement of the Unfamiliar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did Abdur Razzaq describe the people of Calicut?
cards.back: On the one hand, he did not appreciate what he saw in the port of Calicut (present-day Kozhikode) in Kerala, which was populated by “a people the likes of whom I had never imagined”, describing them as “a strange nation”.
cards.quote: On the one hand, he did not appreciate what he saw in the port of Calicut (present-day Kozhikode) in Kerala, which was populated by “a people the likes of whom I had never imagined”, describing them as “a strange nation”.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Ibn Battuta and the Excitement of the Unfamiliar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which Dutch traveller visited the subcontinent in the early seventeenth century and was shocked by its poverty?
cards.back: Pelsaert, a Dutch traveller, visited the subcontinent during the early decades of the seventeenth century. Like Bernier, he was shocked to see the widespread poverty
cards.quote: Pelsaert, a Dutch traveller, visited the subcontinent during the early decades of the seventeenth century. Like Bernier, he was shocked to see the widespread poverty

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
source.section: Ibn Battuta and the Excitement of the Unfamiliar

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Ibn Battuta vs Bernier: what each chose to describe.
cards.back: If Ibn Battuta chose to describe everything that impressed and excited him because of its novelty, François Bernier belonged to a different intellectual tradition. He was far more preoccupied with comparing and contrasting what he saw in India with the situation in Europe in general and France in particular, focusing on situations which he considered depressing.
cards.quote: If Ibn Battuta chose to describe everything that impressed and excited him because of its novelty, François Bernier belonged to a different intellectual tradition. He was far more preoccupied with comparing and contrasting what he saw in India with the situation in Europe in general and France in particular, focusing on situations which he considered depressing.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What seems to have been Bernier’s idea in focusing on depressing situations?
cards.back: His idea seems to have been to influence policy-makers and the intelligentsia to ensure that they made what he considered to be the “right” decisions.
cards.quote: His idea seems to have been to influence policy-makers and the intelligentsia to ensure that they made what he considered to be the “right” decisions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: His representation of India works on the model of ____, where India is presented as the inverse of Europe.
cards.back: His representation of India works on the model of binary opposition, where India is presented as the inverse of Europe.
cards.quote: His representation of India works on the model of binary opposition, where India is presented as the inverse of Europe.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did Bernier order the perceived differences between India and Europe?
cards.back: He also ordered the perceived differences hierarchically, so that India appeared to be inferior to the Western world.
cards.quote: He also ordered the perceived differences hierarchically, so that India appeared to be inferior to the Western world.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: According to Bernier, what was a fundamental difference between Mughal India and Europe?
cards.back: According to Bernier, one of the fundamental differences between Mughal India and Europe was the lack of private property in land in the former.
cards.quote: According to Bernier, one of the fundamental differences between Mughal India and Europe was the lack of private property in land in the former.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Bernier believe about private property and crown ownership of land?
cards.back: He was a firm believer in the virtues of private property, and saw crown ownership of land as being harmful for both the state and its people.
cards.quote: He was a firm believer in the virtues of private property, and saw crown ownership of land as being harmful for both the state and its people.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Bernier think about ownership of land in the Mughal Empire?
cards.back: He thought that in the Mughal Empire the emperor owned all the land and distributed it among his nobles, and that this had disastrous consequences for the economy and society.
cards.quote: He thought that in the Mughal Empire the emperor owned all the land and distributed it among his nobles, and that this had disastrous consequences for the economy and society.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Bernier argue about landholders under crown ownership of land?
cards.back: Owing to crown ownership of land, argued Bernier, landholders could not pass on their land to their children.
cards.quote: Owing to crown ownership of land, argued Bernier, landholders could not pass on their land to their children.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Bernier say the absence of private property had led to?
cards.back: It had led to the uniform ruination of agriculture, excessive oppression of the peasantry and a continuous decline in the living standards of all sections of society, except the ruling aristocracy.
cards.quote: It had led to the uniform ruination of agriculture, excessive oppression of the peasantry and a continuous decline in the living standards of all sections of society, except the ruling aristocracy.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Bernier assert about the middle groups in Indian society?
cards.back: Bernier confidently asserted: “There is no middle state in India.”
cards.quote: Bernier confidently asserted: “There is no middle state in India.”

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did Bernier describe Indian society?
cards.back: Bernier described Indian society as consisting of undifferentiated masses of impoverished people, subjugated by a small minority of a very rich and powerful ruling class.
cards.quote: Bernier described Indian society as consisting of undifferentiated masses of impoverished people, subjugated by a small minority of a very rich and powerful ruling class.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What do Mughal official documents suggest about the state as sole owner of land?
cards.back: Curiously, none of the Mughal official documents suggest that the state was the sole owner of land.
cards.quote: Curiously, none of the Mughal official documents suggest that the state was the sole owner of land.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How did Abu’l Fazl describe land revenue?
cards.back: Abu’l Fazl, the sixteenth-century official chronicler of Akbar’s reign, describes the land revenue as “remunerations of sovereignty”, a claim made by the ruler on his subjects for the protection he provided rather than as rent on land that he owned.
cards.quote: Abu’l Fazl, the sixteenth-century official chronicler of Akbar’s reign, describes the land revenue as “remunerations of sovereignty”, a claim made by the ruler on his subjects for the protection he provided rather than as rent on land that he owned.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What was land revenue actually, according to NCERT?
cards.back: However, this was actually not a rent or even a land tax, but a tax on the crop
cards.quote: However, this was actually not a rent or even a land tax, but a tax on the crop

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What is “oriental despotism” (the idea developed by Montesquieu)?
cards.back: The French philosopher Montesquieu, for instance, used this account to develop the idea of oriental despotism, according to which rulers in Asia (the Orient or the East) enjoyed absolute authority over their subjects, who were kept in conditions of subjugation and poverty, arguing that all land belonged to the king and that private property was non-existent.
cards.quote: The French philosopher Montesquieu, for instance, used this account to develop the idea of oriental despotism, according to which rulers in Asia (the Orient or the East) enjoyed absolute authority over their subjects, who were kept in conditions of subjugation and poverty, arguing that all land belonged to the king and that private property was non-existent.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Which concept did Karl Marx develop in the nineteenth century from Montesquieu's idea of oriental despotism?
cards.back: This idea was further developed as the concept of the Asiatic mode of production by Karl Marx in the nineteenth century.
cards.quote: This idea was further developed as the concept of the Asiatic mode of production by Karl Marx in the nineteenth century.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Marx argue about India before colonialism?
cards.back: He argued that in India (and other Asian countries), before colonialism, surplus was appropriated by the state.
cards.quote: He argued that in India (and other Asian countries), before colonialism, surplus was appropriated by the state.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: According to Karl Marx, what kind of society emerged in pre-colonial India, where the state appropriated surplus?
cards.back: This led to the emergence of a society that was composed of a large number of autonomous and (internally) egalitarian village communities.
cards.quote: This led to the emergence of a society that was composed of a large number of autonomous and (internally) egalitarian village communities.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In Marx's Asiatic mode of production, how was the system of autonomous village communities under an imperial court regarded?
cards.back: The imperial court presided over these village communities, respecting their autonomy as long as the flow of surplus was unimpeded. This was regarded as a stagnant system.
cards.quote: The imperial court presided over these village communities, respecting their autonomy as long as the flow of surplus was unimpeded. This was regarded as a stagnant system.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How was rural society in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries characterised?
cards.back: In fact, during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, rural society was characterised by considerable social and economic differentiation.
cards.quote: In fact, during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, rural society was characterised by considerable social and economic differentiation.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In sixteenth-seventeenth century rural society, which group at one end of the spectrum enjoyed superior rights in land?
cards.back: At one end of the spectrum were the big zamindars, who enjoyed superior rights in land
cards.quote: At one end of the spectrum were the big zamindars, who enjoyed superior rights in land

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who stood between the big zamindars and the landless labourers in rural society?
cards.back: In between was the big peasant, who used hired labour and engaged in commodity production, and the smaller peasant who could barely produce for his subsistence.
cards.quote: In between was the big peasant, who used hired labour and engaged in commodity production, and the smaller peasant who could barely produce for his subsistence.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Why did Bernier feel artisans had no incentive to improve the quality of their manufactures?
cards.back: For instance, he felt that artisans had no incentive to improve the quality of their manufactures, since profits were appropriated by the state.
cards.quote: For instance, he felt that artisans had no incentive to improve the quality of their manufactures, since profits were appropriated by the state.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Bernier concede about the world’s precious metals?
cards.back: At the same time, he conceded that vast quantities of the world’s precious metals flowed into India, as manufactures were exported in exchange for gold and silver.
cards.quote: At the same time, he conceded that vast quantities of the world’s precious metals flowed into India, as manufactures were exported in exchange for gold and silver.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What community did Bernier notice, hinting at a more complex social reality?
cards.back: He also noticed the existence of a prosperous merchant community, engaged in long-distance exchange.
cards.quote: He also noticed the existence of a prosperous merchant community, engaged in long-distance exchange.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What were the imperial karkhanas, whose working Bernier describes in detail?
cards.back: Bernier is perhaps the only historian who provides a detailed account of the working of the imperial karkhanas or workshops
cards.quote: Bernier is perhaps the only historian who provides a detailed account of the working of the imperial karkhanas or workshops

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What proportion of the population lived in towns in the seventeenth century?
cards.back: In fact, during the seventeenth century about 15 per cent of the population lived in towns. This was, on average, higher than the proportion of urban population in Western Europe in the same period.
cards.quote: In fact, during the seventeenth century about 15 per cent of the population lived in towns. This was, on average, higher than the proportion of urban population in Western Europe in the same period.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Bernier mean by “camp towns”?
cards.back: In spite of this Bernier described Mughal cities as “camp towns”, by which he meant towns that owed their existence, and depended for their survival, on the imperial camp.
cards.quote: In spite of this Bernier described Mughal cities as “camp towns”, by which he meant towns that owed their existence, and depended for their survival, on the imperial camp.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: When did Bernier believe camp towns came into existence and declined?
cards.back: He believed that these came into existence when the imperial court moved in and rapidly declined when it moved out.
cards.quote: He believed that these came into existence when the imperial court moved in and rapidly declined when it moved out.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Kinds of towns that existed, against Bernier’s oversimplified picture.
cards.back:
manufacturing towns
trading towns
port-towns
sacred centres
pilgrimage towns
cards.quote: There were all kinds of towns: manufacturing towns, trading towns, port-towns, sacred centres, pilgrimage towns, etc.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In western India, what were merchants' caste-cum-occupational bodies called, and what was each body's chief called?
cards.back: Merchants often had strong community or kin ties, and were organised into their own caste-cum-occupational bodies. In western India these groups were called mahajans, and their chief, the sheth.
cards.quote: Merchants often had strong community or kin ties, and were organised into their own caste-cum-occupational bodies. In western India these groups were called mahajans, and their chief, the sheth.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: In urban centres such as Ahmedabad the mahajans were collectively represented by the chief of the merchant community who was called the ____.
cards.back: In urban centres such as Ahmedabad the mahajans were collectively represented by the chief of the merchant community who was called the nagarsheth.
cards.quote: In urban centres such as Ahmedabad the mahajans were collectively represented by the chief of the merchant community who was called the nagarsheth.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Name the professional classes among urban groups, with their titles.
cards.back:
physicians (hakim or vaid)
teachers (pundit or mulla)
lawyers (wakil)
painters
architects
musicians
calligraphers
cards.quote: Other urban groups included professional classes such as physicians (hakim or vaid), teachers (pundit or mulla), lawyers (wakil), painters, architects, musicians, calligraphers, etc.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Who were the travellers who left written accounts, and what interested them?
cards.back: Travellers who left written accounts were generally men who were interested in and sometimes intrigued by the condition of women in the subcontinent.
cards.quote: Travellers who left written accounts were generally men who were interested in and sometimes intrigued by the condition of women in the subcontinent.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How were slaves treated in markets, according to the travellers’ accounts?
cards.back: For instance, slaves were openly sold in markets, like any other commodity, and were regularly exchanged as gifts.
cards.quote: For instance, slaves were openly sold in markets, like any other commodity, and were regularly exchanged as gifts.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Ibn Battuta purchase in Sind as gifts for Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq?
cards.back: When Ibn Battuta reached Sind he purchased “horses, camels and slaves” as gifts for Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
cards.quote: When Ibn Battuta reached Sind he purchased “horses, camels and slaves” as gifts for Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: For what purpose did the Sultan employ female slaves, besides music and dance?
cards.back: Female slaves were also employed by the Sultan to keep a watch on his nobles.
cards.quote: Female slaves were also employed by the Sultan to keep a watch on his nobles.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: For what were slaves generally used, according to Ibn Battuta?
cards.back: Slaves were generally used for domestic labour, and Ibn Battuta found their services particularly indispensable for carrying women and men on palanquins or dola.
cards.quote: Slaves were generally used for domestic labour, and Ibn Battuta found their services particularly indispensable for carrying women and men on palanquins or dola.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How was the price of female slaves for domestic labour, according to Ibn Battuta?
cards.back: The price of slaves, particularly female slaves required for domestic labour, was very low, and most families who could afford to do so kept at least one or two of them.
cards.quote: The price of slaves, particularly female slaves required for domestic labour, was very low, and most families who could afford to do so kept at least one or two of them.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: How were most female slaves obtained?
cards.back: Most female slaves were captured in raids and expeditions.
cards.quote: Most female slaves were captured in raids and expeditions.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did European travellers highlight as a crucial marker of difference between Western and Eastern societies?
cards.back: Contemporary European travellers and writers often highlighted the treatment of women as a crucial marker of difference between Western and Eastern societies.
cards.quote: Contemporary European travellers and writers often highlighted the treatment of women as a crucial marker of difference between Western and Eastern societies.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: Not surprisingly, Bernier chose the practice of ____ for detailed description.
cards.back: Not surprisingly, Bernier chose the practice of sati for detailed description.
cards.quote: Not surprisingly, Bernier chose the practice of sati for detailed description.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did Bernier note about women who died in sati?
cards.back: He noted that while some women seemed to embrace death cheerfully, others were forced to die.
cards.quote: He noted that while some women seemed to embrace death cheerfully, others were forced to die.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What role did women’s labour play, apart from the practice of sati?
cards.back: Their labour was crucial in both agricultural and non-agricultural production.
cards.quote: Their labour was crucial in both agricultural and non-agricultural production.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What did women from merchant families do?
cards.back: Women from merchant families participated in commercial activities, sometimes even taking mercantile disputes to the court of law.
cards.quote: Women from merchant families participated in commercial activities, sometimes even taking mercantile disputes to the court of law.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: What shaped the observations of the travellers?
cards.back: However, their observations were often shaped by the contexts from which they came.
cards.quote: However, their observations were often shaped by the contexts from which they came.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II

cards.subject: history
cards.unit: Themes in Indian History Part II
cards.front: From which country did the traveller Marco Polo come?
cards.back: Marco Polo (from Italy)
cards.quote: Marco Polo (from Italy)

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part II
